metadata.title: Several new product identities in relation to two-variable Rogers-Ramanujan type sums and mock theta functions

extraction_notes.note: The layout figure (fig:layout) summarizing logical implications between results is omitted in this source; its arrows could not be used for edges, so dependencies were taken from the text only.

Table tbl:spaces (memberships of products in T- and S-spaces) is cited by many proofs but is a float, not a node; its \cref refs were attached as uses edges from the claim that introduces it (S-type symmetry of double products).

Numbered displays that the text names as cited results were retyped from equation to theorem (origin external): Jacobi's triple, quintuple, septuple, sextuple product identities, the Rogers-Ramanujan identities, Watson's mock theta identities (5.7) and Slater's identities (5.13).
Cross-product identity (5.9), only 'suggested by numerical generation' and called more difficult, is a conjecture; its companion (5.10), said to be provable easily, is a claim with rigor semi_formal.

The proof of Prop. 3.12 has two parser 'author labels' (iii) and (i) that are really part of \cref{lem:basic}.(iii) and \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}.(i) mid-sentence; no step can start there without splitting sentences, so the finishing step's two errors on that proof are left as false positives.

Several 'Proof that A <=> B' environments are equivalences; each proof was given a single proves edge to the result it establishes in the paper's logic (Thm 1.3 from Thm 5.2; Thm 1.4 from Thm 5.5; Prop 1.2 from the Rogers-Ramanujan identities), with no reverse edge.

nodes.name: q-Pochhammer and modified theta notation
nodes.statement: Denote $q := e^{2\pi i \tau}$, $x := e^{2\pi i z}$, $(x; q) := \prod_{n = 0}^\infty \left(1 - q^n x\right)$, and $\left\langle x; q \right\rangle := (x; q)(q/x; q)$ (the standard notations have a subscript of $\infty$, which we drop for brevity; this will be helpful in identities like \cref{eq:nonuple}).
nodes.statement_short: Sets $q=e^{2\pi i\tau}$, $x=e^{2\pi i z}$, the infinite product $(x;q)$ and the double product $\langle x;q\rangle=(x;q)(q/x;q)$.

nodes.name: Jacobi's triple product identity
nodes.statement: (q; q)\left\langle x; q \right\rangle = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^n q^{\binom{n}{2}} x^n.
nodes.statement_short: $(q;q)\langle x;q\rangle=\sum_n(-1)^nq^{\binom n2}x^n$.
nodes.label: eq:triple

nodes.name: Quasiperiodic function space T_D(f) (introduction)
nodes.statement: More generally, if $D \subset \mathbb{C}$ is open, connected and closed under $\mathbb{Z}$-translation, and $f \in \textnormal{Hol}(\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}) \setminus \{0\}$, then the space \[ \mathcal{T}_D(f) := \left\{F \in \textnormal{Hol}(D/\mathbb{Z})\ :\ F(z) = f(z) F(z+\tau)\ \text{ when } z, z + \tau \in D\right\} \] can be shown to be finite-dimensional over $\mathbb{C}$ for various choices of $D$ and $f$.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal T_D(f)$: 1-periodic holomorphic $F$ on $D$ with $F(z)=f(z)F(z+\tau)$; finite-dimensional for many $D,f$.

nodes.name: Canonical theta basis [alpha x^d; k]
nodes.statement: In particular, given a positive integer $d$ and a nonzero $\alpha \in \mathbb{C}$, the space $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$ has a canonical basis consisting of the theta functions \[ \vect{\alpha x^d}{k} = \vect{\alpha x^d}{k}(z) := \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2} + kn} x^{dn+k}, \] where $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ varies in any complete residue system modulo $d$ (we introduce this notation because it will admit a natural generalization to other functions of the form $\vect{f}{k}$).
nodes.statement_short: The theta series $[\alpha x^d;k]=\sum_n\alpha^nq^{d\binom n2+kn}x^{dn+k}$, $k$ mod $d$, form a canonical basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(\alpha x^d)$.

nodes.name: Quintuple product identity
nodes.statement: (q; q)\left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle &= \vect{qx^3}{0} - \vect{qx^3}{1} ,
nodes.statement_short: Quintuple product $(q;q)\langle x;q\rangle\langle qx^2;q^2\rangle=[qx^3;0]-[qx^3;1]$.
nodes.label: eq:quintuple

nodes.name: Septuple product identity
nodes.statement: (q; q) \left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle x^2; q^2 \right\rangle &= - \frac{\vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2}}{\left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle} + \frac{\vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3}}{\left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle}.
nodes.statement_short: Septuple product expanded in the paired canonical basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(-qx^5)$ with Rogers-Ramanujan product coefficients.
nodes.label: eq:septuple

nodes.name: Lower half-plane H^- (introduction)
nodes.statement: We will find that the fifth-order mock theta functions are intimately related to the canonical basis vectors of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(qx^2 - x\right)$ (where ${\mathbb{H}}^- := \{\textnormal{Im}\ z < 0\}$), while the third-order ones are similarly connected to the space $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(qx^2 - q^{-1}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduces $\mathbb H^-$ while announcing the link of fifth- and third-order mock theta functions with $\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^-}(qx^2-x)$ and $\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^-}(qx^2-q^{-1})$.

nodes.name: First nonuple product identity
nodes.statement: As an identity of functions in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(q^2x^7\right)$, \begin{equation} \begin{split} (q;q) \left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle^2 \left\langle x^2; q^2 \right\rangle &= - \frac{\vect{q^2x^7}{1} + \vect{q^2x^7}{2}}{\left\langle q^2 ; q^7 \right\rangle^2 \left\langle q; q^7\right\rangle} + \frac{\vect{q^2x^7}{0} + \vect{q^2x^7}{3}}{\left\langle q ; q^7 \right\rangle^2 \left\langle q^3; q^7\right\rangle} \\[4pt] & + q\frac{\vect{q^2x^7}{-1} + \vect{q^2x^7}{4}}{\left\langle q^3 ; q^7 \right\rangle^2 \left\langle q^2; q^7\right\rangle} - q\frac{2\vect{q^2x^7}{5}}{\left\langle q; q^7\right\rangle \left\langle q^2; q^7 \right\rangle \left\langle q^3; q^7 \right\rangle }. \end{split} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Nonuple product expanded in the canonical basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(q^2x^7)$ with level-7 double-product coefficients.
nodes.label: prop:nonuple

nodes.name: First nonuple product identity (display)
nodes.statement: \begin{split} (q;q) \left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle^2 \left\langle x^2; q^2 \right\rangle &= - \frac{\vect{q^2x^7}{1} + \vect{q^2x^7}{2}}{\left\langle q^2 ; q^7 \right\rangle^2 \left\langle q; q^7\right\rangle} + \frac{\vect{q^2x^7}{0} + \vect{q^2x^7}{3}}{\left\langle q ; q^7 \right\rangle^2 \left\langle q^3; q^7\right\rangle} \\[4pt] & + q\frac{\vect{q^2x^7}{-1} + \vect{q^2x^7}{4}}{\left\langle q^3 ; q^7 \right\rangle^2 \left\langle q^2; q^7\right\rangle} - q\frac{2\vect{q^2x^7}{5}}{\left\langle q; q^7\right\rangle \left\langle q^2; q^7 \right\rangle \left\langle q^3; q^7 \right\rangle }. \end{split}
nodes.label: eq:nonuple

nodes.name: Lower half-plane H^- and the space T_{H^-}(qx^2-x)
nodes.statement: Passing to spaces such as $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(qx^2-x\right)$ (where ${\mathbb{H}}^- := \{\textnormal{Im}\ z < 0\}$), which is two-dimensional and corresponds to a meromorphic line bundle, we begin to encounter Rogers--Ramanujan type sums.

nodes.name: Finite q-Pochhammer symbol (x;q)_n
nodes.statement: In fact, the two renowned one-variable Rogers--Ramanujan identities \cite[p.~290]{hardy1979introduction}, \begin{equation} \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_n} = \frac{1}{\left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle} \qquad\quad \text{ and }\qquad\quad \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{(q; q)_n} = \frac{1}{\left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle}, \end{equation} where $(x; q)_n := \prod_{k = 0}^{n-1} \left(1 - xq^k\right)$, are together equivalent to the following new product identity.
nodes.statement_short: Recalls the Rogers-Ramanujan identities and defines $(x;q)_n=\prod_{k<n}(1-xq^k)$.

nodes.name: Rogers-Ramanujan identities
nodes.statement: \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_n} = \frac{1}{\left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle} \qquad\quad \text{ and }\qquad\quad \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{(q; q)_n} = \frac{1}{\left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle},
nodes.statement_short: $\sum q^{n^2}/(q;q)_n=1/\langle q;q^5\rangle$ and $\sum q^{n^2+n}/(q;q)_n=1/\langle q^2;q^5\rangle$.
nodes.label: eq:rog-ram

nodes.name: Two-variable Rogers-Ramanujan product identity
nodes.statement: In $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(qx^2-x\right)$, one has \begin{equation} (q; q) \left\langle x; q \right\rangle (qx; q)\ = \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}, n \ge 0} \frac{q^{\binom{m}{2} + \binom{n+1}{2}}}{(q; q)_n} (-x)^{m+n} \ =\ \frac{\vect{qx^2 - x}{0}}{\left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle} - \frac{\vect{qx^2 - x}{1}}{\left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle}, \end{equation} where for $k \in \{0, 1\}$, $\vect{qx^2 - x}{k}$ is the unique function in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(qx^2-x\right)$ whose Fourier expansion in $z \in {\mathbb{H}}^-$ has coefficient of $x^j$ equal to $\mathbbm{1}_{j = k}$, for $j \in \{0, 1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: $(q;q)\langle x;q\rangle(qx;q)$ equals a two-variable Rogers-Ramanujan double sum and a combination of the canonical basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^-}(qx^2-x)$.
assumptions: $\vect{qx^2 - x}{k}$ is the unique function in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(qx^2-x\right)$ whose Fourier expansion in $z \in {\mathbb{H}}^-$ has coefficient of $x^j$ equal to $\mathbbm{1}_{j = k}$
nodes.label: prop:2var-rog-ram

nodes.name: Two-variable Rogers-Ramanujan identity (display)
nodes.statement: (q; q) \left\langle x; q \right\rangle (qx; q)\ = \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}, n \ge 0} \frac{q^{\binom{m}{2} + \binom{n+1}{2}}}{(q; q)_n} (-x)^{m+n} \ =\ \frac{\vect{qx^2 - x}{0}}{\left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle} - \frac{\vect{qx^2 - x}{1}}{\left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle},
nodes.label: eq:2var-rog-ram

nodes.name: Remark on poles and m-versions of Rogers-Ramanujan
nodes.statement: The functions $\vect{qx^2-x}{k}$ can be expressed as explicit series in ${\mathbb{H}}^-$ (see \cref{cor:kind2}), and can then be meromorphically continued to $\mathbb{C}$; their poles must cancel out in the right-hand side of \cref{eq:2var-rog-ram} since the left-hand side is entire. In fact, $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2 - x\right) = 1$ while $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(qx^2 - x\right) = 2$. Also, the Rogers--Ramanujan identities in \cref{eq:rog-ram} follow from the second equality in \cref{eq:2var-rog-ram} by identifying coefficients of $x^0$ and $x^1$. In fact, identifying coefficients of $x^{1-m}$ for $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ leads to the so-called $m$-versions of the Rogers--Ramanujan identities, involving $\sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2 + mn}/(q; q)_n$ (see, e.g., \cite[(3.5)]{garrett1999variants}).
nodes.statement_short: Canonical vectors of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^-}(qx^2-x)$ continue meromorphically; RR identities and their m-versions follow by comparing coefficients.

nodes.name: Septuple identity vs. Rogers-Ramanujan (main theorem)
nodes.statement: For $0 < |q| < 1$, one has \[ -\frac{\left\langle x^2; q\right\rangle}{(qx; q)} \ =\ \frac{\vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2}}{\vect{qx^2 - x}{0}} \ =\ \frac{\vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3}}{\vect{qx^2 - x}{1}}, \] as an identity of meromorphic functions of $z \in \mathbb{C}$ (where $x = e^{2\pi i z}$). The left-hand side above equals minus the ratio of the septuple product in \cref{eq:septuple} to the product in \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram}.
nodes.statement_short: The paired canonical basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(-qx^5)$ is proportional to the canonical basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^-}(qx^2-x)$, with factor $-\langle x^2;q\rangle/(qx;q)$.
nodes.label: thm:bases-proportional

nodes.name: Octuple identity vs. Rogers-Ramanujan variation
nodes.statement: For $0 < |q| < 1$, one has \[ -\frac{\left(-x^{-1}; q\right) \left\langle x; q\right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle }{(q; q^2)(qx; q)} \ =\ \frac{\vect{-qx^4}{1}}{\vect{qx^2 - q^{-1}}{0}} \ =\ \frac{\vect{-qx^4}{0} + \vect{-qx^4}{2}}{\vect{qx^2 - q^{-1}}{1}}, \] as an identity of meromorphic functions of $z \in \mathbb{C}$ (where $x = e^{2\pi i z}$). The left-hand side above equals minus the ratio of the octuple product in \cref{eq:octuple} to the product in \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram-var}. Here, $\vect{qx^2 - q^{-1}}{k} \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left( qx^2 - q^{-1}\right)$ are defined analogously to $\vect{qx^2 - x}{k}$ in \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram}.
nodes.statement_short: Canonical-basis vectors of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(-qx^4)$ are proportional to those of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^-}(qx^2-q^{-1})$.
nodes.label: thm:bases-proportional-2

nodes.name: Dedekind eta and generalized Dedekind eta functions
nodes.statement: First, denote the Dedekind eta function and the generalized Dedekind eta functions of level $N \ge 1$ (following \cite[Corollary 2]{yang2004transformation}) by \begin{equation} \eta(\tau) := e^{\pi i \tau / 12}(q; q), \qquad\qquad \textnormal E_g(\tau) := e^{N B(g/N) \pi i \tau} \left\langle q^g; q^N \right\rangle, \end{equation} where $B(t) := t^2 - t + \frac{1}{6}$, $g \in \mathbb{Z}$, and the level $N$ must be specified a priori (the generalized eta functions $\textnormal E_g(\tau)$ should not be confused with the Eisenstein series $E_{2k}(\tau)$).
nodes.statement_short: Defines $\eta(\tau)$ and the level-$N$ generalized eta functions $E_g(\tau)=e^{NB(g/N)\pi i\tau}\langle q^g;q^N\rangle$.

nodes.name: Eta and generalized eta function formulas
nodes.statement: \eta(\tau) := e^{\pi i \tau / 12}(q; q), \qquad\qquad \textnormal E_g(\tau) := e^{N B(g/N) \pi i \tau} \left\langle q^g; q^N \right\rangle,
nodes.label: eq:generalized-eta

nodes.name: Eta quotient polynomial
nodes.statement: For $\tau \in {\mathbb{H}}^+$, let $\textnormal E_g(\tau)$ denote the generalized eta functions of level $N = 7$. Then one has the polynomial factorization \[ X^3 - 2\frac{\eta(14\tau)^2}{\eta(7\tau)^2} X^2 - \frac{\eta(2\tau)\eta(7\tau)^3}{\eta(\tau)\eta(14\tau)^3} X + \frac{\eta(\tau)\eta(14\tau)}{\eta(2\tau)\eta(7\tau)} = \prod_{g = 1}^3 \left(X - \frac{\textnormal E_{g}(2\tau)}{\textnormal E_{3g}(\tau)}\right). \]
nodes.statement_short: The three level-7 quotients $E_g(2\tau)/E_{3g}(\tau)$ are the roots of a cubic whose coefficients are Dedekind eta quotients.
assumptions: let $\textnormal E_g(\tau)$ denote the generalized eta functions of level $N = 7$
nodes.label: cor:eta-poly

nodes.name: Fifth-order mock theta functions f_j and psi_j
nodes.statement: Our second corollary involves four of Ramanujan's famous fifth-order mock theta functions \cite{watson1937mock,andrews1989ramanujan}: \begin{equation} f_j(q) := \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+jn}}{(-q; q)_n}, \qquad \ \psi_j(q) := \sum_{n+j \ge 1} q^{\binom{n+1}{2}} (-q; q)_{n+j-1}, \qquad\text{for } j \in \{0, 1\}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Ramanujan's fifth-order mock theta functions $f_0,f_1,\psi_0,\psi_1$.

nodes.name: Fifth-order mock theta function series
nodes.statement: f_j(q) := \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+jn}}{(-q; q)_n}, \qquad \ \psi_j(q) := \sum_{n+j \ge 1} q^{\binom{n+1}{2}} (-q; q)_{n+j-1}, \qquad\text{for } j \in \{0, 1\}.
nodes.label: eq:mock-theta

nodes.name: Fifth-order mock theta sums
nodes.statement: For $j \in \{0, 1\}$, one has \[ (q; q)^2\left(q; q^2\right)\Big( f_j(q) + 2\psi_j(q) \Big) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{\frac{n(5n+2j+1)}{2}} (10 n + 2j + 1). \]
nodes.statement_short: $(q;q)^2(q;q^2)(f_j+2\psi_j)$ equals a weighted theta series $\sum q^{n(5n+2j+1)/2}(10n+2j+1)$.
nodes.label: cor:mock-theta-fifth

nodes.name: Remark relating corollary to main theorem and mock theta conjectures
nodes.statement: \cref{cor:mock-theta-fifth} follows from \cref{thm:bases-proportional} by taking $x \to -1$, and \cref{thm:bases-proportional-2} is similarly related to third-order mock theta functions; we also obtain individual identities for $\psi_j$ in \cref{prop:mock-theta-individual}. More difficult identities for $f_j$ and $\psi_j$ are given by Ramanujan's famous mock theta conjectures \cite{andrews1989ramanujan}, proven by Hickerson \cite{hickerson1988proof} and more recently by Folsom \cite{folsom2008short} using Maass forms.

nodes.name: Two-variable 2x2 determinant identity
nodes.statement: For $x, q \in \mathbb{C}$ with $|q| < 1$, one has \[ \det \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n(n+1)}}{(q; q)_{2n}} x^{2n} & \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{(n+1)^2}}{(q; q)_{2n+1}} x^{2n+1} \vspace{0.3cm} \\ \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n(n+1)}}{(q; q)_{2n+1}} x^{2n+1} & \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_{2n}} x^{2n} \end{pmatrix} = 1. \]
nodes.statement_short: A $2\times2$ matrix of two-variable Rogers-Ramanujan type sums has determinant 1.
nodes.label: prop:2x2-determinant

nodes.name: Question: two-variable analogue for the nonuple identity and W_3 characters
nodes.statement: As noted by Andrews, Schilling and Warnaar \cite[(5.2)]{andrews1999a2}, the Rogers--Ramanujan products $\langle q; q^5 \rangle^{-1}$ and $\langle q^2; q^5 \rangle^{-1}$ are characters of a certain $\textnormal W_2$ algebra, which they denote by $M(2, 5)_2$. We remarked that these products coincide with the $q$-coefficients of the canonical basis vectors in the septuple identity \cref{eq:septuple}, and explained this correspondence through \cref{thm:bases-proportional}. A similar phenomenon occurs for the octuple (\cref{prop:octuple}) and nonuple (\cref{prop:nonuple}) identities: \begin{center} \begin{tabular}{c|c|c|c|c} Algebra & Product identity & Rog.--Ram.\ type id. & 2-Var.\ generaliz. & Correspondence\\ \hline $M(2, 5)_2$ & Septuple, \cref{eq:septuple} & \cref{eq:rog-ram} & \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram} & \cref{thm:bases-proportional} \\ \hline $M(2, 4)_2$ & Octuple, \cref{eq:octuple} & \cref{eq:rog-ram-var}& \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram-var} & \cref{thm:bases-proportional-2} \\ \hline $M(3, 7)_3$ & Nonuple, \cref{eq:nonuple} & \cite[Theorem 1.1]{corteel2019varvec} & (Open question) & (Open question) \end{tabular} \end{center} Indeed, the $q$-coefficients in the right-hand side of the nonuple identity \cref{eq:nonuple} coincide with the 4 characters of the $\textnormal W_3$ algebra $M(3, 7)_3$ (up to factors of $\pm 1, \pm q, \pm 2q$), and \cite[Theorem 5.2]{andrews1999a2} gives $A_2$ Rogers--Ramanujan identities for 3 out of these characters (see also \cite{warnaar2006hall}); the more recent work of Corteel and Welsh also provides the fourth identity \cite[Theorem 1.1]{corteel2019varvec}. Can one complete the bottom row of the table above with an analogue of \cref{thm:bases-proportional}, leading to a new proof of Theorem 1.1 from \cite{corteel2019varvec}, and possibly to applications on higher-order mock theta functions? \begin{remark} There is also a product identity whose $q$-coefficients are the characters of $M(2, u^2 + v^2)_2$, for any relatively prime positive integers $u, v$ such that $u + v$ is odd; see our \cref{cor:character-identity}. These might be connected as in \cref{qtn:characters} to the Andrews--Gordon identities \cite[Theorem 7.8]{andrews1998theory}, which generalize \cref{eq:rog-ram}; \cref{thm:bases-proportional} would correspond to the case $(u, v) = (1, 1)$. As pointed out by Professor Ole Warnaar (private communication), the analogue of \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram} in this case could be a summation of variants of the Andrews--Gordon identities as in \cite[(3.21)]{berkovich2001variants}; the difficulty lies in relating such a summation to an infinite product in a suitable $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f)$ space. \end{remark}
nodes.statement_short: Is there an analogue of the main theorem connecting the nonuple identity with the $M(3,7)_3$ characters (Corteel-Welsh)?
nodes.label: qtn:characters

nodes.name: Remark on M(2,u^2+v^2)_2 characters and Andrews-Gordon identities
nodes.statement: There is also a product identity whose $q$-coefficients are the characters of $M(2, u^2 + v^2)_2$, for any relatively prime positive integers $u, v$ such that $u + v$ is odd; see our \cref{cor:character-identity}. These might be connected as in \cref{qtn:characters} to the Andrews--Gordon identities \cite[Theorem 7.8]{andrews1998theory}, which generalize \cref{eq:rog-ram}; \cref{thm:bases-proportional} would correspond to the case $(u, v) = (1, 1)$. As pointed out by Professor Ole Warnaar (private communication), the analogue of \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram} in this case could be a summation of variants of the Andrews--Gordon identities as in \cite[(3.21)]{berkovich2001variants}; the difficulty lies in relating such a summation to an infinite product in a suitable $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f)$ space.

nodes.name: Two constructions of quasiperiodic functions
nodes.statement: Given an entire $1$-periodic function $f \in \textnormal{Hol}(\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z})$, there are two main ways to construct a function with a $\mathcal{T}_D(f)$-type quasiperiodicity from scratch: the expressions \begin{equation} \prod_{n \ge 0} f(z + n\tau) \qquad\quad \text{and} \qquad\quad \sum_{n < 0}\ \prod_{-n \le j < 0} f(z + j\tau)^{-1} \ +\ 1 \ +\ \sum_{n > 0}\ \prod_{0 \le j < n} f(z + j\tau) \end{equation} are, if well-defined, quasiperiodic with $F(z) = f(z)F(z + \tau)$.
nodes.statement_short: The infinite product $\prod f(z+n\tau)$ and the two-sided sum of partial products are $\tau$-quasiperiodic with factor $f$.

nodes.name: Product and sum constructions
nodes.statement: \prod_{n \ge 0} f(z + n\tau) \qquad\quad \text{and} \qquad\quad \sum_{n < 0}\ \prod_{-n \le j < 0} f(z + j\tau)^{-1} \ +\ 1 \ +\ \sum_{n > 0}\ \prod_{0 \le j < n} f(z + j\tau)
nodes.label: eq:two-ways

nodes.name: M-coefficients
nodes.statement: Going further, the product of two basis vectors $\vect{\alpha x^a}{k}$ and $\vect{\beta x^b}{j}$ (where $a, b, k, j \in \mathbb{Z}$, $a, b \ge 1$, $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{C}^\times$) is an element of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha \beta x^{a+b}\right)$, so we must have \begin{equation} \vect{\alpha x^a}{k}\vect{\beta x^b}{j} = \sum_{0 \le \ell < a+b} M_\ell(q) \vect{\alpha \beta x^{a+b}}{\ell}, \end{equation} for some \emph{M-coefficients} $\{M_\ell(q)\}_\ell$.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficients $M_\ell(q)$ expanding a product of two canonical theta vectors in the canonical basis of the product space.

nodes.name: M-coefficient expansion
nodes.statement: \vect{\alpha x^a}{k}\vect{\beta x^b}{j} = \sum_{0 \le \ell < a+b} M_\ell(q) \vect{\alpha \beta x^{a+b}}{\ell},
nodes.label: eq:m-coeffs

nodes.name: Twisting of a quasiperiodic series
nodes.statement: In a similar spirit, \emph{twisting} the $n$th term in a series as in \cref{eq:two-ways} by a factor of $w(z + n\tau)$ (for suitable functions $w$ with period $1$) should preserve the quasiperiodicity at $z \mapsto z + \tau$.

nodes.name: W-coefficients
nodes.statement: In particular, by twisting the series defining $\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}$, we should be able to write (when well-defined) \begin{equation} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2} + kn} x^{dn+k}\ w(z+ n\tau) = \sum_{0 \le \ell < d} W_\ell(q) \vect{\alpha x^d}{\ell}, \end{equation} for some \emph{W-coefficients} $\{W_\ell(q)\}_\ell$, provided that the left-hand side is entire.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficients $W_\ell(q)$ expanding a twisted theta series in the canonical basis.

nodes.name: W-coefficient expansion
nodes.statement: \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2} + kn} x^{dn+k}\ w(z+ n\tau) = \sum_{0 \le \ell < d} W_\ell(q) \vect{\alpha x^d}{\ell},
nodes.label: eq:w-coeffs

nodes.name: Punctured plane and half-planes
nodes.statement: Denote $\mathbb{C}^\times := \mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}$, ${\mathbb{H}}^+ := \{z \in \mathbb{C} : \textnormal{Im}\ z > 0\}$, ${\mathbb{H}}^- := \{z \in \mathbb{C} : \textnormal{Im}\ z < 0\}$.

nodes.name: Standing conventions for tau, z, x, q
nodes.statement: Throughout the paper we keep $\tau \in {\mathbb{H}}^+$ fixed and let $z \in \mathbb{C}$ vary, and write $x = e^{2\pi i z}$, $q = e^{2\pi i \tau}$ and $q^r = e^{2\pi i r \tau}$ for $r \in \mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Spaces Hol(D) and Hol(D/Z)
nodes.statement: Given a domain $D$ (an open connected subset of $\mathbb{C}$), denote by $\textnormal{Hol}(D)$ the space of all holomorphic functions on $D$; if $D$ is closed under $\mathbb{Z}$-translation, denote by $\textnormal{Hol}(D/\mathbb{Z})$ the space of all functions in $\textnormal{Hol}(D)$ with period $1$.

nodes.name: Translation and scaling operators T_w, S_u
nodes.statement: Given $w \in \mathbb{C}$ and $u \in \mathbb{Z} \setminus \{0\}$, define the linear maps $T_w : \textnormal{Hol}(D) \to \textnormal{Hol}(D - w)$ and $S_u : \textnormal{Hol}(D) \to \textnormal{Hol}(u^{-1} D)$ by \[ (T_w f)(z) := f(z+w), \qquad\qquad (S_u f)(z) := f(u z), \] which are a translation and a scaling of the function's argument.

nodes.name: Spaces T_D(f) and S_D(f)
nodes.statement: Given such $D$ and a \emph{meromorphic} function $f$ on $\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}$, $f \not\equiv 0$, we denote \begin{align} \mathcal{T}_D(f) &:= \left\{F \in \textnormal{Hol}(D/\mathbb{Z})\ :\ F = f \cdot T_\tau F \text{ on } D \cap (D - \tau)\right\}, \\ \mathcal{S}_D(f) &:= \left\{F \in \textnormal{Hol}(D/\mathbb{Z})\ :\ F = f \cdot S_{-1} F \text{ on } D \cap (-D)\right\}, \end{align} where $F = f \cdot T_\tau F$ and $F = f \cdot S_{-1}F$ are understood as equalities of meromorphic functions.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal T_D(f)$: $F=f\cdot T_\tau F$; $\mathcal S_D(f)$: $F=f\cdot S_{-1}F$, for 1-periodic holomorphic $F$ on $D$.

nodes.name: Definition of T_D(f)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{T}_D(f) &:= \left\{F \in \textnormal{Hol}(D/\mathbb{Z})\ :\ F = f \cdot T_\tau F \text{ on } D \cap (D - \tau)\right\},
nodes.label: eq:T-spaces

nodes.name: Definition of S_D(f)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{S}_D(f) &:= \left\{F \in \textnormal{Hol}(D/\mathbb{Z})\ :\ F = f \cdot S_{-1} F \text{ on } D \cap (-D)\right\},
nodes.label: eq:S-spaces

nodes.name: q-Pochhammer symbol for negative n
nodes.statement: Next, we extend the notation $(x; q)_n := \prod_{k=0}^{n-1} \left(1 - xq^k\right)$ from \cref{sec:intro} to all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ by setting \begin{equation} \forall n < 0, \qquad\quad \frac{1}{(x; q)_n} := \frac{(q^n x; q)}{\left(x; q\right)} = \left(q^n x; q\right)_{-n}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Extends $(x;q)_n$ to $n<0$ via $1/(x;q)_n=(q^nx;q)_{-n}$.

nodes.name: Negative-index q-Pochhammer convention
nodes.statement: \forall n < 0, \qquad\quad \frac{1}{(x; q)_n} := \frac{(q^n x; q)}{\left(x; q\right)} = \left(q^n x; q\right)_{-n}.
nodes.label: eq:finite-product-negative

nodes.name: Infinite q-Pochhammer as a limit
nodes.statement: As before, we write $(x; q) := \lim_{n \to \infty} (x; q)_n$, implying that $(x; q) \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1-x)$.

nodes.name: Modified theta function
nodes.statement: The double product $\left\langle x; q\right\rangle := (x; q) (q/x; q)$ is commonly referred to as a modified theta function, and often found in literature as $\left\langle x; q \right\rangle_\infty$ \cite{chu2007unification} or $\theta(x; q)$ \cite[(11.2.1)]{gasper2004basic}.

nodes.name: Quasiperiodicity of double products
nodes.statement: It shortly follows that $\left\langle \alpha x^d; q^d \right\rangle \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(-\alpha x^d\right)$ for any $\alpha \in \mathbb{C}^\times$, a symmetry which is crucial to most proofs of product identities.

nodes.name: S-type symmetry of double products (table of function spaces)
nodes.statement: But more surprisingly, if $\alpha = -sq^b$ for $s \in \{\pm 1\}$ and $b \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that $d \mid 2b$, a short computation left to the reader shows that $\left\langle \alpha x^d; q^d \right\rangle$ also satisfies a simple $\mathcal{S}$-type symmetry recorded in \cref{tbl:spaces}.
nodes.statement_short: For $\alpha=-sq^b$ with $d\mid 2b$, $\langle\alpha x^d;q^d\rangle$ lies in an $\mathcal S_{\mathbb C}$-space as recorded in the table of function spaces.

nodes.name: Three root-of-unity product manipulations
nodes.statement: For completion, we also state three easy manipulations of infinite products as in \cref{tbl:spaces}, which may be used implicitly throughout the paper: for any positive integer $d$, one has \[ \big(x^d; q^d\big) = \prod_{\zeta^d = 1} \left(\zeta x; q\right), \qquad\qquad \big\langle x^d; q^d\big\rangle = \prod_{\zeta^d = 1} \left\langle \zeta x; q\right\rangle, \qquad\qquad \big( x; q \big) = \prod_{j=0}^{d-1} \big(q^j x; q^d \big) , \] where $\zeta$ ranges over the $d$th complex roots of unity.
nodes.statement_short: $(x^d;q^d)=\prod_\zeta(\zeta x;q)$, $\langle x^d;q^d\rangle=\prod_\zeta\langle\zeta x;q\rangle$, $(x;q)=\prod_j(q^jx;q^d)$.

nodes.name: Canonical basis notation [f;k]
nodes.statement: The notation $\vect{f}{k}$ will be used for certain canonical elements of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f)$, generalizing the functions $\vect{\alpha x^d}{k} := \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2} + kn} x^{dn+k}$ from \cref{sec:intro}; see \cref{prop:canonical-basis-vectors}.

nodes.name: Fourier coefficients on a strip
nodes.statement: Given a nonempty open horizontal strip $S \subset \mathbb{C}$, a function $F \in \textnormal{Hol}(S/\mathbb{Z})$ and $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, write \[ \widehat{F}(n) := \int_w^{w+1} F(z) e^{-2\pi i n z} dz, \qquad\qquad F(z) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \widehat{F}(n) x^n, \] for any $w \in S$ (the choice of $w$ is irrelevant by contour-shifting).

nodes.name: Degree in x of a Laurent polynomial
nodes.statement: If $F(z)$ is a Laurent polynomial in $x$, we write $\deg_x F$ for its degree in $x$, i.e.\ the largest $n$ such that $\widehat{F}(n) \neq 0$.

nodes.name: Binomial coefficient and indicator notation
nodes.statement: Finally, we write $\binom{n}{k} := n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)/k!$ for $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $k \ge 0$, and $\mathbbm{1}_{P}$ for the truth value of a proposition $P$ (e.g., $\mathbbm{1}_{x < y}$ equals $1$ whenever $x < y$, and $0$ otherwise).

nodes.name: Extended quasiperiodic function spaces
nodes.statement: Let $D \subset \mathbb{C}$ be a $\mathbb{Z}$-invariant domain, $m$ a positive integer, and $f_1, \ldots, f_m$ meromorphic functions on $\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}$ (i.e., on $\mathbb{C}$ with period $1$), with $f_m \not\equiv 0$ (i.e., $f_m$ is not the zero function). We define the complex vector space \[ \mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m) := \left\{F \in \textnormal{Hol}(D/\mathbb{Z}) : F = f_1 \cdot T_\tau F + \cdots + f_m \cdot T_{m\tau} F \right\}, \] where the equality holds as an identity of meromorphic functions on $D \cap (D - \tau) \cap \cdots \cap (D - m\tau)$. More generally, given an $m \times m$ matrix $M(z)$ whose entries are meromorphic functions on $\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}$ such that $\det M(z) \not\equiv 0$, let \[ \mathcal{T}_D(M) := \left\{ \vec{F} \in \textnormal{Hol}(D/\mathbb{Z})^m : \vec{F} = M \cdot T_\tau \vec{F} \right\}, \] where the equality holds as an identity of $m$ meromorphic functions on $D \cap (D - \tau)$, and $(T_\tau \vec{F})(z) = \vec{F}(z+\tau)$ as before. In particular, we have a linear bijection \[ \mathcal{T}_D\left(f_1, \ldots, f_m\right) \ \cong \ \mathcal{T}_{D \cap (D - \tau) \cap \cdots \cap (D - (m-1)\tau)} \begin{psmall} f_1 & f_2 & \cdots & f_{m-1} & f_m \\ 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ & & \ddots & & \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & 1 & 0 \end{psmall} \qquad \text{by} \quad F \mapsto \begin{psmall} F \\ T_\tau F \\ \vdots \\ T_{(m-1)\tau} F \end{psmall}. \] While much of this paper is concerned with the spaces $\mathcal{T}_D(f)$ (in fact, \cref{sec:higher-prod-id} only works with $\mathcal{T}_D\left(\alpha x^d\right)$), we will encounter more general spaces $\mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$ and $\mathcal{T}_D(M)$ in \cref{sec:rog-ram}.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal T_D(f_1,\dots,f_m)$: $F=\sum_j f_jT_{j\tau}F$; and the vector version $\mathcal T_D(M)$ for a matrix $M$.
nodes.label: def:T-spaces

nodes.name: Two-variable Rogers-Ramanujan fraction
nodes.statement: Consider the entire $1$-periodic function $F(z) := \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2} (q; q)_n^{-1} x^n$ (this is $\chi(x/q)$ from \cite[p.~329]{rogers1893second}). A short computation shows that \[ \forall z \in \mathbb{C} : \quad F(z) = F(z+\tau) + qxF(z+2\tau), \] so $F = T_\tau F + qxT_{2\tau} F$ and thus $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(1, qx\right)$. This vector space turns out to be one-dimensional, which can be used to prove an identity due to Rogers generalizing the Rogers--Ramanujan identities in \cref{eq:rog-ram}; see \cref{prop:rogers}. By iterating this functional equation in matrix form, one can also recover the Rogers--Ramanujan continued fraction identity \cite[p.~328 (4)]{rogers1893second}, \[ \begin{pmatrix} F(z) \\ F(z+\tau) \end{pmatrix} = \prod_{n \ge 1} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & q^n x \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \cdot \begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad \frac{F(z)}{F(z+\tau)} = 1 + \frac{qx}{1 + \frac{q^2x}{1 + \frac{q^3 x}{1 + \cdots}}}. \] where the infinite product of matrices above is computed from the left to the right.
nodes.statement_short: $F(z)=\sum q^{n^2}x^n/(q;q)_n$ lies in $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(1,qx)$; iterating gives the Rogers-Ramanujan continued fraction.
nodes.label: ex:two-var-rog-ram

nodes.name: Line bundles and theta functions
nodes.statement: Take $D = \mathbb{C}$ and $m = 1$ in \cref{def:T-spaces}, and let $f$ be any invertible function in $\textnormal{Hol}(\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z})$. For $m, n \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $z \in \mathbb{C}$, define $\phi_{m\tau + n}(z)$ as $\prod_{k=0}^{m-1} f(z+k\tau)^{-1}$ if $m \ge 0$, and as $\prod_{k=-m}^{-1} f(z+k\tau)$ otherwise. Then $(\phi_\gamma)_{\gamma \in \Gamma}$ form a system of multipliers for the lattice $\Gamma := \mathbb{Z}\tau + \mathbb{Z}$, meaning that they are holomorphic invertible and they satisfy the cocycle condition $\phi_{\gamma+ \delta}(z) = \phi_\gamma(z+\delta) \phi_\delta(z)$ (see, for example, \cite[\S 2.3]{beauville2013theta}). Such a system induces a holomorphic line bundle $L \cong (\mathbb{C} \times \mathbb{C})/\Gamma$ over $\mathbb{C}/\Gamma$, where $\gamma \in \Gamma$ acts on $\mathbb{C} \times \mathbb{C}$ by $\gamma(z, t) = (z + \gamma, \phi_\gamma(z)t)$; a section of this line bundle has the form \[ \mathbb{C}/\Gamma \to L \cong \left(\mathbb{C} \times \mathbb{C}\right)/\Gamma, \qquad\qquad z \mapsto (z, F(z)), \] where $F \in \textnormal{Hol}(\mathbb{C})$ satisfies $F(z + \gamma) = \phi_\gamma(z) F(z)$, and this reduces to $F(z) = f(z)F(z+\tau)$ by our choice of $\left\{\phi_\gamma\right\}_{\gamma \in \Gamma}$. Hence the sections of $L \to C$ are canonically identified with the elements $F$ of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f)$, and these are called the \emph{theta functions} associated to $L$. Canonical examples are Jacobi's theta functions (see \cite{jacobi1829fundamenta} or \cite[p.~464]{whittaker2020course}), and more generally the functions $\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}$. While the triple, quintuple, septuple, etc.\ products all lie in such vector spaces induced by invertible functions $f$, allowing $f$ to have zeros at the cost of reducing the domain of holomorphicity $D$ of $F$ is essential for stating and proving results like \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram}, \cref{thm:bases-proportional} or \cref{thm:bases-proportional-2}. If $D$ contains a horizontal strip of length $\ge \textnormal{Im}\ \tau$ (thus a copy of $\mathbb{C}/\Gamma$), the more general spaces $\mathcal{T}_D(f)$ correspond similarly to \emph{meromorphic} line bundles, while the spaces $\mathcal{T}_D(M)$ (where $M$ is an $m \times m$ matrix) correspond to \emph{vector} bundles of rank $m$ (of the form $E \to \mathbb{C}/\Gamma$ where $E \cong \left(\mathbb{C} \times \mathbb{C}^m\right)/\Gamma$) and \emph{generalized} (or \emph{non-abelian}) theta functions (see \cite[\S 6.2]{beauville2013theta} or \cite{gunning1982generalized}). It can be helpful, however, to consider smaller domains $D$ not containing any copy of $\mathbb{C}/\Gamma$, as we illustrate \cref{prop:fractional}. For the reader familiar with this language, the properties in the following lemma will come naturally; e.g., \cref{lem:basic}.(iii) is motivated by the fact that multiplying a vector bundle by a line bundle yields back a vector bundle of the same rank.
nodes.statement_short: Elements of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(f)$ are sections of a line bundle on $\mathbb C/\Gamma$ (theta functions); $\mathcal T_D(M)$ corresponds to vector bundles.

nodes.name: Basic facts about T_D
nodes.statement:
Let $F \in \mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$ and $G \in \mathcal{T}_D(g)$ be as in \cref{def:T-spaces}.  egin{enumerate}[label=(oman*).] \item If $E$ is another $Z$-invariant domain and $\varnothing 
eq D \subset E$, then $\mathcal{T}_E(f_1, \ldots, f_m) \subset \mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$, where a function in $	extnormal{Hol}(E/\mathbb{Z})$ is uniquely identified with its restriction to $	extnormal{Hol}(D/\mathbb{Z})$. \item For $w \in \mathbb{C}$, one has $ T_w F \in \mathcal{T}_{D-w}\left(T_w f_1, \ldots, T_w f_might)$. \item Letting $g_n := \prod_{j=0}^{m-1} T_{j	au} g$, one has $FG \in \mathcal{T}_D\left(f_1 g_1, f_2 g_2, \ldots, f_m g_might)$; so if $m = 1$, then $FG \in \mathcal{T}_D(f_1g)$. Also, if $G$ has no zeros in $D$, then $G^{-1} \in \mathcal{T}_D(g^{-1})$. \item If $u \in \mathbb{Z}$, $u \ge 1$ and $D \cap T_{-	au} D \cap \cdots \cap T_{-u	au} D 
eq \varnothing$, then \[ S_u G \in \mathcal{T}_{u^{-1}D}\Bigg(\prod_{j=0}^{u-1} S_u T_{j	au} g\Bigg). \] \item If $D$ contains an open horizontal strip of width $> m\cdot 	extnormal{Im}\tau$, then $F$ has a meromorphic continuation to all of $\mathbb{C}$, which still satisfies $F = F_1 \cdot T_	au F + \cdots + f_m \cdot T_{m	au} F$. \item If $D$ contains an open horizontal strip of width $> 	extnormal{Im}\ 	au$, and $0 
eq H \in \mathcal{T}_D(g)$, then $G/H$ extends to an elliptic function on $\mathbb{C}$ with periods $1, 	au$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Restriction, translation, multiplication, scaling, meromorphic continuation and elliptic quotients for $\mathcal T_D$ spaces.
assumptions: Let $F \in \mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$ and $G \in \mathcal{T}_D(g)$ be as in \cref{def:T-spaces}.
nodes.label: lem:basic

nodes.name: Proof of Basic facts about T_D
nodes.statement: Statements (i) and (ii) are immediate, while (iii) and (iv) follow by repeatedly applying (ii) for $w = j\tau$. For (v), let $S \subset D$ be an open horizontal strip of width $> m \cdot \textnormal{Im}\ \tau$; then we can iteratively define $F := f_1 \cdot T_\tau F + \cdots + f_m \cdot T_{m\tau} F$ on the strips $S + n\tau$ for $n \in \{1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$, and \[ F := T_{-m\tau} \frac{F - f_1 \cdot T_\tau F - \cdots - f_m T_{m\tau} F}{f_m} \] on $S - n\tau$ for $n \in \{1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$; note that $F$ is well-defined on $\mathbb{C}$ by the uniqueness of meromorphic continuation. Finally, (vi) follows from (v) applied to $G$ and $H$, and then (iii) applied for $D' = \mathbb{C} \setminus \{\textnormal{poles of $G$, $H$ or $H^{-1}$}\}$ (one has $H^{-1} \in \mathcal{T}_{D'}(g^{-1})$, and so $G/H \in \mathcal{T}_{D'}(1)$).
nodes.statement_short: Direct: (i)-(iv) from definitions and translation; (v) by continuing strip by strip; (vi) from (v) and (iii).

nodes.name: Parts (i)-(v)
nodes.statement: Statements (i) and (ii) are immediate, while (iii) and (iv) follow by repeatedly applying (ii) for $w = j\tau$. For (v), let $S \subset D$ be an open horizontal strip of width $> m \cdot \textnormal{Im}\ \tau$; then we can iteratively define $F := f_1 \cdot T_\tau F + \cdots + f_m \cdot T_{m\tau} F$ on the strips $S + n\tau$ for $n \in \{1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$, and \[ F := T_{-m\tau} \frac{F - f_1 \cdot T_\tau F - \cdots - f_m T_{m\tau} F}{f_m} \] on $S - n\tau$ for $n \in \{1, 2, 3, \ldots\}$; note that $F$ is well-defined on $\mathbb{C}$ by the uniqueness of meromorphic continuation.
nodes.statement_short: (i)-(iv) are immediate; continue F to all of C strip by strip for (v)

nodes.name: Part (vi)
nodes.statement: Finally, (vi) follows from (v) applied to $G$ and $H$, and then (iii) applied for $D' = \mathbb{C} \setminus \{\textnormal{poles of $G$, $H$ or $H^{-1}$}\}$ (one has $H^{-1} \in \mathcal{T}_{D'}(g^{-1})$, and so $G/H \in \mathcal{T}_{D'}(1)$).
nodes.statement_short: Apply (v) and (iii) to get an elliptic quotient

nodes.name: Remark on meromorphic continuation of T_D elements
nodes.statement: By \cref{lem:basic}.(v), we can treat the elements of $\mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$ as meromorphic functions on $\mathbb{C}$ if $D$ is wide enough; the same is true in more general spaces $\mathcal{T}_D(M)$, where the continuation requires inverting the matrix $M$. The restriction of holomorphicity on $D$, however, will be crucial.

nodes.name: Spaces given by constants
nodes.statement: Suppose a domain $D$ contains a horizontal strip $S$ of length $> \textnormal{Im}\ \tau$. Note that $\mathcal{T}_D(1) = \left\{ F \in \textnormal{Hol}(D) : F = T_1 F = T_\tau F \text{ in } D \cap (D - \tau)\right\}$. The proof of \cref{lem:basic}.(ii) then shows that any function $F \in \mathcal{T}_D(1)$ can be continued to an \emph{entire} elliptic function on $\mathbb{C}$, thus a constant. More generally, if $f_1 \equiv \alpha$ is any nonzero constant, then for $F \in \mathcal{T}_D(\alpha)$, considering the Fourier series of $F(z) = \alpha F(z+\tau)$ in $S \cap (S - \tau) \neq \varnothing$ yields \[ \widehat{F}(n) = \alpha q^n \widehat{F}(n) \] for any $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. So if $\alpha = q^{-n}$ for some $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, we find that $\mathcal{T}_D(\alpha)$ is one-dimensional, spanned by $x^n$; otherwise, $\mathcal{T}_D(\alpha) = \{0\}$. We give a more general upper bound for $\dim \mathcal{T}_D$ in \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal T_D(\alpha)$ is spanned by $x^n$ if $\alpha=q^{-n}$, and is zero otherwise.
nodes.label: ex:constants

nodes.name: Upper bounds for dim T_D
nodes.statement:
Let $P_0(z), P_1(z), \ldots, P_m(z)$ be complex polynomials in $x = e^{2\pi i z}$ with $P_0 
eq 0$ and $ ig(\widehat{P_0}(0), \ldots, \widehat{P_m}(0) ig) 
eq (0, \ldots, 0)$, and let $d := \max(\deg_x P_0, \ldots, \deg_x P_m)$. For $1 \le j \le m$, take $f_j := P_j/P_0$. Suppose $D \subset \mathbb{C}$ is a $\mathbb{Z}$-invariant domain, containing an open horizontal strip $S$ of width $> m \cdot 	extnormal{Im}\ 	au$. Letting $V := \mathcal{T}_D\left(f_1, \ldots, f_might)$, the following hold true.  egin{enumerate}[label=(oman*).] \item One has $\dim V \le d + m$. \item For $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, denote $A_n := P_0 - q^n P_1 - \cdots - q^{mn} P_m$. Assume additionally that $\exists n_0 \in \mathbb{Z}$, \[  orall n \ge n_0 + d :\ \widehat{A_n}(0) 
eq 0 \qquad 	ext{ and } \qquad  orall n < n_0 :\ \widehat{A_n}(d) 
eq 0. \] Then one has $\dim V \le d$, with equality iff $ orall k \in \{0, 1, \ldots, d-1\}$, $\exists F_k \in V$ such that \[ \widehat{F_k}(j) = \mathbbm{1}_{j = n_0 + k} \quad 	ext{ in } S, \quad\quad\hspace{0.2cm}  orall j \in \{0, 1, \ldots, d-1\}, \] In this case, $\{F_0, \ldots, F_{d-1}\}$ is a (uniquely determined) basis of $V$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For rational $f_j=P_j/P_0$ in $x$, $\dim\mathcal T_D(f_1..f_m)\le d+m$, and $\le d$ under nonvanishing conditions on $\widehat{A_n}$, with a unique normalized basis in the equality case.
assumptions: $D \subset \mathbb{C}$ is a $\mathbb{Z}$-invariant domain, containing an open horizontal strip $S$ of width $> m \cdot \textnormal{Im}\ \tau$
nodes.label: prop:upper-bounds

nodes.name: Spaces given by constants, continued
nodes.statement: For $m = 1$, $P_0(z) = 1$ and $P_1(z) = \alpha \in \mathbb{C}^\times$, part (i) implies that $\dim \mathcal{T}_D(\alpha) \le 1$ whenever $D$ contains a horizontal strip of width $> \textnormal{Im}\ \tau$. If $\alpha \not\in \left\{q^n : n \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}$, then in part (ii) we have $A_n(z) = 1 - \alpha q^n$, so any choice of $n_0$ yields $\dim \mathcal{T}_D(\alpha) = 0$. This recovers \cref{ex:constants}.
nodes.label: ex:constants-ctd

nodes.name: Two-variable Rogers-Ramanujan fraction, continued
nodes.statement: For $m = 2$, $P_0(z) = P_1(z) = 1$ and $P_2(z) = qx$, we have $A_n(z) = 1 - q^n - q^{2n+1}x$. Hence using $n_0 = 0$ in \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii), we find that $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{+}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(1, qx) \le 1$. In \cref{ex:two-var-rog-ram} we found a nonzero element $G$ of this space, so it must be the unique such function up to scalars.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition on upper bounds gives $\dim\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^+}(1,qx)\le1$, so the series of the earlier example spans it.
nodes.label: ex:two-var-rog-ram-ctd

nodes.name: Proof of Upper bounds for dim T_D
nodes.statement:
For $F \in \mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$, we have $F = f_1 \cdot T_	au F + \cdots + f_m \cdot T_{m	au} F$ and thus $P_0 \cdot F = P_1 \cdot T_	au F + \cdots + P_m \cdot T_{m	au} F$. Taking the Fourier series in $S \cap (S - m	au) 
eq \varnothing$ then yields \[  orall n \in \mathbb{Z} : \qquad\quad \sum_{k=0}^d \widehat{P_0}(k) \widehat{F}(n-k) = \sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{k=0}^d \widehat{P_j}(k) q^{j(n-k)} \widehat{F}(n-k), \] which rearranges (by subtracting the right side from the left side and swapping sums) to  egin{equation} \sum_{k=0}^d \widehat{A_{n-k}}(k) \widehat{F}(n-k) = 0. \end{equation} If $d = 0$, we find that $\widehat{F}(n) = 0$ whenever $\widehat{A_n}(0) 
eq 0$. So (ii) holds trivially since if all $\widehat{A_n}(0) 
eq 0$, we must have $F = 0$. For statement (i), note that one can have $\widehat{A_n}(0) = 0$ for at most $m$ values of $n$, say among $\{n_1, \ldots, n_m\}$, since $\widehat{A_n}(0)$ is a nonzero polynomial in $q^n$ of degree $\le m$. Hence $V$ injects linearly into a subspace of $\mathbb{C}^m$ by the map $F \mapsto  ig(\widehat{F}(n_1), \ldots, \widehat{F}(n_m)  ig)$, proving $\dim V \le m$. Now assume that $d \ge 1$. When $\widehat{A_n}(0) 
eq 0$, \cref{eq:recursion} implies that $\widehat{F}(n)$ is a linear function of $\widehat{F}(n-1), \ldots, \widehat{F}(n-d)$. Similarly, when $\widehat{A_n}(d) 
eq 0$, $\widehat{F}(n)$ is a linear function of $\widehat{F}(n+1), \ldots, \widehat{F}(n+d)$. Hence under the assumption of (ii), $V$ injects linearly into $\mathbb{C}^d$ by $F \mapsto  ig(\widehat{F}(n_0), \ldots, \widehat{F}(n_0 + d-1) ig)$, proving that $\dim V = d$ with equality iff each standard basis vector of $\mathbb{C}^d$ is attained by this injection; the preimages of these vectors correspond to $F_0, \ldots, F_{d-1}$. To prove (i), note as before that $\widehat{A_n}(0)$ and $\widehat{A_n}(d)$ can each be zero for at most $m$ values of $n$ (since $\widehat{A_n}(d)$ is also a polynomial in $q^n$ of degree $\le m$, which is not constantly $0$ by the definition of $d$). Say that $\widehat{A_n}(d)$ has zeros only if $n \in \{n_1, \ldots, n_m\}$, and let $N \in \mathbb{Z}$ be large enough such that $\widehat{A_n}(0) 
eq 0$ for all $n \ge N+d$. Then by our previous reasoning, $V$ injects linearly into $\mathbb{C}^{d+m}$ by $F \mapsto  ig(\widehat{F}(N), \ldots, \widehat{F}(N+d-1), \widehat{F}(n_1), \ldots, \widehat{F}(n_m)  ig)$, proving $\dim V \le d + m$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare Fourier coefficients to get a linear recursion; nonvanishing of extreme coefficients makes $F$ determined by finitely many coefficients, giving injections into $\mathbb C^d$ or $\mathbb C^{d+m}$.

nodes.name: Fourier recursion
nodes.statement: For $F \in \mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$, we have $F = f_1 \cdot T_\tau F + \cdots + f_m \cdot T_{m\tau} F$ and thus $P_0 \cdot F = P_1 \cdot T_\tau F + \cdots + P_m \cdot T_{m\tau} F$. Taking the Fourier series in $S \cap (S - m\tau) \neq \varnothing$ then yields \[ \forall n \in \mathbb{Z} : \qquad\quad \sum_{k=0}^d \widehat{P_0}(k) \widehat{F}(n-k) = \sum_{j=1}^m \sum_{k=0}^d \widehat{P_j}(k) q^{j(n-k)} \widehat{F}(n-k), \] which rearranges (by subtracting the right side from the left side and swapping sums) to \begin{equation} \sum_{k=0}^d \widehat{A_{n-k}}(k) \widehat{F}(n-k) = 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Compare Fourier coefficients to obtain the recursion for $\widehat F$

nodes.name: Case d=0
nodes.statement: If $d = 0$, we find that $\widehat{F}(n) = 0$ whenever $\widehat{A_n}(0) \neq 0$. So (ii) holds trivially since if all $\widehat{A_n}(0) \neq 0$, we must have $F = 0$. For statement (i), note that one can have $\widehat{A_n}(0) = 0$ for at most $m$ values of $n$, say among $\{n_1, \ldots, n_m\}$, since $\widehat{A_n}(0)$ is a nonzero polynomial in $q^n$ of degree $\le m$. Hence $V$ injects linearly into a subspace of $\mathbb{C}^m$ by the map $F \mapsto \big(\widehat{F}(n_1), \ldots, \widehat{F}(n_m) \big)$, proving $\dim V \le m$.
nodes.statement_short: For $d=0$, $F$ is determined by at most $m$ coefficients

nodes.name: Case d>=1, part (ii)
nodes.statement: Now assume that $d \ge 1$. When $\widehat{A_n}(0) \neq 0$, \cref{eq:recursion} implies that $\widehat{F}(n)$ is a linear function of $\widehat{F}(n-1), \ldots, \widehat{F}(n-d)$. Similarly, when $\widehat{A_n}(d) \neq 0$, $\widehat{F}(n)$ is a linear function of $\widehat{F}(n+1), \ldots, \widehat{F}(n+d)$. Hence under the assumption of (ii), $V$ injects linearly into $\mathbb{C}^d$ by $F \mapsto \big(\widehat{F}(n_0), \ldots, \widehat{F}(n_0 + d-1)\big)$, proving that $\dim V = d$ with equality iff each standard basis vector of $\mathbb{C}^d$ is attained by this injection; the preimages of these vectors correspond to $F_0, \ldots, F_{d-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Nonvanishing extreme coefficients give an injection into $\mathbb C^d$

nodes.name: Part (i)
nodes.statement: To prove (i), note as before that $\widehat{A_n}(0)$ and $\widehat{A_n}(d)$ can each be zero for at most $m$ values of $n$ (since $\widehat{A_n}(d)$ is also a polynomial in $q^n$ of degree $\le m$, which is not constantly $0$ by the definition of $d$). Say that $\widehat{A_n}(d)$ has zeros only if $n \in \{n_1, \ldots, n_m\}$, and let $N \in \mathbb{Z}$ be large enough such that $\widehat{A_n}(0) \neq 0$ for all $n \ge N+d$. Then by our previous reasoning, $V$ injects linearly into $\mathbb{C}^{d+m}$ by $F \mapsto \big(\widehat{F}(N), \ldots, \widehat{F}(N+d-1), \widehat{F}(n_1), \ldots, \widehat{F}(n_m) \big)$, proving $\dim V \le d + m$.
nodes.statement_short: Injection into $\mathbb C^{d+m}$ proves $\dim V\le d+m$

nodes.name: Fourier coefficient recursion
nodes.statement: \sum_{k=0}^d \widehat{A_{n-k}}(k) \widehat{F}(n-k) = 0.
nodes.label: eq:recursion

nodes.name: Remark on sharpening the dimension bound
nodes.statement: The bound in \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(i) may be sharpened by determining the zeros of $\widehat{A_n}(0)$ and $\widehat{A_n}(d)$ in particular cases. Also, the linear relation in $\cref{eq:recursion}$ gives a formula for the Fourier coefficients $\widehat{F_k}(n)$ (for $k \in \{0, \ldots, d-1\}$ and $n \in \mathbb{Z}$) in terms of finite matrix products; however, applications will require alternative formulae for $F_k$, which we give in \cref{subsec:canonical-basis-vectors}.

nodes.name: Basic facts about S_D
nodes.statement:
Let $D$ be a $\mathbb{Z}$-invariant domain and $f, g$ be meromorphic functions on $\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}$.  egin{enumerate}[label = (oman*).] \item If $F \in \mathcal{S}_D(f)$ and $G \in \mathcal{S}_D(g)$, then $FG \in \mathcal{S}_D(fg)$. \item If $D \cap (-D) 
eq \varnothing$ and $\mathcal{S}_D(g) 
eq \{0\}$, then one has $g(z)g(-z) = 1$ wherever defined. \item If $D \cap (-D) \cap (D-	au) \cap (-D-	au) 
eq \varnothing$ and $\mathcal{T}_D(f) \cap \mathcal{S}_D(g) 
eq \{0\}$, then wherever defined, \[ f(z)f(-z-	au) = g(z)g(-z-	au). \] \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Products of $\mathcal S_D$-functions; necessary conditions $g(z)g(-z)=1$ and $f(z)f(-z-\tau)=g(z)g(-z-\tau)$.
assumptions: Let $D$ be a $\mathbb{Z}$-invariant domain and $f, g$ be meromorphic functions on $\mathbb{C}/\mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.label: lem:basic-S

nodes.name: Proof of Basic facts about S_D
nodes.statement: Statement (i) is clear, and (ii) follows by iterating the functional equation of any $F \in \mathcal{S}_D(f)$ with $F \neq 0$; note that having $f(z) f(-z) = 1$ on a nonempty open set extends to $f(z)f(-z) = 1$ everywhere. For (iii), let $F \in \mathcal{T}_D(f) \cap \mathcal{S}_D(g) \setminus \{0\}$, and use these two symmetries of $F$ to obtain \[ \begin{aligned} g(z)F(-z) = F(z) &= f(z)F(z+\tau) \\ &= f(z)g(z+\tau) F(-z-\tau) = f(z)g(z+\tau)f(-z-\tau)F(-z), \end{aligned} \] as an identity of meromorphic functions in $z \in D \cap (-D) \cap (D-\tau) \cap (-D-\tau)$. Since this is a nonempty open set and $F$ is not the zero function, we can cancel $F(-z)$ and multiply by $g(-z-\tau)$ to obtain the desired claim (note that $g(z+\tau)g(-z-\tau) = 1$ as meromorphic functions by (ii)).
nodes.statement_short: Iterate the functional equations of a nonzero $F$ and cancel $F(-z)$.

nodes.name: Parts (i)-(iii) setup
nodes.statement: Statement (i) is clear, and (ii) follows by iterating the functional equation of any $F \in \mathcal{S}_D(f)$ with $F \neq 0$; note that having $f(z) f(-z) = 1$ on a nonempty open set extends to $f(z)f(-z) = 1$ everywhere. For (iii), let $F \in \mathcal{T}_D(f) \cap \mathcal{S}_D(g) \setminus \{0\}$, and use these two symmetries of $F$ to obtain \[ \begin{aligned} g(z)F(-z) = F(z) &= f(z)F(z+\tau) \\ &= f(z)g(z+\tau) F(-z-\tau) = f(z)g(z+\tau)f(-z-\tau)F(-z), \end{aligned} \] as an identity of meromorphic functions in $z \in D \cap (-D) \cap (D-\tau) \cap (-D-\tau)$.
nodes.statement_short: (i), (ii) by iterating functional equations; for (iii) combine both symmetries

nodes.name: Cancel F(-z)
nodes.statement: Since this is a nonempty open set and $F$ is not the zero function, we can cancel $F(-z)$ and multiply by $g(-z-\tau)$ to obtain the desired claim (note that $g(z+\tau)g(-z-\tau) = 1$ as meromorphic functions by (ii)).
nodes.statement_short: Cancel $F(-z)$ to obtain the relation

nodes.name: Remark: monomial choices satisfying the S_D conditions
nodes.statement: A choice of meromorphic functions $f$, $g$ which satisfy the conditions in \cref{lem:basic-S}.(ii)-(iii) is given by $f(z) = \pm q^{c} x^d$ and $g(z) = \pm x^{d-2c}$, for $c, d \in \mathbb{Z}$. These come up in the next result.

nodes.name: Spaces given by monomials
nodes.statement: Let $d$ be any integer, and $D$ be a $\mathbb{Z}$-invariant domain containing an open horizontal strip $S$ of width $> \textnormal{Im}\ \tau$. \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] For any $\alpha \in \mathbb{C}^\times$ (which may depend on the fixed $q$), one has \[ \dim \mathcal{T}_D\big(\alpha x^d\big) = \begin{cases} d, \qquad &d > 0, \\ \mathbbm{1}_{\alpha \in \left\{q^n : n \in \mathbb{Z} \right\}}, \qquad &d = 0, \\ 0, \qquad &d < 0. \end{cases} \] Moreover, for $d \ge 0$, any $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right) \setminus \{0\}$ has exactly $d$ zeros (counting multiplicities) in every fundamental region $\{w - t - u\tau : t, u \in [0, 1) \}$, for $w \in \mathbb{C}$. \item[(ii)] For $c \in \mathbb{Z}$ and $s, t \in \{\pm 1\}$, \begin{equation} \dim \left( \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}} \big(sq^c x^d \big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}} \big(tx^{d-2c}\big) \right) = \max\left( 1 + \left\lfloor \frac{d}{2} \right\rfloor - \mathbbm{1}_{2 \mid d} \mathbbm{1}_{t = -1} - \mathbbm{1}_{st = -1} ,\ 0\right). \end{equation} So for $d \in \{1, 2\}$, one obtains $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(s q^cx\right) \subset \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(s x^{1-2c}\right)$ and $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(q^cx^2\right) \subset \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^{2-2c}\right)$. Moreover, all elements of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}} \big(sq^c x^d \big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}} \big(tx^{d-2c}\big)$ have common zeros at: \[ \begin{cases} z = m\tau + n, &\textnormal{if }\ t = -1, \\ z = m\tau + n + \frac{1}{2}, &\textnormal{if }\ t = (-1)^{d+1}, \\ z = \left(m + \frac{1}{2}\right)\tau + \frac{n}{2}, &\textnormal{if }\ st = -1, \qquad\qquad\qquad \forall m,n \in \mathbb{Z}. \end{cases} \] \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: $\dim\mathcal T_D(\alpha x^d)=d$ for $d>0$ (with $d$ zeros per fundamental region); dimension formula and common zeros for $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(sq^cx^d)\cap\mathcal S_{\mathbb C}(tx^{d-2c})$.
assumptions: Let $d$ be any integer, and $D$ be a $\mathbb{Z}$-invariant domain containing an open horizontal strip $S$ of width $> \textnormal{Im}\ \tau$.
nodes.label: prop:monomial-spaces

nodes.name: Dimension of T cap S spaces
nodes.statement: \dim \left( \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}} \big(sq^c x^d \big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}} \big(tx^{d-2c}\big) \right) = \max\left( 1 + \left\lfloor \frac{d}{2} \right\rfloor - \mathbbm{1}_{2 \mid d} \mathbbm{1}_{t = -1} - \mathbbm{1}_{st = -1} ,\ 0\right).
nodes.label: eq:dimension

nodes.name: Remark: generalizes Hickerson's Theorems 1.7 and 1.8
nodes.statement: The content of this proposition generalizes that of Theorems 1.7 and 1.8 from \cite{hickerson1988proof}, which take $D = \mathbb{C}$, $t = -1$, $c = 0$, $d > 0$ and $d$ odd for the second part. The case $d > 0$ from (i) is also generalized by \cite[Theorem 3.5]{beauville2013theta} in the language of line bundles.

nodes.name: Proof of Spaces given by monomials
nodes.statement:
For part (i), case $d = 0$ was settled in \cref{ex:constants}. If $d < 0$, suppose that $\dim \mathcal{T}_D\left(\alpha x^{d}ight)

Fixing a nonzero Fourier coefficient $\widehat{F}(n_0)$, we find inductively that $\widehat{F}(n_0 - nd)$ grows on the order of $q^{dn^2/2}$, which contradicts the convergence of the Fourier series of $F$ anywhere since $\left\vert q^dight\vert > 1$. Now suppose that $d > 0$. Take $m = 1$, $P_0(z) = 1$ and $P_1(z) = \alpha x^d$ in \cref{prop:upper-bounds}, and consider $A_n(z) = 1 - \alpha q^n x^d$. We have $\widehat{A_n}(0)

eq 0$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, so \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii) yields that $\dim \mathcal{T}_D\left(\alpha x^d ight) \le d$, with equality iff there exist $\{F_k\}_{0 \le k < d} \subset \mathcal{T}_D\left(\alpha x^d ight)$ such that  egin{equation} \widehat{F_k}(j) = \mathbbm{1}_{j=k}, \qquad  orall j, k \in \{0, 1, \ldots, d-1\}, \end{equation} where the Fourier series are taken in $S$. Such functions are the canonical basis vectors from \cref{sec:intro}, \[ \left\{\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}ight\}_{0 \le k < d} = \left\{\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d inom{n}{2}+k_jn}x^{dn+k}ight\}_{0 \le k < d}, \] given by locally uniformly convergent Fourier series in $z \in \mathbb{C} \supset D$. Thus these are entire $1$-periodic functions satisfying $\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}(z) = \alpha x^d \vect{\alpha x^d}{k}(z+	au)$ and \cref{eq:fourier}, proving that $\dim \mathcal{T}_D\left(\alpha x^dight) = d$. In fact, for any $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, $\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}$ has nonzero Fourier coefficients only at multiples of $d$ plus $k$, so the functions $\{\vect{\alpha x^d}{k_j}\}_{0 \le j < d}$ give a basis of $\mathcal{T}_D\left(\alpha x^dight)$ for any complete residue system $\{k_0, \ldots, k_{d-1}\}$ modulo $d$. Since we have $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^dight) \subset \mathcal{T}_D\left(\alpha x^d ight)$ by \cref{lem:basic}.(i), the equality of dimensions forces an equality of vector spaces; i.e.\ each function in $\mathcal{T}_D\left(\alpha x^d ight)$ can be holomorphically continued to $\mathbb{C}$. Concerning the claim about zeros in (i), the case $d = 0$ is immediate since then $F$ can only be a scalar multiple of $x^n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. For $d > 0$, note that $\left\langle -\alpha x^d; q^d ightangle \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^dight)$ has zeros whenever $x^d = -\alpha^{-1}q^{nd}$ for $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, thus exactly $d$ zeros in any fundamental region as in part (i). A quick computation shows that $S_{-1}\vect{sx^d}{k} = x^{-d} \vect{sx^d}{d-k}$ for $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ (using that $s \in \{\pm 1\}$), and so $\vect{sx^d}{k} + t\vect{sx^d}{d-k} \in \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(tx^dight)$ as anticipated in \cref{tbl:spaces}. In fact, we claim that the functions  egin{equation} \left\{\vect{sx^d}{k} + t\vect{sx^d}{d-k}ight\}_{0 \le k \le \lfloor d/2 floor} \end{equation} span $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(sx^dight) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(tx^dight)$. Indeed, any $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(sx^dight)$ can be written as $\sum_{k=0}^{d-1} \widehat{F}(k) \vect{sx^d}{k}$ and $\sum_{k=1}^d \widehat{F}(k) \vect{sx^d}{k}$, by identifying Fourier coefficients in two basis representations of $F$.
