nodes.name: Part (i), d<=0
nodes.statement: For part (i), case $d = 0$ was settled in \cref{ex:constants}. If $d < 0$, suppose that $\dim \mathcal{T}_D\left(\alpha x^{d}\right) \neq 0$, and let $0 \neq F \in \mathcal{T}_D\left(\alpha x^{d}\right)$. Then as in \cref{eq:recursion} we have $\widehat{F}(n) = \alpha q^{n-d} \widehat{F}(n-d)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Fixing a nonzero Fourier coefficient $\widehat{F}(n_0)$, we find inductively that $\widehat{F}(n_0 - nd)$ grows on the order of $q^{dn^2/2}$, which contradicts the convergence of the Fourier series of $F$ anywhere since $\left\vert q^d\right\vert > 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Case $d=0$ by the example; $d<0$ by coefficient growth contradiction

nodes.name: Part (i), d>0
nodes.statement: Now suppose that $d > 0$. Take $m = 1$, $P_0(z) = 1$ and $P_1(z) = \alpha x^d$ in \cref{prop:upper-bounds}, and consider $A_n(z) = 1 - \alpha q^n x^d$. We have $\widehat{A_n}(0) \neq 0$ and $\widehat{A_n}(d) \neq 0$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, so \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii) yields that $\dim \mathcal{T}_D\left(\alpha x^d \right) \le d$, with equality iff there exist $\{F_k\}_{0 \le k < d} \subset \mathcal{T}_D\left(\alpha x^d \right)$ such that \begin{equation} \widehat{F_k}(j) = \mathbbm{1}_{j=k}, \qquad \forall j, k \in \{0, 1, \ldots, d-1\}, \end{equation} where the Fourier series are taken in $S$. Such functions are the canonical basis vectors from \cref{sec:intro}, \[ \left\{\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}\right\}_{0 \le k < d} = \left\{\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+k_jn}x^{dn+k}\right\}_{0 \le k < d}, \] given by locally uniformly convergent Fourier series in $z \in \mathbb{C} \supset D$. Thus these are entire $1$-periodic functions satisfying $\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}(z) = \alpha x^d \vect{\alpha x^d}{k}(z+\tau)$ and \cref{eq:fourier}, proving that $\dim \mathcal{T}_D\left(\alpha x^d\right) = d$. In fact, for any $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, $\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}$ has nonzero Fourier coefficients only at multiples of $d$ plus $k$, so the functions $\{\vect{\alpha x^d}{k_j}\}_{0 \le j < d}$ give a basis of $\mathcal{T}_D\left(\alpha x^d\right)$ for any complete residue system $\{k_0, \ldots, k_{d-1}\}$ modulo $d$. Since we have $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right) \subset \mathcal{T}_D\left(\alpha x^d \right)$ by \cref{lem:basic}.(i), the equality of dimensions forces an equality of vector spaces; i.e.\ each function in $\mathcal{T}_D\left(\alpha x^d \right)$ can be holomorphically continued to $\mathbb{C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Upper-bound proposition and canonical theta series give $\dim=d$

nodes.name: Zeros in part (i)
nodes.statement: Concerning the claim about zeros in (i), the case $d = 0$ is immediate since then $F$ can only be a scalar multiple of $x^n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. For $d > 0$, note that $\left\langle -\alpha x^d; q^d \right\rangle \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$ has zeros whenever $x^d = -\alpha^{-1}q^{nd}$ for $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, thus exactly $d$ zeros in any fundamental region as in part (i). Since the ratio of any two nonzero functions in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$ is an elliptic function (by \cref{lem:basic}.(vi)), the same is true for any $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right) \setminus \{0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Count zeros via a double product and elliptic quotients

nodes.name: Part (ii) dimension
nodes.statement: For part (ii), the case $d \le 0$ is easily verified, so take $d > 0$. We can also assume WLOG that $c = 0$ due to the linear bijection given by multiplication by $x^c$, \[ \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(sq^c x^d \big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(tx^{d-2c}\big) \xlongrightarrow{x^c} \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(s x^d \big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(tx^{d}\big), \] which also preserves canonical bases and zeros; note that $x^c \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(q^{-c}\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^{2c}\right)$. A quick computation shows that $S_{-1}\vect{sx^d}{k} = x^{-d} \vect{sx^d}{d-k}$ for $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ (using that $s \in \{\pm 1\}$), and so $\vect{sx^d}{k} + t\vect{sx^d}{d-k} \in \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(tx^d\right)$ as anticipated in \cref{tbl:spaces}. In fact, we claim that the functions \begin{equation} \left\{\vect{sx^d}{k} + t\vect{sx^d}{d-k}\right\}_{0 \le k \le \lfloor d/2 \rfloor} \end{equation} span $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(sx^d\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(tx^d\right)$. Indeed, any $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(sx^d\right)$ can be written as $\sum_{k=0}^{d-1} \widehat{F}(k) \vect{sx^d}{k}$ and $\sum_{k=1}^d \widehat{F}(k) \vect{sx^d}{k}$, by identifying Fourier coefficients in two basis representations of $F$. Hence \[ F = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k=0}^{d-1} \left(\widehat{F}(k) \vect{sx^d}{k} + \widehat{F}(d-k) \vect{sx^d}{d-k} \right). \] Assuming additionally that $F \in \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(tx^d\right)$, we find that $\widehat{F}(k) = t\widehat{F}(d-k)$ by identifying Fourier series, and thus $F$ is spanned by the sums in \cref{eq:pair-basis}. Since $\vect{sx^d}{k} + \vect{sx^d}{d-k}$ has null Fourier coefficients anywhere else other than at multiples of $d$ plus-minus $k$, it is clear that the vectors in \cref{eq:pair-basis} are linearly independent \emph{provided} that they are nonzero. But to have $\vect{sx^d}{k} + t\vect{sx^d}{d-k} = 0$ we would need in particular that $k \equiv d-k \pmod{d}$, so $k \in \{0, d/2\}$. Treating these two cases separately leads to the two terms subtracted from $1 + \lfloor d/2 \rfloor$ in \cref{eq:dimension}. For $d \in \{1, 2\}$ one has $1 + \lfloor d/2 \rfloor = d$, so for the right choices of $s, t \in \{\pm 1\}$ one can force an equality of vector spaces $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(sq^c x^d \right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(tx^{d-2c} \right) = \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(sq^c x^d \right)$, proving the claimed inclusions.
nodes.statement_short: Pair canonical vectors under $S_{-1}$ to compute the dimension

nodes.name: Reduce to c=0
nodes.statement: For part (ii), the case $d \le 0$ is easily verified, so take $d > 0$. We can also assume WLOG that $c = 0$ due to the linear bijection given by multiplication by $x^c$, \[ \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(sq^c x^d \big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(tx^{d-2c}\big) \xlongrightarrow{x^c} \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(s x^d \big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(tx^{d}\big), \] which also preserves canonical bases and zeros; note that $x^c \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(q^{-c}\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^{2c}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $d>0$, $c=0$ via multiplication by $x^c$

nodes.name: S-symmetry of canonical vectors
nodes.statement: A quick computation shows that $S_{-1}\vect{sx^d}{k} = x^{-d} \vect{sx^d}{d-k}$ for $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ (using that $s \in \{\pm 1\}$), and so $\vect{sx^d}{k} + t\vect{sx^d}{d-k} \in \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(tx^d\right)$ as anticipated in \cref{tbl:spaces}.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $S_{-1}$ on canonical vectors

nodes.name: Paired vectors span
nodes.statement: In fact, we claim that the functions \begin{equation} \left\{\vect{sx^d}{k} + t\vect{sx^d}{d-k}\right\}_{0 \le k \le \lfloor d/2 \rfloor} \end{equation} span $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(sx^d\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(tx^d\right)$. Indeed, any $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(sx^d\right)$ can be written as $\sum_{k=0}^{d-1} \widehat{F}(k) \vect{sx^d}{k}$ and $\sum_{k=1}^d \widehat{F}(k) \vect{sx^d}{k}$, by identifying Fourier coefficients in two basis representations of $F$. Hence \[ F = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k=0}^{d-1} \left(\widehat{F}(k) \vect{sx^d}{k} + \widehat{F}(d-k) \vect{sx^d}{d-k} \right). \] Assuming additionally that $F \in \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(tx^d\right)$, we find that $\widehat{F}(k) = t\widehat{F}(d-k)$ by identifying Fourier series, and thus $F$ is spanned by the sums in \cref{eq:pair-basis}.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: the paired vectors span $\mathcal T\cap\mathcal S$

nodes.name: Symmetrize expansion
nodes.statement: Indeed, any $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(sx^d\right)$ can be written as $\sum_{k=0}^{d-1} \widehat{F}(k) \vect{sx^d}{k}$ and $\sum_{k=1}^d \widehat{F}(k) \vect{sx^d}{k}$, by identifying Fourier coefficients in two basis representations of $F$. Hence \[ F = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{k=0}^{d-1} \left(\widehat{F}(k) \vect{sx^d}{k} + \widehat{F}(d-k) \vect{sx^d}{d-k} \right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Average two basis representations of $F$

nodes.name: Use S-symmetry
nodes.statement: Assuming additionally that $F \in \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(tx^d\right)$, we find that $\widehat{F}(k) = t\widehat{F}(d-k)$ by identifying Fourier series, and thus $F$ is spanned by the sums in \cref{eq:pair-basis}.
nodes.statement_short: The $\mathcal S$-symmetry pairs coefficients

nodes.name: Independence and degenerate cases
nodes.statement: Since $\vect{sx^d}{k} + \vect{sx^d}{d-k}$ has null Fourier coefficients anywhere else other than at multiples of $d$ plus-minus $k$, it is clear that the vectors in \cref{eq:pair-basis} are linearly independent \emph{provided} that they are nonzero. But to have $\vect{sx^d}{k} + t\vect{sx^d}{d-k} = 0$ we would need in particular that $k \equiv d-k \pmod{d}$, so $k \in \{0, d/2\}$. Treating these two cases separately leads to the two terms subtracted from $1 + \lfloor d/2 \rfloor$ in \cref{eq:dimension}.
nodes.statement_short: Independence except for $k\in\{0,d/2\}$, giving the formula

nodes.name: Inclusions for d=1,2
nodes.statement: For $d \in \{1, 2\}$ one has $1 + \lfloor d/2 \rfloor = d$, so for the right choices of $s, t \in \{\pm 1\}$ one can force an equality of vector spaces $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(sq^c x^d \right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(tx^{d-2c} \right) = \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(sq^c x^d \right)$, proving the claimed inclusions.
nodes.statement_short: Dimensions match, giving the inclusions

nodes.name: Common zeros
nodes.statement: Finally, for the statement about common zeros in (ii), consider the maps \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} [column sep = huge, row sep = tiny] \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big({-s}x^{d-1}\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(x^{d-1}\big) \arrow{r}{\left\langle x; q \right\rangle} & \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(sx^d\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big({-x^d}\big), \\ \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(sx^{d-1}\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big({(-1)^{d+1}x^{d-1}}\big) \arrow{r}{\left\langle -x; q \right\rangle} & \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(sx^d\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big({(-1)^{d+1}x^d}\big), \\ \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big({-s}x^{d-2}\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big({-s}x^{d-2}\big) \arrow{r}{x\left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle} & \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(sx^d\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big({-sx^d}\big), \end{tikzcd} \end{center} where we used that $\left\langle \pm x; q\right\rangle \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\mp x\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\mp x\right)$ and $x\left\langle qx^2; q^2\right\rangle \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(-x^2\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^2\right)$. These are injective linear maps of vector spaces of equal finite dimensions by \cref{eq:dimension} (e.g., for the first map both spaces have dimension $\max\left(\lfloor(d+1)/2\rfloor - \mathbbm{1}_{s = 1}, 0\right)$). Thus the three maps above are bijections, and determining the zeros of $\left\langle x; q\right\rangle$, $\left\langle -x; q\right\rangle$ and $\left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle$ completes our proof.
nodes.statement_short: Bijective multiplication maps transfer the zeros of double products

nodes.name: Canonical Fourier normalization
nodes.statement: \widehat{F_k}(j) = \mathbbm{1}_{j=k}, \qquad \forall j, k \in \{0, 1, \ldots, d-1\},
nodes.label: eq:fourier

nodes.name: Paired basis of T cap S
nodes.statement: \left\{\vect{sx^d}{k} + t\vect{sx^d}{d-k}\right\}_{0 \le k \le \lfloor d/2 \rfloor}
nodes.label: eq:pair-basis

nodes.name: Bijections between T cap S spaces by multiplicative factors
nodes.statement: For $c, d \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $d \ge 1$, the map \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} [column sep = huge] \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big({-q^c x^d}\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(x^{d-2c}\big) \arrow{r}{x^{-1}\left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle^{-1}} & \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big({q^c x^{d-2}}\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(x^{d-2-2c}\big) \end{tikzcd} \end{center} which divides by $x\left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle$, is a bijection of $\lfloor d/2 \rfloor$-dimensional vector spaces. If $d$ is odd, \begin{center} \small \begin{tikzcd} [column sep = huge] \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big({-q^c x^d}\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(x^{d-2c}\big) \arrow{r}{x^{-1}\left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle^{-1}} \arrow{rd}[swap]{\left\langle -x; q \right\rangle^{-1}} & \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big({q^c x^{d-2}}\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(x^{d-2c-2}\big) \arrow{r}{\left\langle -x; q \right\rangle^{-1}} & \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big({q^c x^{d-3}}\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(x^{d-2c-3}\big) \\ & \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big({-q^c x^{d-1}}\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(x^{d-2c-1}\big) \arrow{ru}[swap]{x^{-1}\left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle^{-1}} \end{tikzcd} \end{center} give more such bijections by multiplicative factors.
nodes.statement_short: Dividing by $x\langle qx^2;q^2\rangle$ (and by $\langle -x;q\rangle$ for odd $d$) gives bijections of $\lfloor d/2\rfloor$-dimensional $\mathcal T\cap\mathcal S$ spaces.
nodes.label: cor:bijections

nodes.name: Spaces given by polynomials
nodes.statement: Suppose $f(z)$ is a Laurent polynomial in $x = e^{2\pi i z}$ with $\deg_x f = d \ge 1$, such that $f(z)$ has no zeros in $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < -\textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$. Then one has \[ \dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(f \right) = d \qquad \text{ and } \qquad \dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(f \right) \le d, \] and if $d \ge 2$, equality is reached in the right side if and only if $f$ is a monomial in $x$. Moreover, any nonzero $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f)$ has exactly $d$ zeros (counting multiplicity) in any fundamental region $\{w - t - u\tau : t, u \in [0, 1) \}$, for $w \in {\mathbb{H}}^-$.
nodes.statement_short: For a Laurent polynomial $f$ of degree $d$ without zeros below $-\textnormal{Im}\,\tau$: $\dim\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^-}(f)=d$, $\dim\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(f)\le d$ with equality iff monomial.
assumptions: $f(z)$ is a Laurent polynomial in $x = e^{2\pi i z}$ with $\deg_x f = d \ge 1$
nodes.label: prop:polynomial-spaces

nodes.name: Proof of Spaces given by polynomials
nodes.statement: Write $f(z) = \alpha x^d \cdot g(-z)$, where $\alpha = \widehat{f}(d)$ and $g(z)$ is a polynomial in $x$ with free coefficient $\widehat{g}(0) = 1$. Then consider the function \[ G(z) := \prod_{n \ge 1} g(-z + n\tau) = \prod_{n \ge 1} \left(1 + \widehat{g}(1) q^nx^{-1} + \widehat{g}(2) q^{2n}x^{-2} + \cdots \right), \] where the product converges locally uniformly in $\mathbb{C}$ (given that $\sum_{n \ge 1} q^n$ converges); note that $G$ is designed to satisfy $G(z)g(-z) = G(z+\tau)$, hence $G \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(g(-z)^{-1}\right)$. Moreover, since $f(z)$ is nonzero on $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < - \textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$, each $g(-z+n\tau)$ is nonzero on $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < (n-1)\textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$, so $G$ is nonzero on $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < 0\} = {\mathbb{H}}^-$ by standard properties of infinite products, and thus $G^{-1} \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(g(-z)\right)$. Applying \cref{lem:basic}.(iii) twice, we find that multiplication by $G(z)$ induces a bijective linear map \begin{equation} \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}} (f) \xlongrightarrow{\cdot\ G(z)} \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\big(\alpha x^d \big) = \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(\alpha x^d \big), \end{equation} proving $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f) = \dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right) = d$ by \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}. By \cref{lem:basic}.(i), this immediately implies that $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f) \le d$. Now say $f(z)$ is not a monomial in $x$, so it must have a zero $z_0 \in \mathbb{C}$, which results in a zero $w_0$ of $G(z)$. For $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, consider the product \[ F_k(z) := x^k \big\langle {-\alpha} q^k x^d; q^d \big\rangle \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(q^{-k} \cdot \alpha q^k x^d\big) = \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(\alpha x^d\big). \] Then $F_0(z)$ has zeros precisely when $-\alpha x^d = q^{nd}$ for some $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, i.e.\ when $z = u + (dn\tau + 2m\pi i)/d$ for some $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ and a fixed $u \in \mathbb{C}$. Hence $F_k(z) = x^k F_0(z + k\tau/d) = 0$ iff $z = u + ((dn-k)+ 2m\pi i)/d$ for some $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, which implies that $F_j$ and $F_k$ have no common zeros when $j \not\equiv k \pmod{d}$. So assuming $d \ge 2$, there is some $F_j$ with $F_j(w_0) \neq 0$, which implies that \[ F_j \cdot G^{-1} \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f) \setminus \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f) \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f) < d. \] This settles the equality case of $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f) \le d$ (together with \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}.(i)). The statement about zeros in fundamental regions of ${\mathbb{H}}^-$ follows from the analogous statement in \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}.(i) and the bijection in \cref{eq:bijection} (since $G$ has no zeros in ${\mathbb{H}}^-$).
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by an infinite product $G$ to biject $\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^-}(f)$ with $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(\alpha x^d)$; use zeros of $G$ to exhibit non-entire elements when $f$ is not a monomial.

nodes.name: Construct G
nodes.statement: Write $f(z) = \alpha x^d \cdot g(-z)$, where $\alpha = \widehat{f}(d)$ and $g(z)$ is a polynomial in $x$ with free coefficient $\widehat{g}(0) = 1$. Then consider the function \[ G(z) := \prod_{n \ge 1} g(-z + n\tau) = \prod_{n \ge 1} \left(1 + \widehat{g}(1) q^nx^{-1} + \widehat{g}(2) q^{2n}x^{-2} + \cdots \right), \] where the product converges locally uniformly in $\mathbb{C}$ (given that $\sum_{n \ge 1} q^n$ converges); note that $G$ is designed to satisfy $G(z)g(-z) = G(z+\tau)$, hence $G \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(g(-z)^{-1}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Factor $f$ and define the infinite product $G$

nodes.name: G nonvanishing on lower half-plane
nodes.statement: Moreover, since $f(z)$ is nonzero on $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < - \textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$, each $g(-z+n\tau)$ is nonzero on $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < (n-1)\textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$, so $G$ is nonzero on $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < 0\} = {\mathbb{H}}^-$ by standard properties of infinite products, and thus $G^{-1} \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(g(-z)\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: $G$ has no zeros in $\mathbb H^-$

nodes.name: Bijection by G
nodes.statement: Applying \cref{lem:basic}.(iii) twice, we find that multiplication by $G(z)$ induces a bijective linear map \begin{equation} \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}} (f) \xlongrightarrow{\cdot\ G(z)} \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\big(\alpha x^d \big) = \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(\alpha x^d \big), \end{equation} proving $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f) = \dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right) = d$ by \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplication by $G$ is a bijection onto $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(\alpha x^d)$

nodes.name: Bound for T_C(f)
nodes.statement: By \cref{lem:basic}.(i), this immediately implies that $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f) \le d$.
nodes.statement_short: Restriction gives $\dim\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(f)\le d$

nodes.name: Non-monomial case
nodes.statement: Now say $f(z)$ is not a monomial in $x$, so it must have a zero $z_0 \in \mathbb{C}$, which results in a zero $w_0$ of $G(z)$. For $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, consider the product \[ F_k(z) := x^k \big\langle {-\alpha} q^k x^d; q^d \big\rangle \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(q^{-k} \cdot \alpha q^k x^d\big) = \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(\alpha x^d\big). \]
nodes.statement_short: A zero of $f$ gives a zero of $G$; introduce products $F_k$

nodes.name: Zeros of F_k
nodes.statement: Then $F_0(z)$ has zeros precisely when $-\alpha x^d = q^{nd}$ for some $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, i.e.\ when $z = u + (dn\tau + 2m\pi i)/d$ for some $m \in \mathbb{Z}$ and a fixed $u \in \mathbb{C}$. Hence $F_k(z) = x^k F_0(z + k\tau/d) = 0$ iff $z = u + ((dn-k)+ 2m\pi i)/d$ for some $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, which implies that $F_j$ and $F_k$ have no common zeros when $j \not\equiv k \pmod{d}$.
nodes.statement_short: The $F_k$ have disjoint zero sets mod $d$

nodes.name: Non-entire element
nodes.statement: So assuming $d \ge 2$, there is some $F_j$ with $F_j(w_0) \neq 0$, which implies that \[ F_j \cdot G^{-1} \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f) \setminus \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f) \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f) < d. \]
nodes.statement_short: Some $F_j/G$ is not entire, so strict inequality

nodes.name: Equality case
nodes.statement: This settles the equality case of $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f) \le d$ (together with \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}.(i)).
nodes.statement_short: Settles the equality case

nodes.name: Zero count
nodes.statement: The statement about zeros in fundamental regions of ${\mathbb{H}}^-$ follows from the analogous statement in \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}.(i) and the bijection in \cref{eq:bijection} (since $G$ has no zeros in ${\mathbb{H}}^-$).
nodes.statement_short: Transfer zero count through the bijection

nodes.name: Bijection by multiplication with G
nodes.statement: \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}} (f) \xlongrightarrow{\cdot\ G(z)} \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\big(\alpha x^d \big) = \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(\alpha x^d \big),
nodes.label: eq:bijection

nodes.name: Remark: bijections preserving canonical bases behind the main theorems
nodes.statement: Combining \cref{cor:bijections} with the inclusion $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2\right) \subset \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}(1)$ from \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}, and the map in \cref{eq:bijection}, we obtain bijections by multiplicative factors \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} [column sep = huge, row sep = tiny] \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big({-q}x^5\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(x^3\big) \arrow{rr}{x^{-1}\left([-qx^3;0] + [-qx^3;1]\right)^{-1}} && \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(qx^2\big) \arrow{rr}{(q; q)\left(x^{-1}; q\right)^{-1}} \arrow{rrd}[swap,xshift=0.3cm]{(q; q)\left(x^{-2}; q^2\right)^{-1}} && \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\big(qx^2 - x\big) \\ \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big({-q}x^4\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(x^2\big) \arrow{rru}[swap]{x^{-1}[-qx^2;0]^{-1}} && && \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\big(qx^2 - q^{-1}\big) \end{tikzcd} \end{center} where we used that $\left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle = \vect{-qx^2}{0}$ and $(q; q)\left\langle -x; q\right\rangle\left\langle qx^2; q^2\right\rangle = \vect{-qx^3}{0} + \vect{-qx^3}{1}$ by \cref{eq:triple,eq:quintuple} with adequate substitutions. What is special about the two resulting bijections (following the top and the bottom maps above) is that they preserve canonical bases: $\left\{\vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2}, \vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3}\right\}$ go to $\left\{\vect{qx^2 - x}{0}, \vect{qx^2-x}{1}\right\}$ by the top chain of maps, while $\left\{\vect{-qx^4}{1}, \vect{-qx^4}{0} + \vect{-qx^4}{2}\right\}$ go to $\left\{\vect{qx^2 - q^{-1}}{0}, \vect{qx^2-q^{-1}}{1}\right\}$ by the bottom one. This is the content of our main results in \cref{thm:bases-proportional,thm:bases-proportional-2}. \begin{figure}[ht] \centering \includegraphics[scale = 0.6]{5Zeros} \qquad\qquad \includegraphics[scale = 0.6]{2Zeros} \caption{Plots of $\vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2}$ (left) and $(q; q)\left(x^{-1}; q\right)\vect{qx^2 - x}{0}$ (right) on $\{\textnormal{Re}\ z, \textnormal{Im}\ z \in [0, 1)\}$, for $\tau = i$ (\emph{using domain coloring; plot made in Wolfram Mathematica}).} \end{figure} \FloatBarrier As predicted by \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}.(i), $\vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2} \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(-qx^5\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^3\right)$ has five zeros in the fundamental region $\{t + u\tau : t,u \in [0, 1)\}$. Three of these zeros, at $z \in \left\{1/2, \tau/2, (1+\tau)/2\right\}$, correspond to the zeros of $\vect{-qx^3}{0} + \vect{-qx^3}{1}$ and are eliminated by the bijection in \cref{cor:bijections}; the remaining two nontrivial zeros coincide with the zeros of $\left(x^{-1}; q\right)\vect{qx^2 - x}{0} \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2\right)$, as seen in \cref{fig:plots}. For $\tau = i$, the nontrivial zeros lie approximately $0.24657 + 0.5i$ and $0.75343 + 0.5i$; note that they sum up to $1 + i$ since $\left(x^{-1}; q\right)\vect{qx^2 - x}{0}$ has a symmetry by a nonzero multiplicative factor at $z \mapsto 1 + \tau - z$ (by combining $1$-periodicity with the symmetries from $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2\right) \subset \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}(1)$).
nodes.statement_short: Chains of multiplicative bijections send the paired bases of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(-qx^5)$, $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(-qx^4)$ to the canonical bases of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^-}(qx^2-x)$, $\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^-}(qx^2-q^{-1})$; zeros illustrated numerically.

nodes.name: Canonical basis
nodes.statement: Let $f(z)$ be a polynomial in $x = e^{2\pi i z}$ with $\deg_x f = d \ge 1$, such that $f(z)$ has no zeros in $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < -\textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$, and $\widehat{f}(0) \not\in \left\{q^{-n} : n \ge d \right\}$. Then $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f)$ has a canonical basis $\{\vect{f}{k}\}_{0 \le k < d}$ uniquely determined by \[ \widehat{\vect{f}{k}}(j) = \mathbbm{1}_{j=k} \quad \text{ in } {\mathbb{H}}^-, \qquad\quad \forall j, k \in \{0, 1, \ldots, d-1\}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Under nonvanishing conditions on $f$, $\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^-}(f)$ has a unique basis $[f;k]$ with $\widehat{[f;k]}(j)=\mathbb 1_{j=k}$ for $0\le j<d$.
assumptions: Let $f(z)$ be a polynomial in $x = e^{2\pi i z}$ with $\deg_x f = d \ge 1$
nodes.label: prop:canonical-basis-vectors

nodes.name: Proof of Canonical basis
nodes.statement: \cref{prop:polynomial-spaces} implies that $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f) = d$, so we aim to apply the `only if' part of the equality case in \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii). We have $P_0(z) = 1$ and $P_1(z) = f(z)$, so for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, \[ A_n(z) = P_0(z) - q^n P_1(z) = 1 - q^n \left(\widehat{f}(0) + \widehat{f}(1)x + \cdots + \widehat{f}(d)x^d \right). \] Our assumptions imply that $\widehat{A_n}(0) = 1 - q^n \widehat{f}(0) \neq 0$ for all $n \ge d$, and $\widehat{A_n}(d) = q^n \widehat{f}(d) \neq 0$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Hence using $n_0 = 0$, the conditions of \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii) are fulfilled.
nodes.statement_short: Apply the equality case of the upper-bound proposition with $n_0=0$, checking the nonvanishing of $\widehat{A_n}(0)$ and $\widehat{A_n}(d)$.

nodes.name: Reduce to upper-bound criterion
nodes.statement: \cref{prop:polynomial-spaces} implies that $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f) = d$, so we aim to apply the `only if' part of the equality case in \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii).
nodes.statement_short: Dimension is $d$; apply the equality case of the upper bound

nodes.name: Compute A_n
nodes.statement: We have $P_0(z) = 1$ and $P_1(z) = f(z)$, so for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, \[ A_n(z) = P_0(z) - q^n P_1(z) = 1 - q^n \left(\widehat{f}(0) + \widehat{f}(1)x + \cdots + \widehat{f}(d)x^d \right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Write out $A_n$

nodes.name: Check conditions
nodes.statement: Our assumptions imply that $\widehat{A_n}(0) = 1 - q^n \widehat{f}(0) \neq 0$ for all $n \ge d$, and $\widehat{A_n}(d) = q^n \widehat{f}(d) \neq 0$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$. Hence using $n_0 = 0$, the conditions of \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii) are fulfilled.
nodes.statement_short: Hypotheses give nonvanishing with $n_0=0$

nodes.name: Remark: expansion in the canonical basis
nodes.statement: In the proof of \cref{prop:polynomial-spaces}, dividing the canonical basis of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$ by $G(z)$ yields a basis of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f)$, but this usually differs from the canonical basis $\{\vect{f}{k}\}_{0 \le k < d}$ (when well-defined); in fact, computing the relationship between these two bases is one of the main difficulties in proving \cref{thm:bases-proportional,thm:bases-proportional-2}. The advantage of expressing product identities in terms of the canonical basis is that for any $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f)$, by identifying Fourier coefficients one can write \begin{equation} F = \sum_{k=0}^{d-1} \widehat{F}(k) \vect{f}{k}, \end{equation} and the coefficients $\{\widehat{F}(k)\}_k$ may be objects of interest (in \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram-var} for example, they are the two Rogers--Ramanujan series from \cref{eq:rog-ram}). In particular, if $f(z)$ is a second-degree polynomial in $x$ with no zeros in $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < -\textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$ and $\widehat{f}(0) \not\in \left\{q^{-n} : n \ge 2\right\}$, \cref{prop:polynomial-spaces,prop:canonical-basis-vectors} imply that $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f) \le 1$ and $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f) = 2$, with a basis $\{\vect{f}{0}, \vect{f}{1}\}$. So if we are given an entire function $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f)$, it must be unique up to a scalar, and it is natural to express it as in \cref{eq:fourier-coeffs-basis}; this is the subject of \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram} for $f(z) = qx^2 - x$.

nodes.name: Expansion of F in the canonical basis
nodes.statement: F = \sum_{k=0}^{d-1} \widehat{F}(k) \vect{f}{k},
nodes.label: eq:fourier-coeffs-basis

nodes.name: Canonical basis vectors of T(qx^2 - x): poles and residues
nodes.statement: For $f(z) = qx^2 - x$ and $k \in \{0, 1\}$, $\vect{qx^2-x}{k}$ is a well-defined holomorphic function in ${\mathbb{H}}^-$ by \cref{prop:polynomial-spaces}. By \cref{lem:basic}.(v), it can be continued meromorphically to $\mathbb{C}$, with simple poles at $z = n\tau + m$ for $n, m \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $n \ge 0$; these poles are cancelled when multiplying by $\left(x^{-1}; q\right)$, as expected since we know $\left(x^{-1}; q\right)\vect{qx^2 - x}{k} \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2\right)$ is entire. Using \cref{eq:triple}, \cref{eq:quintuple}, and our main result in \cref{thm:bases-proportional}, one can easily compute the residues of these functions at the periodic poles $z \in \mathbb{Z}$; up to a factor of $2\pi i$, these are \[ \lim_{x \to 1} (x-1)\vect{qx^2 - x}{k} = \begin{cases} \left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1}, &k = 0, \\ \left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1}, &k = 1, \end{cases} \] which is consistent with the pole cancellation in \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram}. One can also verify this numerically as an identity of $q$-series: expand $F(z) := \vect{qx^2-x}{k} = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \widehat{F}(n) x^n$ in ${\mathbb{H}}^-$ and write \[ \lim_{x \to 1} (x-1)\vect{qx^2 - x}{k} = \lim_{n \to -\infty} \widehat{F}(n), \] since $(x-1)\vect{qx^2 - x}{k}$ has the Fourier series $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \big(\widehat{F}(n-1) - \widehat{F}(n)\big) x^n$ in $\left\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < \textnormal{Im}\ \tau \right\} \supset \mathbb{Z}$, and $\widehat{F}(n) \to 0$ as $n \to \infty$ (note that $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \widehat{F}(n) x^n$ converges absolutely for $z \in {\mathbb{H}}^-$, i.e.\ $|x| > 1$). \begin{table}[ht] \centering \tiny \captionsetup{width=\linewidth} nodes.name: Formulae for canonical vectors, first kind
nodes.statement: Suppose $f(z) = \alpha x^d + \beta$ is a polynomial in $x$ of degree $d \ge 1$ and free coefficient $\beta \in \mathbb{C} \setminus \left\{ q^{-n} : n \ge d \right\}$, such that $f(z) \neq 0$ in $\left\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < -\textnormal{Im}\ \tau\right\}$. Then for $0 \le k < d$, one has \begin{equation} \vect{\alpha x^d + \beta}{k} \ =\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n \frac{q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn}}{\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d\right)_n} x^{dn+k} \ =\ \frac{\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}}{\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d \right) \left(-\alpha^{-1}\beta x^{-d} q^d; q^d \right)}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For $f=\alpha x^d+\beta$, $[f;k]$ is an explicit series with $(\beta q^{d+k};q^d)_n$ denominators, equal to $[\alpha x^d;k]$ divided by two infinite products.
assumptions: $f(z) = \alpha x^d + \beta$ is a polynomial in $x$ of degree $d \ge 1$
nodes.label: prop:exact-formulae-kind1

nodes.name: First-kind canonical vector formula
nodes.statement: \vect{\alpha x^d + \beta}{k} \ =\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n \frac{q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn}}{\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d\right)_n} x^{dn+k} \ =\ \frac{\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}}{\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d \right) \left(-\alpha^{-1}\beta x^{-d} q^d; q^d \right)}.
nodes.label: eq:kind1

nodes.name: Proof of Formulae for canonical vectors, first kind
nodes.statement:
Note that $\left( eta q^{d+k}; q^dight)_n$ has no zeros for $n \ge 0$ by our assumption on $ eta$, and in fact we have $\left( eta q^{d+k}; q^dight)_n^{-1} = 1 + O(q) = O(1)$ for $n \ge 0$; hence the coefficients of $x^{dn+k}$ in the middle series above decrease like $q^{dn^2/2}$. For $n < 0$, we defined $\left( eta q^{d+k}; q^dight)_n = \left( eta q^{d+k-dn}; q^dight)_{-n}^{-1}$, and thus \[  egin{aligned}  rac{\alpha^n q^{d inom{n}{2}+kn}}{ ig( eta q^{d+k}; q^d  ig)_n} = \alpha^n q^{d inom{n}{2}+kn} \prod_{j=1}^{|n|} \left(1 -  eta q^{d+k-dj}ight) &= \alpha^{-|n|} q^{d inom{|n|+1}{2}-k|n|} \cdot O\left(| eta|^{|n|} |q|^{\sum_{j=1}^{|n|} (d+k-dj)} ight) \ &= O\left(|q^d eta/\alpha|^{|n|} ight). \end{aligned} \] assuming without loss of generality that $ eta 
eq 0$ (when the given series coincides with $\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}$). But since $\alpha x^d +  eta 
eq 0$ in the range $\{	extnormal{Im}\ z < -	extnormal{Im}\ 	au\}$ (when $|x^d|$ spans $\left(|q|^{-d}, +\inftyight)$), we must have $| eta/\alpha| \le |q|^{-d}$, i.e.\ $|q^d  eta / \alpha| \le 1$. Hence the bound above reduces to $O(1)$. This shows that the middle series in \cref{eq:kind1} converges absolutely and locally uniformly to a holomorphic function $R(z)$ for $z \in {\mathbb{H}}^-$ (using that $|x^{-1}| < 1$ to bound $\sum_{n < 0} x^{dn+k}$, and the quadratic-exponent decrease of $q^{dn(n-1)/2} x^n$ for $n \ge 0$). We clearly have $\widehat{R}(j) = \mathbbm{1}_{j=k}$ for $0 \le j < d$, so to prove the first equality in \cref{eq:kind1} it remains to show that $R \in \mathcal{T}_{{\mathbb{H}^{	extnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}}(\alpha x^d +  eta)$. Indeed, we have \[  egin{aligned} \left(\alpha x^d +  etaight) R(z+	au) &= \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^{n+1}  rac{q^{d inom{n+1}{2}+k(n+1)}}{\left( eta q^{d+k}; q^dight)_n} x^{d(n+1)+k} +  eta \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n  rac{q^{d inom{n+1}{2}+k(n+1)}}{\left( eta q^{d+k}; q^dight)_n} x^{dn+k} \ &= \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n  rac{q^{d inom{n}{2}+kn}}{\left( eta q^{d+k}; q^dight)_n} x^{dn+k} \left(1 -  eta q^{d+k+d(n-1)} +  eta q^{dn+k} ight) \quad = R(z). \end{aligned} \] For the second equality in \cref{eq:kind1}, we require two simple identities that will be proven (non-circularly) in the next subsection: \cref{eq:basic1} and \cref{eq:basic2}. For $z \in {\mathbb{H}}^-$, consider the function \[ F(z) :=  rac{\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}}{\left(-\alpha^{-1} eta x^{-d} q^d; q^dight)} \ \stackrel{	ext{by \cref{eq:basic2}}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=} \ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d inom{n}{2} + kn} x^{dn+k} \cdot \sum_{n \ge 0}  rac{1}{\left(q^d; q^dight)_n}  ig({-\alpha^{-1} eta} x^{-d} q^d  ig)^n. \] We have $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{	extnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(\alpha x^d\left(1 + \alpha^{-1} eta x^{-d}ight) ight) = \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{	extnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(\alpha x^d +  eta ight)$ by \cref{tbl:spaces}, and thus $F$ has a basis representation as in \cref{eq:fourier-coeffs-basis}. But by multiplying out the Fourier series above, we see that \[  orall j \in \{0, 1, \ldots, d-1\} : \qquad\quad \widehat{F}(j) =  egin{cases} 0, &j 
eq k, \ \sum_{n \ge 0}  rac{q^{d inom{n}{2}}}{\left(q^d; q^dight)_n} \left(- eta q^{d+k}ight)^n, &j = k, \end{cases} \] and the latter sum reduces to $\left( eta q^{d+k}; q^d ight)$ by \cref{eq:basic1}. nodes.statement_short: Show the series converges in $\mathbb H^-$, has the right Fourier normalization and satisfies the functional equation; then identify it with $[\alpha x^d;k]$ over an infinite product using the q-binomial expansions.

nodes.name: Terms n>=0
nodes.statement: Note that $\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d\right)_n$ has no zeros for $n \ge 0$ by our assumption on $\beta$, and in fact we have $\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d\right)_n^{-1} = 1 + O(q) = O(1)$ for $n \ge 0$; hence the coefficients of $x^{dn+k}$ in the middle series above decrease like $q^{dn^2/2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the coefficients for $n\ge0$

nodes.name: Terms n<0
nodes.statement: For $n < 0$, we defined $\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d\right)_n = \left(\beta q^{d+k-dn}; q^d\right)_{-n}^{-1}$, and thus \[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn}}{\big(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d \big)_n} = \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} \prod_{j=1}^{|n|} \left(1 - \beta q^{d+k-dj}\right) &= \alpha^{-|n|} q^{d\binom{|n|+1}{2}-k|n|} \cdot O\left(|\beta|^{|n|} |q|^{\sum_{j=1}^{|n|} (d+k-dj)} \right) \\ &= O\left(|q^d\beta/\alpha|^{|n|} \right). \end{aligned} \] assuming without loss of generality that $\beta \neq 0$ (when the given series coincides with $\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}$). But since $\alpha x^d + \beta \neq 0$ in the range $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < -\textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$ (when $|x^d|$ spans $\left(|q|^{-d}, +\infty\right)$), we must have $|\beta/\alpha| \le |q|^{-d}$, i.e.\ $|q^d \beta / \alpha| \le 1$. Hence the bound above reduces to $O(1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the coefficients for $n<0$ using $|q^d\beta/\alpha|\le1$

nodes.name: Convergence
nodes.statement: This shows that the middle series in \cref{eq:kind1} converges absolutely and locally uniformly to a holomorphic function $R(z)$ for $z \in {\mathbb{H}}^-$ (using that $|x^{-1}| < 1$ to bound $\sum_{n < 0} x^{dn+k}$, and the quadratic-exponent decrease of $q^{dn(n-1)/2} x^n$ for $n \ge 0$).
nodes.statement_short: The series converges to a holomorphic $R$ on $\mathbb H^-$

nodes.name: Functional equation
nodes.statement: We clearly have $\widehat{R}(j) = \mathbbm{1}_{j=k}$ for $0 \le j < d$, so to prove the first equality in \cref{eq:kind1} it remains to show that $R \in \mathcal{T}_{{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}}(\alpha x^d + \beta)$. Indeed, we have \[ \begin{aligned} \left(\alpha x^d + \beta\right) R(z+\tau) &= \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^{n+1} \frac{q^{d\binom{n+1}{2}+k(n+1)}}{\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d\right)_n} x^{d(n+1)+k} + \beta \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n \frac{q^{d\binom{n+1}{2}+k(n+1)}}{\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d\right)_n} x^{dn+k} \\ &= \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n \frac{q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn}}{\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d\right)_n} x^{dn+k} \left(1 - \beta q^{d+k+d(n-1)} + \beta q^{dn+k} \right) \quad = R(z). \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Check normalization and $R\in\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^-}(\alpha x^d+\beta)$

nodes.name: Product form
nodes.statement: For the second equality in \cref{eq:kind1}, we require two simple identities that will be proven (non-circularly) in the next subsection: \cref{eq:basic1} and \cref{eq:basic2}. For $z \in {\mathbb{H}}^-$, consider the function \[ F(z) := \frac{\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}}{\left(-\alpha^{-1}\beta x^{-d} q^d; q^d\right)} \ \stackrel{\text{by \cref{eq:basic2}}}{=\joinrel=\joinrel=} \ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2} + kn} x^{dn+k} \cdot \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{1}{\left(q^d; q^d\right)_n} \big({-\alpha^{-1}\beta} x^{-d} q^d \big)^n. \]
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $F$ = theta vector over an infinite product, expanded by the q-binomial theorem

nodes.name: F in the space
nodes.statement: We have $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(\alpha x^d\left(1 + \alpha^{-1}\beta x^{-d}\right) \right) = \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(\alpha x^d + \beta \right)$ by \cref{tbl:spaces}, and thus $F$ has a basis representation as in \cref{eq:fourier-coeffs-basis}.
nodes.statement_short: $F$ lies in the same space

nodes.name: Fourier coefficients of F
nodes.statement: But by multiplying out the Fourier series above, we see that \[ \forall j \in \{0, 1, \ldots, d-1\} : \qquad\quad \widehat{F}(j) = \begin{cases} 0, &j \neq k, \\ \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{d\binom{n}{2}}}{\left(q^d; q^d\right)_n} \left(-\beta q^{d+k}\right)^n, &j = k, \end{cases} \] and the latter sum reduces to $\left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d \right)$ by \cref{eq:basic1}.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $\widehat F(j)$ and sum with Euler's formula

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: We thus have $F(z) = \left(\beta q^{d+k}; q^d \right) \vect{\alpha x^d + \beta}{k}$, completing our proof.
nodes.statement_short: $F$ is a multiple of $[\alpha x^d+\beta;k]$

nodes.name: Canonical basis of T(qx^2 - y)
nodes.statement: For $|y| \le |q|^{-1}$, the canonical basis vectors of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(qx^2 - y\right)$ are \[ \begin{aligned} \vect{qx^2 - y}{0} &= \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(-q^2y; q^2\right)_n} x^{2n} \ \ \hspace{0.11cm} = \frac{\vect{qx^2}{0}}{\left(-q^2y; q^2\right)\left(qx^{-2}y; q^2\right)}, \\ \vect{qx^2 - y}{1} &= \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{\left(-q^3y; q^2\right)_n} x^{2n+1} = \frac{\vect{qx^2}{1}}{\left(-q^3y; q^2\right)\left(qx^{-2}y; q^2\right)}. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Explicit series and product formulas for $[qx^2-y;0]$ and $[qx^2-y;1]$.
nodes.label: cor:kind1

nodes.name: Remark: sharpness of the canonical basis conditions
nodes.statement: Since we know that $\vect{\alpha x^d + \beta}{k}$ exists based on more abstract arguments (recall the proof of \cref{prop:canonical-basis-vectors}), we could have identified its Fourier series in \cref{eq:kind1} directly from the recurrence relation in \cref{eq:recursion}. However, the first part of the proof of \cref{prop:exact-formulae-kind1} is instructive for the next proposition, where the analogous summation is usually not a Fourier series; also, the fact that the conditions of \cref{prop:canonical-basis-vectors} barely make the series in \cref{eq:kind1} converge shows that they are sharp.

nodes.name: Formulae for canonical vectors, second kind
nodes.statement: Suppose $f(z)$ is a polynomial in $x$ of degree $d \ge 1$ with null free coefficient, and that $f(z)$ has no zeros in $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < - \textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$. Write $f(z) = \alpha x^d g(-z)$, where $\alpha = \widehat{f}(d)$, and let $G(z) := \prod_{n \ge 1} g(-z+n\tau)$. Then for $0 \le k < d$, \begin{equation} \vect{f}{k} = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2} + kn} x^{dn+k} \frac{G\left(z+(n-1)\tau\right)}{G(z)} g_k\left(-z-(n-1)\tau\right), \end{equation} where $g_k(z) := \sum_{j=0}^k \widehat{g}(j) x^{j}$ is the truncation of $g$ to degree $\le k$. In particular, for $\deg_x g \le k < d$, \[ \vect{f}{0} = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}} x^{dn} \frac{G(z+(n-1)\tau)}{G(z)} \qquad \text{and} \qquad \vect{f}{k} = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2} + kn} x^{dn+k} \frac{G(z+n\tau)}{G(z)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: For $f$ with zero constant term, $[f;k]$ is a twisted theta series with factors $G(z+(n-1)\tau)/G(z)$ and truncations $g_k$.
assumptions: $f(z)$ is a polynomial in $x$ of degree $d \ge 1$ with null free coefficient
nodes.label: prop:exact-formulae-kind2

nodes.name: Second-kind canonical vector formula
nodes.statement: \vect{f}{k} = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2} + kn} x^{dn+k} \frac{G\left(z+(n-1)\tau\right)}{G(z)} g_k\left(-z-(n-1)\tau\right),
nodes.label: eq:kind2

nodes.name: Remark: second-kind formula as the second construction
nodes.statement: For $\deg_x g \le k < d$, if $R(z)$ denotes the right-hand side of \cref{eq:kind2}, then $x^{-k} R(z)$ is precisely the second construction in \cref{eq:two-ways} for the factor $q^k f(z)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Formulae for canonical vectors, second kind
nodes.statement: First, recall from the proof of \cref{prop:polynomial-spaces} that $G \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(g(-z)^{-1}\right)$ is well-defined and multiplication by $G$ induces a bijection $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f) \to \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(\alpha x^d)$ as in $\cref{eq:bijection}$. We leave to the reader to verify that the series in the right-hand side of \cref{eq:kind2} converges absolutely and locally uniformly for $z \in {\mathbb{H}}^-$ to a function $R(z)$, which is similar to the proof of \cref{prop:exact-formulae-kind1}; the fact that $\widehat{f}(0) = 0$ and thus $\deg_x g \le d-1$ is crucial here, to ensure that $\widehat{R}(n)$ decreases like $q^{cn^2}$ as $n \to \infty$ for some $c > 0$. Now $R(z)G(z)$ is just a \emph{twisted} version of the series $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} x^{dn+k}$ in the sense of \cref{eq:w-coeffs}; thus $R \cdot G \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$, and so $R \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}} (f)$. It remains to identify the Fourier coefficients $\widehat{R}(j)$ for $0 \le j < d$. Note that the Fourier expansions of $G(z + (n-1)\tau)/G(z)$ and $g_k(-z-(n-1)\tau)$ only contain negative powers of $x$, so only the terms $n \ge 0$ in $\cref{eq:kind2}$ contribute to the Fourier coefficients $\{\widehat{R}(j)\}_{0 \le j < d}$. But for $n \ge 1$, one has \[ x^{dn+k} \frac{G\left(z+(n-1)\tau\right)}{G(z)} g_k\left(-z-(n-1)\tau\right) = x^{dn+k} \Bigg(\prod_{j=2-n}^0 g(-z+j\tau)\Bigg) \Bigg( \sum_{j=0}^k \widehat{g}(j) \left(q^{n-1} x\right)^{-j}\Bigg), \] which only contains powers of $x$ with exponents $\ge dn+k - (d-1)(n-1) - k \ge d$. Hence the only relevant term is the one given by $n = 0$, which is \[ x^k \frac{G(z-\tau)}{G(z)} g_k(-z+\tau) = x^k \frac{g_k(-z+\tau)}{g(-z+\tau)} = x^k - x^k\frac{g(-z+\tau) - g_k(-z+\tau)}{g(-z+\tau)}. \] But by the definition of $g_k$, the difference $g(-z+\tau) - g_k(-z+\tau)$ only contains powers of $x$ with exponents less than $-k$. We conclude that $\widehat{R}(j) = \mathbbm{1}_{j=k}$ for $0 \le j < d$, and thus $R = \vect{f}{k}$.
nodes.statement_short: The series times $G$ is a twisted theta series, hence lies in the right space; only the $n=0$ term contributes to the low Fourier coefficients, giving the normalization.

nodes.name: Recall G
nodes.statement: First, recall from the proof of \cref{prop:polynomial-spaces} that $G \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(g(-z)^{-1}\right)$ is well-defined and multiplication by $G$ induces a bijection $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f) \to \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(\alpha x^d)$ as in $\cref{eq:bijection}$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall $G$ and the bijection

nodes.name: Convergence
nodes.statement: We leave to the reader to verify that the series in the right-hand side of \cref{eq:kind2} converges absolutely and locally uniformly for $z \in {\mathbb{H}}^-$ to a function $R(z)$, which is similar to the proof of \cref{prop:exact-formulae-kind1}; the fact that $\widehat{f}(0) = 0$ and thus $\deg_x g \le d-1$ is crucial here, to ensure that $\widehat{R}(n)$ decreases like $q^{cn^2}$ as $n \to \infty$ for some $c > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: The series converges to $R$ on $\mathbb H^-$

nodes.name: R in the space
nodes.statement: Now $R(z)G(z)$ is just a \emph{twisted} version of the series $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} x^{dn+k}$ in the sense of \cref{eq:w-coeffs}; thus $R \cdot G \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$, and so $R \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}} (f)$.
nodes.statement_short: $RG$ is a twisted theta series, so $R\in\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^-}(f)$

nodes.name: Reduce to coefficients
nodes.statement: It remains to identify the Fourier coefficients $\widehat{R}(j)$ for $0 \le j < d$.
nodes.statement_short: Remains to identify low Fourier coefficients

nodes.name: Only n>=0 contribute
nodes.statement: Note that the Fourier expansions of $G(z + (n-1)\tau)/G(z)$ and $g_k(-z-(n-1)\tau)$ only contain negative powers of $x$, so only the terms $n \ge 0$ in $\cref{eq:kind2}$ contribute to the Fourier coefficients $\{\widehat{R}(j)\}_{0 \le j < d}$.
nodes.statement_short: Negative-index terms contain only negative powers

nodes.name: Terms n>=1
nodes.statement: But for $n \ge 1$, one has \[ x^{dn+k} \frac{G\left(z+(n-1)\tau\right)}{G(z)} g_k\left(-z-(n-1)\tau\right) = x^{dn+k} \Bigg(\prod_{j=2-n}^0 g(-z+j\tau)\Bigg) \Bigg( \sum_{j=0}^k \widehat{g}(j) \left(q^{n-1} x\right)^{-j}\Bigg), \] which only contains powers of $x$ with exponents $\ge dn+k - (d-1)(n-1) - k \ge d$.
nodes.statement_short: Terms $n\ge1$ only contain powers $\ge d$

nodes.name: Term n=0
nodes.statement: Hence the only relevant term is the one given by $n = 0$, which is \[ x^k \frac{G(z-\tau)}{G(z)} g_k(-z+\tau) = x^k \frac{g_k(-z+\tau)}{g(-z+\tau)} = x^k - x^k\frac{g(-z+\tau) - g_k(-z+\tau)}{g(-z+\tau)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Expand the $n=0$ term

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: But by the definition of $g_k$, the difference $g(-z+\tau) - g_k(-z+\tau)$ only contains powers of $x$ with exponents less than $-k$. We conclude that $\widehat{R}(j) = \mathbbm{1}_{j=k}$ for $0 \le j < d$, and thus $R = \vect{f}{k}$.
nodes.statement_short: Normalization holds, so $R=[f;k]$

nodes.name: Canonical basis of T(qx^2 - yx)
nodes.statement: For $|y| \le 1$, the canonical basis vectors of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(qx^2 - yx\right)$ are \[ \vect{qx^2-yx}{0} = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \frac{(q^{-n+1}x^{-1}y; q)}{(x^{-1}y; q)} , \qquad\quad \vect{qx^2-yx}{1} = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2+n} x^{2n+1} \frac{(q^{-n}x^{-1}y; q)}{(x^{-1}y; q)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Explicit series for $[qx^2-yx;0]$ and $[qx^2-yx;1]$.
nodes.label: cor:kind2

nodes.name: Fourier identification
nodes.statement: Suppose $\mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$, $S \subset D$, $d \ge 1$ and $n_0 \in \mathbb{Z}$ are as in the hypothesis of \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii). Then given $F, G \in \mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$, one has $F = G$ iff $\widehat{F}(k) = \widehat{G}(k)$ for all $k \in \{n_0, n_0 + 1, \ldots, n_0 + d-1\}$ (taking Fourier series in the strip $S$). If $d = 1$ and the limits below exist and are nonzero, one also has \[ F = G \qquad \iff \qquad \lim_{n \to \infty} \widehat{F}(n) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \widehat{G}(n). \]
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: Two elements of a $\mathcal T_D$ space satisfying the upper-bound hypotheses agree iff $d$ consecutive Fourier coefficients agree (or, for $d=1$, their limits).
assumptions: $\mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$, $S \subset D$, $d \ge 1$ and $n_0 \in \mathbb{Z}$ are as in the hypothesis of \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii)
nodes.label: lem:proofs-by-fourier

nodes.name: Proof of Fourier identification
nodes.statement: In the proof of \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii), we showed (using the linear relation of Fourier coefficients \cref{eq:recursion}) that $\mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$ injects into $\mathbb{C}^d$ by $F \mapsto \big(\widehat{F}(n_0), \ldots, \widehat{F}(n_0 + d-1)\big)$, proving the first claim. Note that this does \emph{not} require an equality in $\dim \mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m) \le d$. For the second claim, having $d = 1$ implies that $\dim \mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m) \le 1$ by \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii), which easily establishes the desired equivalence.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity of the coefficient map from the upper-bound proof; for $d=1$ the space is at most one-dimensional.

nodes.name: First claim
nodes.statement: In the proof of \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii), we showed (using the linear relation of Fourier coefficients \cref{eq:recursion}) that $\mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m)$ injects into $\mathbb{C}^d$ by $F \mapsto \big(\widehat{F}(n_0), \ldots, \widehat{F}(n_0 + d-1)\big)$, proving the first claim. Note that this does \emph{not} require an equality in $\dim \mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m) \le d$.
nodes.statement_short: Injectivity of the coefficient map
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Second claim
nodes.statement: For the second claim, having $d = 1$ implies that $\dim \mathcal{T}_D(f_1, \ldots, f_m) \le 1$ by \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii), which easily establishes the desired equivalence.
nodes.statement_short: For $d=1$ the space has dimension at most 1
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Ramanujan's 1psi1 summation
nodes.statement: Let $a, b \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $a, q/b \not\in \{q^n : n \ge 1\}$ and $a \neq 0$. Then for $|b/a| < |x| < 1$, one has \begin{equation} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{(a; q)_n}{(b; q)_n} x^n = \frac{(q; q)(b/a; q)}{(b; q)(q/a; q)} \frac{\left\langle ax; q \right\rangle}{(x; q)(b/ax; q)}. \end{equation} Taking $x \mapsto x/a$ and then $a \to \infty$ recovers Jacobi's triple product identity from \cref{eq:triple}.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: $\sum_n (a;q)_n/(b;q)_n x^n$ equals an explicit ratio of infinite products.
assumptions: $a, b \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $a, q/b \not\in \{q^n : n \ge 1\}$ and $a \neq 0$
nodes.label: prop:ramanujan-1psi1

nodes.name: 1psi1 summation formula
nodes.statement: \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{(a; q)_n}{(b; q)_n} x^n = \frac{(q; q)(b/a; q)}{(b; q)(q/a; q)} \frac{\left\langle ax; q \right\rangle}{(x; q)(b/ax; q)}.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.label: eq:ramanujan-1psi1

nodes.name: Proof of Ramanujan's 1psi1 summation in the T_D framework
nodes.statement:
It suffices to prove the claim when $|b/a| < |q|$ and $a 
ot \in \{q^n : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}$, by the uniqueness of analytic continuation in $a$. Letting $D := \{z : |b/a| < |x| < 1\}$, we note that $D$ includes a horizontal strip of length $> 	extnormal{Im}\ 	au$, and that both sides of \cref{eq:ramanujan-1psi1} yield holomorphic functions of $z$ inside $D$. Using \cref{tbl:spaces}, the right-hand side lies in \[ \mathcal{T}_D\left( rac{-ax}{(1-x)(1-b/aqx)^{-1}} ight) = \mathcal{T}_D\left( rac{(b/q) - ax}{1-x}ight), \] and the same is easily verified for the left-hand side. In the context of \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii), we have $A_n(z) = 1 - x - q^n((b/q) + ax)$; hence $d = 1$, $\widehat{A_n}(0) = 1 - q^{n-1}b 
eq 0$ for any $n \ge 1$, and $\widehat{A_n}(d) = q^n a - 1 
eq 0$ for any $n < 0$. Thus the conditions in \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii) are fulfilled for $n_0 = 0$, and so by \cref{lem:proofs-by-fourier} it suffices to check that $\lim_{n 	o \infty} \widehat{F}(n) = \lim_{n 	o \infty} \widehat{G}(n)$, where $F$ and $G$ denote the left-hand side and the right-hand side of \cref{eq:ramanujan-1psi1}. But clearly \[ \lim_{n 	o \infty} \widehat{F}(n) =  rac{(a; q)}{(b; q)} 
eq 0. \] Concerning the right-hand side, note that $(1-x)G(z)$ extends to a holomorphic function on $D' := \{z : |b/a| < |x| < |q|^{-1}\}$; hence the Fourier series $(1-x)G(z) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \left(\widehat{G}(n) - \widehat{G}(n-1)ight) x^n$ extends to (and converges absolutely and locally uniformly in) $D'$. Plugging in $x = 1$ yields \[ \lim_{x 	o 1} (1-x)G(z) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \left(\widehat{G}(n) - \widehat{G}(n-1)ight), \] where the sum converges absolutely. But the fact that $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \widehat{G}(n) x^n$ also converges absolutely for some $|x| < 1$ forces $\lim_{n 	o -\infty} \widehat{G}(n) = 0$, and thus \[ \lim_{n 	o \infty} \widehat{G}(n) = \lim_{x 	o 1} (1-x)G(z) =  rac{(q; q)(b/a; q)}{(b; q)(q/a; q)}  rac{(a; q)(q/a; q)}{(q; q)(b/a; q)} =  rac{(a; q)}{(b; q)}, \] which completes our proof.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: Both sides lie in a one-dimensional $\mathcal T_D$ space; Fourier identification reduces to comparing the limits of Fourier coefficients, computed via the residue at $x=1$.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: It suffices to prove the claim when $|b/a| < |q|$ and $a \not \in \{q^n : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}$, by the uniqueness of analytic continuation in $a$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to generic $a,b$ by analytic continuation
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Domain D
nodes.statement: Letting $D := \{z : |b/a| < |x| < 1\}$, we note that $D$ includes a horizontal strip of length $> \textnormal{Im}\ \tau$, and that both sides of \cref{eq:ramanujan-1psi1} yield holomorphic functions of $z$ inside $D$.
nodes.statement_short: Both sides holomorphic on an annulus-strip $D$
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Common space
nodes.statement: Using \cref{tbl:spaces}, the right-hand side lies in \[ \mathcal{T}_D\left(\frac{-ax}{(1-x)(1-b/aqx)^{-1}} \right) = \mathcal{T}_D\left(\frac{(b/q) - ax}{1-x}\right), \] and the same is easily verified for the left-hand side.
nodes.statement_short: Both sides lie in the same $\mathcal T_D$ space
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Compute A_n
nodes.statement: In the context of \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii), we have $A_n(z) = 1 - x - q^n((b/q) + ax)$; hence $d = 1$, $\widehat{A_n}(0) = 1 - q^{n-1}b \neq 0$ for any $n \ge 1$, and $\widehat{A_n}(d) = q^n a - 1 \neq 0$ for any $n < 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Check the hypotheses of the upper bound with $d=1$
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Reduce to limits
nodes.statement: Thus the conditions in \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii) are fulfilled for $n_0 = 0$, and so by \cref{lem:proofs-by-fourier} it suffices to check that $\lim_{n \to \infty} \widehat{F}(n) = \lim_{n \to \infty} \widehat{G}(n)$, where $F$ and $G$ denote the left-hand side and the right-hand side of \cref{eq:ramanujan-1psi1}.
nodes.statement_short: Fourier identification reduces to limits of coefficients
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Left-hand limit
nodes.statement: But clearly \[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \widehat{F}(n) = \frac{(a; q)}{(b; q)} \neq 0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Limit of left-hand coefficients
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Right-hand residue
nodes.statement: Concerning the right-hand side, note that $(1-x)G(z)$ extends to a holomorphic function on $D' := \{z : |b/a| < |x| < |q|^{-1}\}$; hence the Fourier series $(1-x)G(z) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \left(\widehat{G}(n) - \widehat{G}(n-1)\right) x^n$ extends to (and converges absolutely and locally uniformly in) $D'$. Plugging in $x = 1$ yields \[ \lim_{x \to 1} (1-x)G(z) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \left(\widehat{G}(n) - \widehat{G}(n-1)\right), \] where the sum converges absolutely.
nodes.statement_short: Express the limit via $(1-x)G$ at $x=1$
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Limits agree
nodes.statement: But the fact that $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \widehat{G}(n) x^n$ also converges absolutely for some $|x| < 1$ forces $\lim_{n \to -\infty} \widehat{G}(n) = 0$, and thus \[ \lim_{n \to \infty} \widehat{G}(n) = \lim_{x \to 1} (1-x)G(z) = \frac{(q; q)(b/a; q)}{(b; q)(q/a; q)} \frac{(a; q)(q/a; q)}{(q; q)(b/a; q)} = \frac{(a; q)}{(b; q)}, \] which completes our proof.
nodes.statement_short: The limits coincide
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Basic infinite product expansions (Euler, q-binomial theorem)
nodes.statement: For $z \in \mathbb{C}$, one has \cite[p.~19]{andrews1998theory} \begin{equation} (x; q) = \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{q^{\binom{n}{2}}}{(q; q)_n} (-x)^n, \end{equation} More generally, for $z \in {\mathbb{H}}^+$ and $y \in \mathbb{C}$, one has the $q$-binomial theorem \cite[Theorem 2.4]{andrews1974applications} \begin{equation} \frac{(xy; q)}{(x; q)} = \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{(y; q)_n}{(q; q)_n} x^n \qquad\quad \xRightarrow{y \mapsto 0} \qquad\quad \frac{1}{(x; q)} = \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{1}{(q; q)_n} x^n. \end{equation} If additionally $|y| < 1$, then \begin{equation} \frac{(xy; q)}{(x; q)(y; q)} = \sum_{m, n \ge 0} \frac{q^{mn} x^m y^n}{(q; q)_m (q; q)_n}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: Euler's expansion of $(x;q)$, the q-binomial theorem, and a double-sum expansion of $(xy;q)/((x;q)(y;q))$.
nodes.label: cor:basic-identities

nodes.name: Euler expansion of (x;q)
nodes.statement: (x; q) = \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{q^{\binom{n}{2}}}{(q; q)_n} (-x)^n,
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.label: eq:basic1

nodes.name: q-binomial theorem
nodes.statement: \frac{(xy; q)}{(x; q)} = \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{(y; q)_n}{(q; q)_n} x^n \qquad\quad \xRightarrow{y \mapsto 0} \qquad\quad \frac{1}{(x; q)} = \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{1}{(q; q)_n} x^n.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.label: eq:basic2

nodes.name: Double-sum expansion
nodes.statement: \frac{(xy; q)}{(x; q)(y; q)} = \sum_{m, n \ge 0} \frac{q^{mn} x^m y^n}{(q; q)_m (q; q)_n}.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.label: eq:basic3

nodes.name: Proof of Basic infinite product expansions in the T_D framework
nodes.statement: \cref{eq:basic1} and \cref{eq:basic2} follow as particular cases of \cref{prop:ramanujan-1psi1}, but can also be deduced by working in the one-dimensional spaces $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1 - x)$ and $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{+}\hspace{-0.03cm}}} \left((1-xy)/(1-x)\right)$. Finally, one easily checks that both sides of \cref{eq:basic3} lie in the space $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{+}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left((1 - xy)/((1 - x)(1 - y))\right)$, and by \cref{lem:proofs-by-fourier} it suffices to identify the coefficients of $x^0$. These Fourier coefficients are $(y; q)^{-1}$ and respectively $\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{1}{(q; q)_n} y^n$, which coincide due to the second identity in \cref{eq:basic2}.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: Special cases of the 1psi1 summation; the double-sum identity by Fourier identification in a one-dimensional space.

nodes.name: First two identities
nodes.statement: \cref{eq:basic1} and \cref{eq:basic2} follow as particular cases of \cref{prop:ramanujan-1psi1}, but can also be deduced by working in the one-dimensional spaces $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1 - x)$ and $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{+}\hspace{-0.03cm}}} \left((1-xy)/(1-x)\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Special cases of the 1psi1 summation
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Double-sum identity
nodes.statement: Finally, one easily checks that both sides of \cref{eq:basic3} lie in the space $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{+}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left((1 - xy)/((1 - x)(1 - y))\right)$, and by \cref{lem:proofs-by-fourier} it suffices to identify the coefficients of $x^0$. These Fourier coefficients are $(y; q)^{-1}$ and respectively $\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{1}{(q; q)_n} y^n$, which coincide due to the second identity in \cref{eq:basic2}.
nodes.statement_short: Fourier identification at $x^0$
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Cauchy's finite triple product identity
nodes.statement: For $z \in \mathbb{C}$ and any $N \ge 1$, \[ (x; q)_N \left(q/x; q\right)_N = \sum_{n = -N}^N \frac{(q; q)_{2N}}{(q; q)_{N-n} (q; q)_{N+n}} (-1)^n q^{\binom{n}{2}} x^n. \] Taking $N \to \infty$ recovers Jacobi's triple product identity from \cref{eq:triple}.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: Finite analogue of Jacobi's triple product: $(x;q)_N(q/x;q)_N$ as a q-binomial-weighted theta sum.
nodes.label: prop:Cauchy

nodes.name: Proof of Cauchy's finite triple product identity in the T_D framework
nodes.statement: We leave to the reader to verify that both sides above lie in \[ \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\frac{q^N - x}{1 - q^{N}x}\right). \] Going back to \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii), we have $d = 1$ and $A_n(z) = 1 - q^{N}x - \left(q^N - x\right)q^n = \left(1 - q^{N+n}\right) - \left(q^{N} - q^{n} \right)x$ in this case. But for any choice of $n_0 \in [-N, N]$, we have $1 - q^{N+n} \neq 0$ for all $n \ge n_0 + 1$, and $q^{N} - q^{n} \neq 0$ for all $n < n_0$. So by \cref{lem:proofs-by-fourier}, it suffices to identify the coefficients of $x^N$ in the two sides of Cauchy's identity, which are $(-1) \cdot (-q) \cdots (-q)^{N-1} = (-1)^N q^{\binom{N}{2}}$.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: Both sides lie in a one-dimensional $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}$ space; compare the coefficients of $x^N$.

nodes.name: Common space
nodes.statement: We leave to the reader to verify that both sides above lie in \[ \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\frac{q^N - x}{1 - q^{N}x}\right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Both sides lie in a $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}$ space of a rational factor
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Check hypotheses
nodes.statement: Going back to \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii), we have $d = 1$ and $A_n(z) = 1 - q^{N}x - \left(q^N - x\right)q^n = \left(1 - q^{N+n}\right) - \left(q^{N} - q^{n} \right)x$ in this case. But for any choice of $n_0 \in [-N, N]$, we have $1 - q^{N+n} \neq 0$ for all $n \ge n_0 + 1$, and $q^{N} - q^{n} \neq 0$ for all $n < n_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute $A_n$ and verify nonvanishing

nodes.name: Compare x^N coefficients
nodes.statement: So by \cref{lem:proofs-by-fourier}, it suffices to identify the coefficients of $x^N$ in the two sides of Cauchy's identity, which are $(-1) \cdot (-q) \cdots (-q)^{N-1} = (-1)^N q^{\binom{N}{2}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare the $x^N$ coefficients

nodes.name: Remark: product formula for canonical theta vectors
nodes.statement: Taking $x \mapsto \alpha x^d$ and $q \mapsto q^d$ in Jacobi's triple product identity \cref{eq:triple} for some $\alpha \in \mathbb{C}^\times$ yields that \[ \big(q^d; q^d\big)\big\langle {-\alpha} x^d; q^d \big\rangle = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}} x^{dn} = \vect{\alpha x^d}{0}, \] and taking $z \mapsto z + k\tau/d$ for $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ gives the more general formula \begin{equation} \vect{\alpha x^d}{k} = \big(q^d; q^d\big)\big\langle {-\alpha} q^k x^d ; q^d \big\rangle x^k. \end{equation} Note that this is consistent with the vector spaces in \cref{tbl:spaces}. In particular, we know exactly where the canonical basis vectors $\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}$ have zeros (recall the proof of \cref{prop:polynomial-spaces}), although the zeros of a sum of two such functions can be nontrivial (recall \cref{ex:plots}).
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Product formula for [alpha x^d; k]
nodes.statement: \vect{\alpha x^d}{k} = \big(q^d; q^d\big)\big\langle {-\alpha} q^k x^d ; q^d \big\rangle x^k.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.label: eq:canonical-formula

nodes.name: Value identification
nodes.statement: Let $d$ be a positive integer, $\alpha \in \mathbb{C}^\times$, and $F, G \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$. If $\alpha = -q^n$ for some $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, assume additionally that $\widehat{F}(d-n) = \widehat{G}(d-n)$. Then one has $F = G$ iff $F(j/d) = G(j/d)$ for all integers $0 \le j < d$.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: Two elements of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(\alpha x^d)$ agree iff they agree at $z=j/d$, $0\le j<d$ (with an extra coefficient condition when $\alpha=-q^n$).
assumptions: Let $d$ be a positive integer, $\alpha \in \mathbb{C}^\times$, and $F, G \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$.
conclusions: one has $F = G$ iff $F(j/d) = G(j/d)$ for all integers $0 \le j < d$
nodes.label: lem:proofs-by-value

nodes.name: Remark: canonical vectors at roots of unity
nodes.statement: When $z = j/d$, $x = e^{2\pi i j/d}$ is a $d$th root of unity, which is helpful since the powers of $x$ occurring in a canonical basis vector $\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}$ are all multiples of $d$ plus $k$. Indeed, \cref{eq:canonical-formula} implies that \begin{equation} \forall j, k \in \mathbb{Z}: \qquad\quad \vect{\alpha x^d}{k}\left(j/d\right) = \big( q^d; q^d \big) \big\langle {-\alpha} q^k; q^d \big\rangle e^{2\pi i (jk/d)}. \end{equation} Specializing product identities at roots of unity to prove them is, of course, not a new idea \cite{cao2012applications}, but it is helpful to phrase it in terms of the $d$-dimensional spaces $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Values of canonical vectors at roots of unity
nodes.statement: \forall j, k \in \mathbb{Z}: \qquad\quad \vect{\alpha x^d}{k}\left(j/d\right) = \big( q^d; q^d \big) \big\langle {-\alpha} q^k; q^d \big\rangle e^{2\pi i (jk/d)}.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.label: eq:canonical-root

nodes.name: Proof of Value identification
nodes.statement: Take $G = 0$ without loss of generality, and suppose $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$ satisfies $F(j/d) = 0$ for all $0 \le j < d$. Writing $F = \sum_{k=0}^{d-1} \widehat{F}(k) \vect{f}{k}$ as in \cref{eq:fourier-coeffs-basis}, the computation in \cref{eq:canonical-root} implies that \[ \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\ 1 & \zeta & \cdots & \zeta^{d-1} \\ & & \ddots \\ 1 & \zeta^{d-1} & \cdots & \zeta^{(d-1)(d-1)} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \widehat{F}(0) \big\langle {-\alpha}; q^d \big\rangle \\ \widehat{F}(1) \big\langle {-\alpha} q; q^d \big\rangle \\ \vdots \\ \widehat{F}(d-1) \big\langle {-\alpha} q^{d-1}; q^d \big\rangle \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \text{where } \zeta = e^{2\pi i /d}. \] But the matrix above is Vandermonde and invertible, and hence $\widehat{F}(k) \left\langle -\alpha q^k; q^d \right\rangle = 0$ for all $0 \le k < d$. Now note that $\left\langle -\alpha q^k; q^d \right\rangle = 0$ only when $\alpha = -q^{d(m+1)-k}$ for some $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, and in this case the assumption of the lemma ensures that $\widehat{F}(k-dm) = 0$. But $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$ implies that $\widehat{F}(n) = \alpha q^{n-d} \widehat{F}(n-d)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, and hence $\widehat{F}(k) = 0$. We thus have $\widehat{F}(k) = 0$ for all $0 \le k < d$, which forces $F = 0$ by its canonical basis representation (or by \cref{lem:proofs-by-fourier}).
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: Values at $d$th roots of unity give a Vandermonde system for the scaled canonical coefficients; invertibility forces all coefficients to vanish.

nodes.name: WLOG G=0 and Vandermonde system
nodes.statement: Take $G = 0$ without loss of generality, and suppose $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$ satisfies $F(j/d) = 0$ for all $0 \le j < d$. Writing $F = \sum_{k=0}^{d-1} \widehat{F}(k) \vect{f}{k}$ as in \cref{eq:fourier-coeffs-basis}, the computation in \cref{eq:canonical-root} implies that \[ \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\ 1 & \zeta & \cdots & \zeta^{d-1} \\ & & \ddots \\ 1 & \zeta^{d-1} & \cdots & \zeta^{(d-1)(d-1)} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \widehat{F}(0) \big\langle {-\alpha}; q^d \big\rangle \\ \widehat{F}(1) \big\langle {-\alpha} q; q^d \big\rangle \\ \vdots \\ \widehat{F}(d-1) \big\langle {-\alpha} q^{d-1}; q^d \big\rangle \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \text{where } \zeta = e^{2\pi i /d}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $G=0$; values at roots of unity give a Vandermonde system
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Invert
nodes.statement: But the matrix above is Vandermonde and invertible, and hence $\widehat{F}(k) \left\langle -\alpha q^k; q^d \right\rangle = 0$ for all $0 \le k < d$.
nodes.statement_short: Invertibility gives vanishing scaled coefficients
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Degenerate case
nodes.statement: Now note that $\left\langle -\alpha q^k; q^d \right\rangle = 0$ only when $\alpha = -q^{d(m+1)-k}$ for some $m \in \mathbb{Z}$, and in this case the assumption of the lemma ensures that $\widehat{F}(k-dm) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the extra hypothesis when a product vanishes
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Recursion
nodes.statement: But $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$ implies that $\widehat{F}(n) = \alpha q^{n-d} \widehat{F}(n-d)$ for all $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, and hence $\widehat{F}(k) = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: The coefficient recursion gives $\widehat F(k)=0$
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: We thus have $\widehat{F}(k) = 0$ for all $0 \le k < d$, which forces $F = 0$ by its canonical basis representation (or by \cref{lem:proofs-by-fourier}).
nodes.statement_short: All canonical coefficients vanish, so $F=0$
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Proof of the quintuple product identity
nodes.statement: To show that $(q; q) \left\langle x; q\right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2\right\rangle = \vect{qx^3}{0} - \vect{qx^3}{1}$, it is easier to take $x \mapsto -x$ and prove \[ (q; q) \left\langle -x; q\right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2\right\rangle \stackrel{?}{=} \left(q^3; q^3\right)\left(\left\langle qx^3; q^3 \right\rangle + x\left\langle q^2 x^3; q^3 \right\rangle \right) \] instead (where we used \cref{eq:canonical-formula} on the right-hand side). Both sides lie in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(-qx^3\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x\right)$ by multiplying the respective factors in \cref{tbl:spaces}, which is one-dimensional by \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}, and spanned by $\vect{-qx^3}{0} + \vect{-qx^3}{1}$. Hence both sides have $\widehat{F}(2) = 0$, and by \cref{lem:proofs-by-value} it suffices to check the equality when $x = \zeta$ is a cube root of unity. The latter reduces to \[ (q; q) \left( -\zeta; q\right) \left( -q\zeta^2; q\right) \left( q\zeta^2; q^2\right) \left( q\zeta; q^2\right) \stackrel{?}{=} \left(q^3; q^3\right)\left(\left\langle q; q^3 \right\rangle + \zeta \left\langle q^2; q^3 \right\rangle \right). \] Using $(-\zeta; q) = (1 + \zeta)(-q\zeta; q)$ and simplifying by $(q; q)(1+\zeta)$, this further reduces to \[ \left( -q\zeta; q\right) \left( -q\zeta^2; q\right) \left( q\zeta; q^2\right)\left( q\zeta^2; q^2\right) \stackrel{?}{=} 1. \] Finally, using $(-x; q) = \left(x^2; q^2\right)/(x; q)$, the left-hand side becomes \[ \frac{\left( q^2\zeta^2; q^2\right) \left( q^2\zeta; q^2\right) \left( q\zeta; q^2\right)\left( q\zeta^2; q^2\right)} {\left( q\zeta; q\right) \left( q\zeta^2; q\right)} = \frac{\left( q\zeta^2; q\right) \left( q\zeta; q\right)} {\left( q\zeta; q\right) \left( q\zeta^2; q\right)} = 1, \] as we wanted.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: Both sides lie in a one-dimensional $\mathcal T\cap\mathcal S$ space; by value identification check cube roots of unity, where the identity reduces to a product equal to 1.

nodes.name: Reformulate
nodes.statement: To show that $(q; q) \left\langle x; q\right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2\right\rangle = \vect{qx^3}{0} - \vect{qx^3}{1}$, it is easier to take $x \mapsto -x$ and prove \[ (q; q) \left\langle -x; q\right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2\right\rangle \stackrel{?}{=} \left(q^3; q^3\right)\left(\left\langle qx^3; q^3 \right\rangle + x\left\langle q^2 x^3; q^3 \right\rangle \right) \] instead (where we used \cref{eq:canonical-formula} on the right-hand side).
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $x\mapsto -x$ and use the canonical formula
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Common space
nodes.statement: Both sides lie in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(-qx^3\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x\right)$ by multiplying the respective factors in \cref{tbl:spaces}, which is one-dimensional by \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}, and spanned by $\vect{-qx^3}{0} + \vect{-qx^3}{1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Both sides in a one-dimensional $\mathcal T\cap\mathcal S$ space
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Value identification
nodes.statement: Hence both sides have $\widehat{F}(2) = 0$, and by \cref{lem:proofs-by-value} it suffices to check the equality when $x = \zeta$ is a cube root of unity. The latter reduces to \[ (q; q) \left( -\zeta; q\right) \left( -q\zeta^2; q\right) \left( q\zeta^2; q^2\right) \left( q\zeta; q^2\right) \stackrel{?}{=} \left(q^3; q^3\right)\left(\left\langle q; q^3 \right\rangle + \zeta \left\langle q^2; q^3 \right\rangle \right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to cube roots of unity
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Simplify
nodes.statement: Using $(-\zeta; q) = (1 + \zeta)(-q\zeta; q)$ and simplifying by $(q; q)(1+\zeta)$, this further reduces to \[ \left( -q\zeta; q\right) \left( -q\zeta^2; q\right) \left( q\zeta; q^2\right)\left( q\zeta^2; q^2\right) \stackrel{?}{=} 1. \]
nodes.statement_short: Cancel common factors
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Finally, using $(-x; q) = \left(x^2; q^2\right)/(x; q)$, the left-hand side becomes \[ \frac{\left( q^2\zeta^2; q^2\right) \left( q^2\zeta; q^2\right) \left( q\zeta; q^2\right)\left( q\zeta^2; q^2\right)} {\left( q\zeta; q\right) \left( q\zeta^2; q\right)} = \frac{\left( q\zeta^2; q\right) \left( q\zeta; q\right)} {\left( q\zeta; q\right) \left( q\zeta^2; q\right)} = 1, \] as we wanted.
nodes.statement_short: The remaining product equals 1
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Proof of the septuple product identity
nodes.statement: Note that both sides of $\cref{eq:septuple}$ lie in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(-qx^5\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^3\right)$ by \cref{tbl:spaces}, a space which is spanned by $\vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3}$ and $\vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2}$ by \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}.
