Hence both sides have $\widehat{F}(4) = 0$, and by \cref{lem:proofs-by-value} it suffices to verify \cref{eq:septuple} when $x = \zeta$ is a fifth root of unity, which reduces by \cref{eq:canonical-root} to \[ (q; q) \left\langle \zeta; q \right\rangle \left\langle \zeta^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle q\zeta^2; q^2 \right\rangle \stackrel{?}{=} \frac{\left(q^5; q^5\right)\left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle \left(1 + \zeta^3\right)}{\left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle} - \frac{\left(q^5; q^5\right)\left\langle q^2; q^5\right\rangle \left(\zeta + \zeta^2\right)}{\left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle}. \] But the right-hand side is just $\left(q^5; q^5\right)\left(1 - \zeta - \zeta^2 + \zeta^3\right)$, whereas grouping $\left\langle \zeta^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle q\zeta^2; q^2 \right\rangle = \left\langle \zeta^2; q \right\rangle$, the left-hand side becomes \[ (q; q) (1 - \zeta) (q \zeta; q) \left(q\zeta^4; q\right) \left(1 - \zeta^2\right) \left(q \zeta^2; q\right) \left(q\zeta^3; q\right) = (1 - \zeta)\left(1 - \zeta^2\right) \left(q^5; q^5\right), \] by factoring $1 - q^{5n} = \prod_{k=0}^4 \left(1 - \zeta^k q^n\right)$. Expand $\left( 1- \zeta\right)\left(1 - \zeta^2\right) = 1 - \zeta - \zeta^2 + \zeta^3$ to finish.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: Both sides lie in a two-dimensional $\mathcal T\cap\mathcal S$ space; value identification at fifth roots of unity reduces it to factoring $1-q^{5n}$.

nodes.name: Common space
nodes.statement: Note that both sides of $\cref{eq:septuple}$ lie in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(-qx^5\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^3\right)$ by \cref{tbl:spaces}, a space which is spanned by $\vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3}$ and $\vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2}$ by \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}.
nodes.statement_short: Both sides in a two-dimensional $\mathcal T\cap\mathcal S$ space
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Value identification
nodes.statement: Hence both sides have $\widehat{F}(4) = 0$, and by \cref{lem:proofs-by-value} it suffices to verify \cref{eq:septuple} when $x = \zeta$ is a fifth root of unity, which reduces by \cref{eq:canonical-root} to \[ (q; q) \left\langle \zeta; q \right\rangle \left\langle \zeta^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle q\zeta^2; q^2 \right\rangle \stackrel{?}{=} \frac{\left(q^5; q^5\right)\left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle \left(1 + \zeta^3\right)}{\left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle} - \frac{\left(q^5; q^5\right)\left\langle q^2; q^5\right\rangle \left(\zeta + \zeta^2\right)}{\left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to fifth roots of unity
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Evaluate both sides
nodes.statement: But the right-hand side is just $\left(q^5; q^5\right)\left(1 - \zeta - \zeta^2 + \zeta^3\right)$, whereas grouping $\left\langle \zeta^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle q\zeta^2; q^2 \right\rangle = \left\langle \zeta^2; q \right\rangle$, the left-hand side becomes \[ (q; q) (1 - \zeta) (q \zeta; q) \left(q\zeta^4; q\right) \left(1 - \zeta^2\right) \left(q \zeta^2; q\right) \left(q\zeta^3; q\right) = (1 - \zeta)\left(1 - \zeta^2\right) \left(q^5; q^5\right), \] by factoring $1 - q^{5n} = \prod_{k=0}^4 \left(1 - \zeta^k q^n\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Factor $1-q^{5n}$
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Expand $\left( 1- \zeta\right)\left(1 - \zeta^2\right) = 1 - \zeta - \zeta^2 + \zeta^3$ to finish.
nodes.statement_short: Expand to finish
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Remark: value identification does not easily give the nonuple identities
nodes.statement: \cref{lem:proofs-by-value} does not lead to an easy proof of our two nonuple product identities (\cref{prop:nonuple} and \cref{prop:nonuple2}), which will require different methods based on \cref{lem:proofs-by-fourier}. Nevertheless, below is another application of \cref{lem:proofs-by-value}, which will be helpful in relation to \cref{thm:bases-proportional-2}.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Squared triple product identity
nodes.statement: In $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^2\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^2\right)$, one has \[ \frac{1}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)}\left((q; q)\left\langle x; q \right\rangle\right)^2 = \left(-q; q^2\right)^2 \vect{x^2}{0} - 2\left(-q^2; q^2\right)^2\vect{x^2}{1}. \]
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: $((q;q)\langle x;q\rangle)^2/(q^2;q^2)$ in the canonical basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(x^2)$.
nodes.label: prop:squared-triple

nodes.name: Proof of Squared triple product identity
nodes.statement: By \cref{lem:proofs-by-value}, it suffices to check the identity for $x \in \{\pm 1\}$, which is easy using \cref{eq:canonical-root}; we leave the details to the reader.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: Value identification: check $x=\pm1$ using the canonical vector values.

nodes.name: Pole identification
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha \in \mathbb{C}^\times$ and $d \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $d \le 0$; if $d = 0$, assume additionally that $\alpha \not\in \left\{q^n : n \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}$. Let $S$ be an open horizontal strip of length $> \textnormal{Im}\ \tau$, and suppose $F, G \in \mathcal{T}_{S \setminus I}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$ where $I \subset S$ is a set of isolated points. Then one has $F = G$ iff $F - G \in \textnormal{Hol}(S)$. Hence if $F$ and $G$ only have simple poles, it suffices to check that their residues at those poles agree.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: For $d\le0$, two elements of $\mathcal T_{S\setminus I}(\alpha x^d)$ agree iff their difference is holomorphic on $S$, e.g. iff residues agree.
nodes.label: lem:proofs-by-pole

nodes.name: Proof of Pole identification
nodes.statement: Note that $F - G \in \textnormal{Hol}(S)$ implies $F - G \in \mathcal{T}_S\left(\alpha x^d\right)$, so it remains to show that $\mathcal{T}_S\left(\alpha x^d\right) = \{0\}$. This was established in \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}.(i) (under the given condition if $d = 0$).
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: The difference lies in $\mathcal T_S(\alpha x^d)$, which is zero by the monomial-spaces proposition.

nodes.name: Quotients of double products
nodes.statement: For $x, q \in \mathbb{C}$ with $0 < |q| < |x| < 1$, one has (as noted, for instance, in \cite[para.\ 486]{tannery1898elements}) \begin{equation} \frac{(q; q)^2}{\left\langle x; q \right\rangle} = \sum_{m, n \geq 0} \left( q^{(2m+1)n} - q^{(2n+1)(m+1)}\right) x^{m-n}, \end{equation} Moreover, one has \begin{equation} \frac{(q; q)^4}{\left\langle x; q\right\rangle^2} = \sum_{m, n \geq 0} \left(m+n+1\right) q^{(m+1)n} x^{m-n}. \end{equation} If additionally $y \in \mathbb{C}$ such that $|q| < |y| < 1$, then as noted by Hickerson \cite[Theorem 1.5]{hickerson1988proof}, \begin{equation} (q; q)^2 \frac{ \left\langle xy; q \right\rangle}{\left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle y; q \right\rangle} = \sum_{m, n \ge 0} q^{mn} x^m y^n - \sum_{m, n \ge 1} q^{mn} x^{-m} y^{-n}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: Lambert-type double-sum expansions of $(q;q)^2/\langle x;q\rangle$, its square, and $(q;q)^2\langle xy;q\rangle/(\langle x;q\rangle\langle y;q\rangle)$.
nodes.label: prop:fractional

nodes.name: Expansion of (q;q)^2/<x;q>
nodes.statement: \frac{(q; q)^2}{\left\langle x; q \right\rangle} = \sum_{m, n \geq 0} \left( q^{(2m+1)n} - q^{(2n+1)(m+1)}\right) x^{m-n},
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.label: eq:inverse

nodes.name: Expansion of (q;q)^4/<x;q>^2
nodes.statement: \frac{(q; q)^4}{\left\langle x; q\right\rangle^2} = \sum_{m, n \geq 0} \left(m+n+1\right) q^{(m+1)n} x^{m-n}.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.label: eq:inverse2

nodes.name: Hickerson's expansion of the double-product quotient
nodes.statement: (q; q)^2 \frac{ \left\langle xy; q \right\rangle}{\left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle y; q \right\rangle} = \sum_{m, n \ge 0} q^{mn} x^m y^n - \sum_{m, n \ge 1} q^{mn} x^{-m} y^{-n}.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.label: eq:fractional

nodes.name: Remark: Fourier coefficients cluster on lines for meromorphic quotients
nodes.statement: In most product identities, the nonzero 2D Fourier coefficients of entire and half-plane-entire functions tend to cluster in parabolas, such as in \cref{eq:triple,eq:quintuple,eq:septuple,eq:nonuple} or (partly) in \cref{tbl:plot1}. But the series in \cref{prop:fractional} have poles when $x = q^n$ ($n \in \mathbb{Z}$), so their nonzero coefficients cluster in a collection of lines rather than parabolas; each line corresponds to a series of the type $(1-q^nx)^{-1} = \sum_{m \ge 0} q^{mn}x^m$ or $(1-q^nx)^{-2} = \sum_{m \ge 0} (m+1) q^{mn}x^m$, indicating the order of the associated pole.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Proof of Quotients of double products
nodes.statement: We view the expressions in \cref{eq:inverse,eq:inverse2,eq:fractional} as functions of $z$ (as usual), and regard $q$ and $y$ as constants. Let $L(z)$ denote the left-hand side and $R(z)$ the right-hand side of \cref{eq:inverse}. One can check that both sides define holomorphic functions on $\{0 < \textnormal{Im}\ z < \textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$, with boundaries imposed on $R(z)$ by the convergence of $\sum_{m \ge 0} x^m$ (coming from $n = 0$), respectively $\sum_{n \ge 0} q^n x^{-n}$ (coming from $m = 0$); in fact, $L(z)$ is a meromorphic in all of $\mathbb{C}$. Now rewrite \[ R(z) = \frac{1}{1 - x} + \sum_{n \ge 1} U_n(z) - \sum_{n \ge 0} V_n(z) \qquad\qquad \text{for } 0 < \textnormal{Im}\ z < \textnormal{Im}\ \tau, \] where $U_n(z) = \sum_{m \ge 0} q^{(2m+1)n} x^{m-n}$ and $V_n(z) = \sum_{m \ge 0} q^{(2n+1)(m+1)} x^{m-n}$. This gives a meromorphic continuation of $R(z)$ to $S := \{-\textnormal{Im}\ \tau < \textnormal{Im}\ z < \textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$, with poles only at $x = 1$ (i.e., at $z = 2\pi i n$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$). Moreover, on $S \cap (S - \tau) = \{-\textnormal{Im}\ \tau < \textnormal{Im}\ z < 0\}$, this continuation satisfies \[ \begin{aligned} -x^{-1} R(z + \tau) &= -\frac{x^{-1}}{1 - qx} - \sum_{n \ge 1} \left(V_n(z) + x^{-n-1}\right) + \sum_{n \ge 0} U_{n+1}(z) \\ &= R(z) - \frac{1}{1-x} -\frac{x^{-1}}{1 - qx} + V_0(z) + \frac{x^{-2}}{1 - x^{-1}} \\ &= R(z) - \frac{1}{1-x} -\frac{x^{-1}}{1 - qx} + \frac{q}{1-qx} + \frac{x^{-1}}{x - 1} \quad = R(z) + x^{-1} - x^{-1} \ = R(z). \end{aligned} \] Thus $R \in \mathcal{T}_{S \setminus I}\left(-x^{-1}\right)$, where $I = \{x = 1\}$. But the same is true for $L(z) = (q; q)^2 \left\langle x; q\right\rangle^{-1}$, since $\left\langle x; q\right\rangle \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(-x\right)$ only has zeros on $\{x = q^n : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}$. Furthermore, near the poles one has \[ \lim_{x \to 1} (1 - x) L(z) = \lim_{x \to q} \frac{(q; q)^2 (1 - x)}{\left\langle x; q\right\rangle} = \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{(q; q)^2}{(qx; q)\left(qx^{-1}; q\right)} = 1, \] \[ \lim_{x \to 1} (1 - x) R(z) = \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{1-x}{1-x} = 1, \] so that $L - R$ is holomorphic on $S$; \cref{lem:proofs-by-pole} now completes the proof of \cref{eq:inverse}. The proof of $\cref{eq:fractional}$ is analogous, by writing the right-hand side as $\frac{1}{1-x} + \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{y^n}{1-q^n x} - \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{q^nx^{-1}y^{-n}}{1-q^n x^{-1}}$ on the same punctured strip $S \setminus I$; the relevant function space is now $\mathcal{T}_{S\setminus I}(y)$, and the fact that $y \not\in \left\{q^n : n \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}$ (since $|q| < |y| < 1$) allows us to apply \cref{lem:proofs-by-pole} (again, by identifying residues at $x = 1$). As for \cref{eq:inverse2}, one can proceed similarly using \cref{lem:proofs-by-pole} for the function space $\mathcal{T}_{S \setminus I}\left(x^{-2}\right)$, except that the presence of double poles at $x = 1$ makes the identification harder. Alternatively, one can recover \cref{eq:inverse2} by taking the derivative in $y$ of \cref{eq:fractional} at $y = q/x$, and multiplying by $q/x$.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space
nodes.statement_short: Continue both sides meromorphically to a strip, show they lie in $\mathcal T_{S\setminus I}(-x^{-1})$ (resp. $(y)$), and match residues at $x=1$ via pole identification; the squared case by differentiating in $y$.

nodes.name: Setup L and R
nodes.statement: We view the expressions in \cref{eq:inverse,eq:inverse2,eq:fractional} as functions of $z$ (as usual), and regard $q$ and $y$ as constants. Let $L(z)$ denote the left-hand side and $R(z)$ the right-hand side of \cref{eq:inverse}.
nodes.statement_short: Regard both sides as functions of $z$
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Holomorphy domains
nodes.statement: One can check that both sides define holomorphic functions on $\{0 < \textnormal{Im}\ z < \textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$, with boundaries imposed on $R(z)$ by the convergence of $\sum_{m \ge 0} x^m$ (coming from $n = 0$), respectively $\sum_{n \ge 0} q^n x^{-n}$ (coming from $m = 0$); in fact, $L(z)$ is a meromorphic in all of $\mathbb{C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Both sides holomorphic on a strip
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Continue R
nodes.statement: Now rewrite \[ R(z) = \frac{1}{1 - x} + \sum_{n \ge 1} U_n(z) - \sum_{n \ge 0} V_n(z) \qquad\qquad \text{for } 0 < \textnormal{Im}\ z < \textnormal{Im}\ \tau, \] where $U_n(z) = \sum_{m \ge 0} q^{(2m+1)n} x^{m-n}$ and $V_n(z) = \sum_{m \ge 0} q^{(2n+1)(m+1)} x^{m-n}$. This gives a meromorphic continuation of $R(z)$ to $S := \{-\textnormal{Im}\ \tau < \textnormal{Im}\ z < \textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$, with poles only at $x = 1$ (i.e., at $z = 2\pi i n$, $n \in \mathbb{Z}$).
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $R$ to continue it meromorphically
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Functional equation
nodes.statement: Moreover, on $S \cap (S - \tau) = \{-\textnormal{Im}\ \tau < \textnormal{Im}\ z < 0\}$, this continuation satisfies \[ \begin{aligned} -x^{-1} R(z + \tau) &= -\frac{x^{-1}}{1 - qx} - \sum_{n \ge 1} \left(V_n(z) + x^{-n-1}\right) + \sum_{n \ge 0} U_{n+1}(z) \\ &= R(z) - \frac{1}{1-x} -\frac{x^{-1}}{1 - qx} + V_0(z) + \frac{x^{-2}}{1 - x^{-1}} \\ &= R(z) - \frac{1}{1-x} -\frac{x^{-1}}{1 - qx} + \frac{q}{1-qx} + \frac{x^{-1}}{x - 1} \quad = R(z) + x^{-1} - x^{-1} \ = R(z). \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Verify the quasiperiodicity of $R$
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Same space
nodes.statement: Thus $R \in \mathcal{T}_{S \setminus I}\left(-x^{-1}\right)$, where $I = \{x = 1\}$. But the same is true for $L(z) = (q; q)^2 \left\langle x; q\right\rangle^{-1}$, since $\left\langle x; q\right\rangle \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(-x\right)$ only has zeros on $\{x = q^n : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}$.
nodes.statement_short: $L$ and $R$ lie in the same punctured space
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Match residues
nodes.statement: Furthermore, near the poles one has \[ \lim_{x \to 1} (1 - x) L(z) = \lim_{x \to q} \frac{(q; q)^2 (1 - x)}{\left\langle x; q\right\rangle} = \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{(q; q)^2}{(qx; q)\left(qx^{-1}; q\right)} = 1, \] \[ \lim_{x \to 1} (1 - x) R(z) = \lim_{x \to 1} \frac{1-x}{1-x} = 1, \] so that $L - R$ is holomorphic on $S$; \cref{lem:proofs-by-pole} now completes the proof of \cref{eq:inverse}.
nodes.statement_short: Residues agree; pole identification gives the first identity
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Third identity
nodes.statement: The proof of $\cref{eq:fractional}$ is analogous, by writing the right-hand side as $\frac{1}{1-x} + \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{y^n}{1-q^n x} - \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{q^nx^{-1}y^{-n}}{1-q^n x^{-1}}$ on the same punctured strip $S \setminus I$; the relevant function space is now $\mathcal{T}_{S\setminus I}(y)$, and the fact that $y \not\in \left\{q^n : n \in \mathbb{Z}\right\}$ (since $|q| < |y| < 1$) allows us to apply \cref{lem:proofs-by-pole} (again, by identifying residues at $x = 1$).
nodes.statement_short: Analogous argument in $\mathcal T_{S\setminus I}(y)$
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Second identity
nodes.statement: As for \cref{eq:inverse2}, one can proceed similarly using \cref{lem:proofs-by-pole} for the function space $\mathcal{T}_{S \setminus I}\left(x^{-2}\right)$, except that the presence of double poles at $x = 1$ makes the identification harder. Alternatively, one can recover \cref{eq:inverse2} by taking the derivative in $y$ of \cref{eq:fractional} at $y = q/x$, and multiplying by $q/x$.
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate the third identity in $y$
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Remark: formal-series proofs would be harder
nodes.statement: Identity \cref{eq:inverse}, with the substitutions $x \mapsto x^2$, $q \mapsto q^2$, also follows from \cref{eq:fractional} by taking $y = -q/x$. We note that it would be more difficult to prove such identities of meromorphic functions if we viewed them strictly as formal series. Indeed, there is no adequate ring of formal series containing the right-hand sides of \cref{eq:inverse,eq:inverse2,eq:fractional} both before and after substituting $x \mapsto xq$; attempting such proofs would lead to expressions of the form $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} x^n$, which correspond in the meromorphic setting to sums of the type $\frac{1}{1-x} + \frac{x^{-1}}{1-x^{-1}} = 0$.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Remark: Besge's identity from the square relation
nodes.statement: From the fact that \cref{eq:inverse2} is the square of \cref{eq:inverse}, one can eventually deduce Besge's identity for the convolution $\sum_{k=1}^{n-1} \sigma(k) \sigma(n-k)$, where $\sigma$ is the sum-of-divisors function.
nodes.section: 3.3 How to identify two functions in the same space

nodes.name: Multiplication identities for T_C(alpha x^d)
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{C}^\times$, and $a, b, u, v$ be positive integers. Then for $k, j \in \mathbb{Z}$ and any complete residue system $R$ of integers modulo $au^2+bv^2$, one has \begin{equation} \vect{\alpha x^a}{k}(u z) \cdot \vect{\beta x^b}{j}(v z) = \sum_{\ell \in R} M_\ell(q) \vect{\alpha^u \beta^v q^{a\binom{u}{2} + b \binom{v}{2}} x^{au^2+bv^2}}{\ell}, \end{equation} where the coefficients $M_\ell(q) \in \mathbb{C}$ also depend on $a, b, \alpha, \beta, u, v$ but not on $z$, and are computed as follows. Let $d := \gcd(au, bv)$, $a' := au/d$, $b' := bv/d$ and $\ell' := (\ell - uk - vj)/d$. If $\ell' \not\in \mathbb{Z}$, then $M_\ell(q) = 0$. Else, letting $(n_0, m_0)$ be an integer solution to $a'n_0 + b'm_0 = 1$, one has \begin{equation} M_\ell(q) = \gamma_\ell \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \big(\alpha^{b'} \beta^{-a'}\big)^n q^{\frac{ab'^2 + ba'^2}{2}n^2 + \delta_\ell n}, \end{equation} \[ \gamma_\ell = \big( \alpha^{n_0} \beta^{m_0} \big)^{\ell'} q^{a\binom{n_0 \ell' }{2} + b\binom{m_0 \ell'}{2} + (kn_0 + jm_0)\ell'}, \qquad\quad \delta_\ell = (ab'n_0 - ba'm_0)\ell' - \frac{ab' - ba'}{2} + kb' - ja'. \]
nodes.statement_short: The product of two scaled canonical theta vectors expands in the canonical basis with M-coefficients given by explicit one-dimensional theta series.
assumptions: Let $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{C}^\times$, and $a, b, u, v$ be positive integers.
nodes.label: lem:m-identities

nodes.name: Product expansion with M-coefficients
nodes.statement: \vect{\alpha x^a}{k}(u z) \cdot \vect{\beta x^b}{j}(v z) = \sum_{\ell \in R} M_\ell(q) \vect{\alpha^u \beta^v q^{a\binom{u}{2} + b \binom{v}{2}} x^{au^2+bv^2}}{\ell},
nodes.label: eq:m-expansion

nodes.name: Formula for M-coefficients
nodes.statement: M_\ell(q) = \gamma_\ell \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \big(\alpha^{b'} \beta^{-a'}\big)^n q^{\frac{ab'^2 + ba'^2}{2}n^2 + \delta_\ell n},
nodes.label: eq:m-coeffs-formula

nodes.name: Remark: special cases of the multiplication identities
nodes.statement: When $u = v = 1$ and $R$ is a complete residue system modulo $a+b$, \cref{lem:m-identities} states that \[ \vect{\alpha x^a}{k} \cdot \vect{\beta x^b}{j} = \sum_{\ell \in R} M_\ell(q) \vect{\alpha \beta x^{a+b}}{\ell}, \] which is precisely the type of identity anticipated in \cref{eq:m-coeffs}; $M_\ell(q)$ is also a bit simpler in this case since $ab' = ba'$. If $\gcd(a, b) = 1$ then $M_\ell(q)$ is always nonzero, and we get $d = 1$, $a' = a$, $b' = b$, $\ell' = \ell - k - j$; so in particular, $\delta_\ell$ becomes $ab(n_0 - m_0)\ell' + kb - ja$. If additionally $b = 1$, then we can take $n_0 = 1$ and $m_0 = 1-a$, which simplifies $M_\ell(q)$ even further. But in practice, one may avoid computing $\gamma_\ell$ and $\delta_\ell$ by the formulae above, since knowing that $M_\ell(q)$ takes the form in \cref{eq:m-coeffs-formula} allows for direct numerical identification (by computing the first few terms of the Fourier series in $\tau$ of the coefficient of $x^\ell$ in the original product).

nodes.name: Proof of Multiplication identities
nodes.statement: By \cref{lem:basic}.(iv), $S_u\left(\vect{\alpha x^a}{k}\right) \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(\alpha^u q^{a\binom{u}{2}} x^{au^2} \big)$ and $S_v\left(\vect{\beta x^b}{j}\right) \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(\beta^v q^{b\binom{v}{2}} x^{bv^2} \big)$. Hence their product lies in the product $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}$-space, which is spanned by the basis vectors on the right-hand side of \cref{eq:m-expansion} for any complete residue system $R$ modulo $au^2+bv^2$ (recall the proof of \cref{prop:polynomial-spaces}). It remains to compute the coefficients $M_\ell(q)$, i.e.\ the coefficients of $x^\ell$ in \[ \vect{\alpha x^a}{k}(u z) \cdot \vect{\beta x^b}{j}(v z) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{a\binom{n}{2} + kn} x^{aun + uk} \cdot \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} \beta^m q^{b\binom{m}{2}+jm} x^{bvm+vj}. \] By multiplying these series and identifying coefficients of $x^\ell$, we find that \[ M_\ell(q) = \sum_{aun+bvm=\ell-uk-vj} \alpha^n \beta^m q^{a\binom{n}{2} + kn + b\binom{m}{2} + jm} = \sum_{a'n + b'm = \ell'} \alpha^n \beta^m q^{a\binom{n}{2} + kn + b\binom{m}{2} + jm}. \] Hence if $\ell' \not\in \mathbb{Z}$, there are no terms in the summation above and thus $M_\ell(q) = 0$. Otherwise, there are infinitely many terms, given precisely by \[ (n, m) = \ell'(n_0, m_0) + p(b', -a'), \qquad\qquad p \in \mathbb{Z}. \] By reindexing and replacing $p$ with $n$, this yields \[ M_\ell(q) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^{n_0\ell' + b'n} \beta^{m_0\ell' - a'n} q^{a\binom{n_0\ell' + b'n}{2} + k(n_0\ell' + b'n) + b \binom{m_0\ell' - a'n}{2} + j(m_0\ell' - a'n)}, \] which simplifies to the expression in \cref{eq:m-coeffs-formula}.
nodes.statement_short: Both sides lie in the same $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}$ space; compute coefficients by multiplying Fourier series and parametrizing the solutions of a linear Diophantine equation.

nodes.name: Scaled factors
nodes.statement: By \cref{lem:basic}.(iv), $S_u\left(\vect{\alpha x^a}{k}\right) \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(\alpha^u q^{a\binom{u}{2}} x^{au^2} \big)$ and $S_v\left(\vect{\beta x^b}{j}\right) \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(\beta^v q^{b\binom{v}{2}} x^{bv^2} \big)$.
nodes.statement_short: Scaled factors lie in monomial spaces

nodes.name: Product space
nodes.statement: Hence their product lies in the product $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}$-space, which is spanned by the basis vectors on the right-hand side of \cref{eq:m-expansion} for any complete residue system $R$ modulo $au^2+bv^2$ (recall the proof of \cref{prop:polynomial-spaces}).
nodes.statement_short: The product lies in the product space spanned by canonical vectors

nodes.name: Coefficients to compute
nodes.statement: It remains to compute the coefficients $M_\ell(q)$, i.e.\ the coefficients of $x^\ell$ in \[ \vect{\alpha x^a}{k}(u z) \cdot \vect{\beta x^b}{j}(v z) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{a\binom{n}{2} + kn} x^{aun + uk} \cdot \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} \beta^m q^{b\binom{m}{2}+jm} x^{bvm+vj}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Remains to compute $M_\ell$

nodes.name: Multiply series
nodes.statement: By multiplying these series and identifying coefficients of $x^\ell$, we find that \[ M_\ell(q) = \sum_{aun+bvm=\ell-uk-vj} \alpha^n \beta^m q^{a\binom{n}{2} + kn + b\binom{m}{2} + jm} = \sum_{a'n + b'm = \ell'} \alpha^n \beta^m q^{a\binom{n}{2} + kn + b\binom{m}{2} + jm}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Coefficient as a sum over a linear Diophantine equation

nodes.name: Parametrize solutions
nodes.statement: Hence if $\ell' \not\in \mathbb{Z}$, there are no terms in the summation above and thus $M_\ell(q) = 0$. Otherwise, there are infinitely many terms, given precisely by \[ (n, m) = \ell'(n_0, m_0) + p(b', -a'), \qquad\qquad p \in \mathbb{Z}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Empty or parametrized by $p\in\mathbb Z$

nodes.name: Simplify
nodes.statement: By reindexing and replacing $p$ with $n$, this yields \[ M_\ell(q) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^{n_0\ell' + b'n} \beta^{m_0\ell' - a'n} q^{a\binom{n_0\ell' + b'n}{2} + k(n_0\ell' + b'n) + b \binom{m_0\ell' - a'n}{2} + j(m_0\ell' - a'n)}, \] which simplifies to the expression in \cref{eq:m-coeffs-formula}.
nodes.statement_short: Reindex to obtain the formula

nodes.name: Remark: three-step strategy for higher-order product identities
nodes.statement: Given $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{C}^\times$ and positive integers $a, b, u, v$, we are interested in the products below: \begin{align} \text{Type 1:}\qquad &\left\langle \alpha x^{u a}; q^a \right\rangle \left\langle \beta x^{v b}; q^b \right\rangle, \\ \text{Type 2:}\qquad &\left\langle \alpha x^{u a}; q^a \right\rangle \left\langle \alpha^2 x^{2u a}q^a; q^{2a} \right\rangle \left\langle \beta x^{v b}; q^b \right\rangle , \\ \text{Type 3:}\qquad &\left\langle \alpha x^{u a}; q^a \right\rangle \left\langle \alpha^2 x^{2u a}q^a; q^{2a} \right\rangle \left\langle \beta x^{v b}; q^b \right\rangle \left\langle \beta^2 x^{2v b} q^b; q^{2b} \right\rangle. \end{align} At the same time, adequate substitutions in \cref{eq:triple,eq:quintuple} yield \begin{align} \left(q^a; q^a\right)\left\langle \alpha x^{u a}; q^a \right\rangle &= \vect{-\alpha x^a}{0}(uz), \\ \left(q^a; q^a\right) \left\langle \alpha x^{u a}; q^a \right\rangle \left\langle \alpha^2 x^{2u a}q^a; q^{2a} \right\rangle &= \vect{\alpha^3 q^a x^{3a}}{0}(uz) - \alpha \vect{\alpha^3 q^a x^{3a}}{a}(uz), \end{align} In this context, one strategy for finding higher-order product identities proceeds as follows: \begin{itemize} \item[\textbf{Step}]\textbf{1.}\ Given an infinite product as in \cref{eq:type1,eq:type2,eq:type3}, use \cref{eq:substitutions-triple,eq:substitutions-quintuple} to express it as a sum of products of the form in \cref{lem:m-identities}, up to scalar factors of $\left(q^a; q^a\right)\left(q^b; q^b\right)$. \item[\textbf{Step}]\textbf{2.}\ Apply \cref{lem:m-identities} repeatedly and group terms to obtain a representation of the given product in the canonical basis of the appropriate $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\gamma x^d\right)$ space. Having an additional $\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}$ structure (using \cref{tbl:spaces} in case $\alpha, \beta \in \{\pm 1\}$) reduces this work by half, since in a space of the form $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(s q^c x^d\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(t x^{d-2c}\right)$, the canonical basis vectors pair up (recall \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}). \item[\textbf{Step}]\textbf{3.}\ After Step 2, the coefficients of the canonical basis vectors $\vect{\gamma x^d}{\ell}$ in the resulting expansion are linear combinations of theta-type series in $q$, as in \cref{eq:m-coeffs-formula}. Use \cref{eq:substitutions-triple,eq:substitutions-quintuple} again, specialized at adequate values $x \mapsto f(q)$, to rewrite each of these $q$-coefficients as infinite products (when applicable). This results in product identities like \cref{eq:septuple} and \cref{eq:nonuple}. \end{itemize} \cref{tbl:products} gathers some results of this approach.
nodes.statement_short: Types 1-3 of products; express them via triple/quintuple substitutions, expand with M-coefficients, then rewrite coefficients as products.

nodes.name: Type-1 product
nodes.statement: \text{Type 1:}\qquad &\left\langle \alpha x^{u a}; q^a \right\rangle \left\langle \beta x^{v b}; q^b \right\rangle,
nodes.label: eq:type1

nodes.name: Type-2 product
nodes.statement: \text{Type 2:}\qquad &\left\langle \alpha x^{u a}; q^a \right\rangle \left\langle \alpha^2 x^{2u a}q^a; q^{2a} \right\rangle \left\langle \beta x^{v b}; q^b \right\rangle ,
nodes.label: eq:type2

nodes.name: Type-3 product
nodes.statement: \text{Type 3:}\qquad &\left\langle \alpha x^{u a}; q^a \right\rangle \left\langle \alpha^2 x^{2u a}q^a; q^{2a} \right\rangle \left\langle \beta x^{v b}; q^b \right\rangle \left\langle \beta^2 x^{2v b} q^b; q^{2b} \right\rangle.
nodes.label: eq:type3

nodes.name: Triple product substitution
nodes.statement: \left(q^a; q^a\right)\left\langle \alpha x^{u a}; q^a \right\rangle &= \vect{-\alpha x^a}{0}(uz),
nodes.label: eq:substitutions-triple

nodes.name: Quintuple product substitution
nodes.statement: \left(q^a; q^a\right) \left\langle \alpha x^{u a}; q^a \right\rangle \left\langle \alpha^2 x^{2u a}q^a; q^{2a} \right\rangle &= \vect{\alpha^3 q^a x^{3a}}{0}(uz) - \alpha \vect{\alpha^3 q^a x^{3a}}{a}(uz),
nodes.label: eq:substitutions-quintuple

nodes.name: General type-1 identity
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{C}^\times$ and $a, b, u, v$ be positive integers. Define $d := \gcd(au, bv)$, $a' := au/d$ and $b' := bv/d$ as before, and let $c := ab'^2 + ba'^2$. Then there exist coefficients $\gamma_\ell \in \mathbb{C}$ and powers $p_\ell \in \mathbb{Z}$ such that for any complete residue system $R$ modulo $au^2 + bv^2$, \[ \left\langle \alpha x^{u a}; q^a \right\rangle \left\langle \beta x^{v b}; q^b \right\rangle = \sum_{\substack{\ell \in R \\ d \mid \ell}} \gamma_\ell \frac{(q^c; q^c)\left\langle -(-\alpha)^{b'}(-\beta)^{-a'}q^{p_\ell} ; q^c \right\rangle}{\left(q^a; q^a\right)\left(q^b; q^b\right)} \vect{(-\alpha)^u (-\beta)^v q^{a\binom{u}{2} + b \binom{v}{2}} x^{au^2+bv^2}}{\ell}. \] It is often preferable to bring $p_\ell$ to the range $[0, c/2]$ using that $\left\langle y; q^c \right\rangle = -y\left\langle q^c y; q^c \right\rangle = \left\langle q^c/y; q^c \right\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Any type-1 product $\langle\alpha x^{ua};q^a\rangle\langle\beta x^{vb};q^b\rangle$ expands in a canonical basis with infinite-product coefficients.
assumptions: Let $\alpha, \beta \in \mathbb{C}^\times$ and $a, b, u, v$ be positive integers.
nodes.label: prop:general-type-1

nodes.name: Proof of General type-1 identity
nodes.statement: Use \cref{eq:substitutions-triple} and then \cref{lem:m-identities} (for $\alpha \mapsto -\alpha$, $\beta \mapsto -\beta$ and $k = j = 0$) to rewrite the left-hand side as \[ \frac{\vect{-\alpha x^a}{0}(uz) \cdot \vect{-\alpha x^b}{0}(vz)}{\left(q^a; q^a\right)\left(q^b; q^b\right)} = \sum_{d \mid \ell \in R} \frac{M_\ell(q)}{\left(q^a; q^a\right)\left(q^b; q^b\right)} \vect{(-\alpha)^u (-\beta)^v q^{a\binom{u}{2} + b \binom{v}{2}} x^{au^2+bv^2}}{\ell}. \] It remains to identify the coefficients $M_\ell(q)$ as infinite products, which follows from their formula in \cref{eq:m-coeffs-formula}, and the triple product identity with adequate substitutions. The resulting choices of $\gamma_\ell$ are as in \cref{lem:m-identities} but for $\alpha \mapsto -\alpha$ and $\beta \mapsto -\beta$, while $p_\ell = \delta_\ell + (c/2)$ where $\delta_\ell$ are as in \cref{lem:m-identities}.
nodes.statement_short: Triple product substitution, then the multiplication lemma; identify M-coefficients as products via the triple product identity.

nodes.name: Expand
nodes.statement: Use \cref{eq:substitutions-triple} and then \cref{lem:m-identities} (for $\alpha \mapsto -\alpha$, $\beta \mapsto -\beta$ and $k = j = 0$) to rewrite the left-hand side as \[ \frac{\vect{-\alpha x^a}{0}(uz) \cdot \vect{-\alpha x^b}{0}(vz)}{\left(q^a; q^a\right)\left(q^b; q^b\right)} = \sum_{d \mid \ell \in R} \frac{M_\ell(q)}{\left(q^a; q^a\right)\left(q^b; q^b\right)} \vect{(-\alpha)^u (-\beta)^v q^{a\binom{u}{2} + b \binom{v}{2}} x^{au^2+bv^2}}{\ell}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Triple substitution and multiplication lemma

nodes.name: Identify coefficients
nodes.statement: It remains to identify the coefficients $M_\ell(q)$ as infinite products, which follows from their formula in \cref{eq:m-coeffs-formula}, and the triple product identity with adequate substitutions.
nodes.statement_short: M-coefficients are products by the triple identity

nodes.name: Parameters
nodes.statement: The resulting choices of $\gamma_\ell$ are as in \cref{lem:m-identities} but for $\alpha \mapsto -\alpha$ and $\beta \mapsto -\beta$, while $p_\ell = \delta_\ell + (c/2)$ where $\delta_\ell$ are as in \cref{lem:m-identities}.
nodes.statement_short: Read off $\gamma_\ell$ and $p_\ell$

nodes.name: Characters chi_j^(2,c) of M(2,c)_2
nodes.statement: Following \cite[(5.2)]{andrews1999a2}, denote $\chi_j^{(2,c)}(q) := (q; q)^{-1}\left(q^c; q^c\right) \left\langle q^j; q^c \right\rangle$ for all $j \in \mathbb{Z}$, and note that these products satisfy $\chi_{j}^{(2,c)}(q) = -q^j \chi_{j+c}^{(2,c)}(q) = \chi_{c-j}^{(2,c)}(q)$.

nodes.name: M(2, u^2+v^2)_2 character identity
nodes.statement: Let $u, v$ be positive integers with $\gcd(u, v) = 1$ and $u + v$ odd, and set $c := u^2 + v^2$. Let $(n_0, m_0)$ be an integer solution to $un_0 + vm_0 = 1$, and take $p := v n_0 - u m_0$ and $r := (u-v+c)/2$. Then there exist factors $\gamma_\ell$ of the form $(-1)^{a_\ell} q^{b_\ell}$ (depending on $u, v, n_0, m_0$) such that, as an identity of functions in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(-q^{\binom{u}{2} + \binom{v}{2}} x^c\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^{u+v}\right)$, \begin{equation} (q; q)\left\langle x^u; q \right\rangle \left\langle x^v; q \right\rangle = \sum_{\ell = (u+v-c+2)/2}^{(u+v-1)/2} \gamma_\ell\ \chi_{p\ell + r}^{(2, c)}(q) \left( \vect{-q^{\binom{u}{2} + \binom{v}{2}} x^{c}}{\ell} + \vect{-q^{\binom{u}{2} + \binom{v}{2}} x^{c}}{u+v-\ell} \right). \end{equation} Moreover, each character of $M(2, c)_2$ (given by $\chi_j^{(2,c)}(q)$ for $1 \le j \le (c-1)/2$) appears exactly once in \cref{eq:character-id}, after applying the symmetries $\chi_{j}^{(2,c)}(q) = -q^j \chi_{j+c}^{(2,c)}(q) = \chi_{c-j}^{(2,c)}(q)$ as needed.
nodes.statement_short: $(q;q)\langle x^u;q\rangle\langle x^v;q\rangle$ expands in paired canonical vectors with coefficients the $M(2,u^2+v^2)_2$ characters, each appearing once.
assumptions: Let $u, v$ be positive integers with $\gcd(u, v) = 1$ and $u + v$ odd
nodes.label: cor:character-identity

nodes.name: Character identity expansion
nodes.statement: (q; q)\left\langle x^u; q \right\rangle \left\langle x^v; q \right\rangle = \sum_{\ell = (u+v-c+2)/2}^{(u+v-1)/2} \gamma_\ell\ \chi_{p\ell + r}^{(2, c)}(q) \left( \vect{-q^{\binom{u}{2} + \binom{v}{2}} x^{c}}{\ell} + \vect{-q^{\binom{u}{2} + \binom{v}{2}} x^{c}}{u+v-\ell} \right).
nodes.label: eq:character-id

nodes.name: Proof of M(2, u^2+v^2)_2 character identity
nodes.statement: Take $a = b = \alpha = \beta = 1$ and $R = \{(u+v-c+2)/2, \ldots, (u+v+c)/2\}$ in \cref{prop:general-type-1}, and compute \[ p_\ell \ =\ \delta_\ell + \frac{c}{2} \ =\ (vn_0 - um_0)\ell - \frac{v-u}{2} + \frac{c}{2} \ =\ p \ell + r, \] using the values $d = 1$ and $k = j = 0$ in \cref{lem:m-identities}. This produces equation \cref{eq:character-id}, except that $\ell$ varies in $R$ and the canonical basis vectors in the right-hand side are not paired. The pairing follows from the symmetry space $\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^{u+v}\right)$ of the left-hand side (and our adequate choice of $R$); the remaining value $\ell = (u+v+c)/2$ can be ignored since by \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}, the space $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(-q^{\binom{u}{2} + \binom{v}{2}} x^c\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^{u+v}\right)$ is spanned by the sums $\vect{-q^{\binom{u}{2} + \binom{v}{2}} x^{c}}{\ell} + \vect{-q^{\binom{u}{2} + \binom{v}{2}} x^{c}}{u+v-\ell}$ for $(u+v-c+2)/2 \le \ell \le (u+v-1)/2$. Finally, it is easy to check that \[ \gcd(p, c) = 1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad p \ell + r \equiv 0 \pmod{c} \qquad \text{for} \qquad \ell \equiv \frac{u+v+c}{2} \pmod{c}, \] so that the index $p\ell+r$ covers each residue classes modulo $c$ \emph{except for $0$} exactly once when $R \setminus \{(u+v+c)/2\}$. Together with the aforementioned symmetries at $j \mapsto j+c$ and $j \mapsto c-j$ of the characters $\chi^{(2,c)}_{j}(q)$, this settles the second part of \cref{cor:character-identity}.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize the general type-1 identity, pair basis vectors via the $\mathcal S$-symmetry, and check the index $p\ell+r$ runs over nonzero residues mod $c$.

nodes.name: Specialize
nodes.statement: Take $a = b = \alpha = \beta = 1$ and $R = \{(u+v-c+2)/2, \ldots, (u+v+c)/2\}$ in \cref{prop:general-type-1}, and compute \[ p_\ell \ =\ \delta_\ell + \frac{c}{2} \ =\ (vn_0 - um_0)\ell - \frac{v-u}{2} + \frac{c}{2} \ =\ p \ell + r, \] using the values $d = 1$ and $k = j = 0$ in \cref{lem:m-identities}.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize the general type-1 identity

nodes.name: Raw expansion
nodes.statement: This produces equation \cref{eq:character-id}, except that $\ell$ varies in $R$ and the canonical basis vectors in the right-hand side are not paired.
nodes.statement_short: Gives the identity with unpaired vectors

nodes.name: Pairing
nodes.statement: The pairing follows from the symmetry space $\mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^{u+v}\right)$ of the left-hand side (and our adequate choice of $R$); the remaining value $\ell = (u+v+c)/2$ can be ignored since by \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}, the space $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\big(-q^{\binom{u}{2} + \binom{v}{2}} x^c\big) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^{u+v}\right)$ is spanned by the sums $\vect{-q^{\binom{u}{2} + \binom{v}{2}} x^{c}}{\ell} + \vect{-q^{\binom{u}{2} + \binom{v}{2}} x^{c}}{u+v-\ell}$ for $(u+v-c+2)/2 \le \ell \le (u+v-1)/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Pair vectors via the $\mathcal S$-symmetry

nodes.name: Residues of indices
nodes.statement: Finally, it is easy to check that \[ \gcd(p, c) = 1 \qquad\text{and}\qquad p \ell + r \equiv 0 \pmod{c} \qquad \text{for} \qquad \ell \equiv \frac{u+v+c}{2} \pmod{c}, \] so that the index $p\ell+r$ covers each residue classes modulo $c$ \emph{except for $0$} exactly once when $R \setminus \{(u+v+c)/2\}$.
nodes.statement_short: The indices $p\ell+r$ cover nonzero residues

nodes.name: Each character once
nodes.statement: Together with the aforementioned symmetries at $j \mapsto j+c$ and $j \mapsto c-j$ of the characters $\chi^{(2,c)}_{j}(q)$, this settles the second part of \cref{cor:character-identity}.
nodes.statement_short: Each character appears exactly once

nodes.name: Examples u=1,v=2 (septuple) and u=2,v=3
nodes.statement: For $u = 1$ and $v = 2$ (thus $c = u^2 + v^2 = 5$), \cref{cor:character-identity} recovers the septuple product identity from \cref{eq:septuple}, which can be rephrased as \[ \begin{aligned} (q; q)\left\langle x; q\right\rangle \left\langle x^2; q\right\rangle = &-\chi_1^{(2,5)}(q) \left(\vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2}\right) \\ &+\chi_2^{(2,5)}(q) \left(\vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3}\right). \end{aligned} \] For $u = 2$ and $v = 3$, one obtains the analogous result \[ \begin{aligned} (q; q)\left\langle x^2; q\right\rangle \left\langle x^3; q \right\rangle = &- q\chi_5^{(2,13)}(q) \left(\vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{-3} + \vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{8}\right) \\ &- q\chi_3^{(2,13)}(q) \left(\vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{-2} + \vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{7}\right) \\ &+ q\chi_2^{(2,13)}(q) \left(\vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{-1} + \vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{6}\right) \\ &+ \hspace{0.16cm} \chi_6^{(2,13)}(q) \left(\vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{0} + \vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{5}\right) \\ &+ q\chi_1^{(2,13)}(q) \left(\vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{1} + \vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{4}\right) \\ &- \hspace{0.16cm} \chi_4^{(2,13)}(q) \left(\vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{2} + \vect{-q^4 x^{13}}{3}\right) , \end{aligned} \] which may be linked to the Andrews--Gordon identities \cite[Theorem 7.8]{andrews1998theory} as explained after \cref{qtn:characters}. On the other hand, the squared triple product identity from \cref{prop:squared-triple} follows by taking $a = b = u = v = 1$ in \cref{prop:general-type-1} (so that $au^2 + bv^2 = c = 2$), a case not covered by \cref{cor:character-identity}. Other such consequences of \cref{prop:general-type-1} are listed below.
nodes.statement_short: Recovers the septuple identity and gives a level-13 analogue.

nodes.name: More type-1 identities
nodes.statement: As an identity of functions in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^4\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^2\right)$, \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \frac{(q; q)\left(q^3; q^3\right)}{\left(q^{12}; q^{12}\right)} \left\langle x; q\right\rangle \left\langle x^3; q^3\right\rangle &= \left\langle-q^6; q^{12} \right\rangle \vect{x^4}{0} + q \left\langle-1; q^{12} \right\rangle \vect{x^4}{2} \\[-5pt] &- \left\langle-q^3; q^{12} \right\rangle\left(\vect{x^4}{1} + \vect{x^4}{3} \right). \end{aligned} \end{equation} (This is the sextuple product identity from \cite{zhu2011sextuple} in an equivalent form.) Moreover, \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \frac{(q; q)^2}{\left(q^{10}; q^{10}\right)} \left\langle x; q\right\rangle \left\langle x^3; q \right\rangle = &- \left\langle -q^3; q^{10}\right\rangle \left(\vect{q^3x^{10}}{1} + \vect{q^3x^{10}}{3}\right) \\[-5pt] &+ \left\langle -q^4; q^{10}\right\rangle \left(\vect{q^3x^{10}}{0} + \vect{q^3x^{10}}{4}\right)\\ &- q\left\langle-q; q^{10}\right\rangle \hspace{0.15cm} \left(\vect{q^3x^{10}}{-1} + \vect{q^3x^{10}}{5}\right) \\ &+ q\left\langle-q^2; q^{10}\right\rangle \left(\vect{q^3x^{10}}{-2} + \vect{q^3x^{10}}{6}\right)\\ &- q\left\langle-q^5; q^{10}\right\rangle \vect{q^3x^{10}}{-3} \ +\ q\left\langle-1; q^{10}\right\rangle\vect{q^3x^{10}}{2} \end{aligned} \end{equation} inside $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(q^3 x^{10}\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^4\right)$. Finally, in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(-q^6 x^{21}\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^9\right)$, \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \left(q^3; q^3\right)\left\langle x^3; q \right\rangle \left\langle x^6; q^3\right\rangle &= \frac{\vect{-q^6 x^{21}}{0} + \vect{-q^6x^{21}}{9}} {\left\langle q; q^7\right\rangle \left\langle q^2; q^7 \right\rangle} \\ &- \frac{\vect{-q^6 x^{21}}{3} + \vect{-q^6x^{21}}{6}} {\left\langle q^2; q^7\right\rangle \left\langle q^3; q^7 \right\rangle} - q \frac{\vect{-q^6 x^{21}}{-3} + \vect{-q^6x^{21}}{12}} {\left\langle q^3; q^7\right\rangle \left\langle q; q^7 \right\rangle}. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Sextuple identity and two further type-1 identities in $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(q^3x^{10})$ and $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(-q^6x^{21})$.

nodes.name: Sextuple product identity
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \frac{(q; q)\left(q^3; q^3\right)}{\left(q^{12}; q^{12}\right)} \left\langle x; q\right\rangle \left\langle x^3; q^3\right\rangle &= \left\langle-q^6; q^{12} \right\rangle \vect{x^4}{0} + q \left\langle-1; q^{12} \right\rangle \vect{x^4}{2} \\[-5pt] &- \left\langle-q^3; q^{12} \right\rangle\left(\vect{x^4}{1} + \vect{x^4}{3} \right). \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:sextuple

nodes.name: Order-10 type-1 identity
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \frac{(q; q)^2}{\left(q^{10}; q^{10}\right)} \left\langle x; q\right\rangle \left\langle x^3; q \right\rangle = &- \left\langle -q^3; q^{10}\right\rangle \left(\vect{q^3x^{10}}{1} + \vect{q^3x^{10}}{3}\right) \\[-5pt] &+ \left\langle -q^4; q^{10}\right\rangle \left(\vect{q^3x^{10}}{0} + \vect{q^3x^{10}}{4}\right)\\ &- q\left\langle-q; q^{10}\right\rangle \hspace{0.15cm} \left(\vect{q^3x^{10}}{-1} + \vect{q^3x^{10}}{5}\right) \\ &+ q\left\langle-q^2; q^{10}\right\rangle \left(\vect{q^3x^{10}}{-2} + \vect{q^3x^{10}}{6}\right)\\ &- q\left\langle-q^5; q^{10}\right\rangle \vect{q^3x^{10}}{-3} \ +\ q\left\langle-1; q^{10}\right\rangle\vect{q^3x^{10}}{2} \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:order-10

nodes.name: Order-21 type-1 identity
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \left(q^3; q^3\right)\left\langle x^3; q \right\rangle \left\langle x^6; q^3\right\rangle &= \frac{\vect{-q^6 x^{21}}{0} + \vect{-q^6x^{21}}{9}} {\left\langle q; q^7\right\rangle \left\langle q^2; q^7 \right\rangle} \\ &- \frac{\vect{-q^6 x^{21}}{3} + \vect{-q^6x^{21}}{6}} {\left\langle q^2; q^7\right\rangle \left\langle q^3; q^7 \right\rangle} - q \frac{\vect{-q^6 x^{21}}{-3} + \vect{-q^6x^{21}}{12}} {\left\langle q^3; q^7\right\rangle \left\langle q; q^7 \right\rangle}. \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:order-21

nodes.name: Proof of More type-1 identities
nodes.statement: For \cref{eq:sextuple}, use \cref{prop:general-type-1} for $\alpha = \beta = u = v = 1$, $a = 1$ and $b = 3$ (so $c = 1 \cdot 3^2 + 3 \cdot 1^2 = 12$ and $au^2 + bv^2 = 4$), then multiply both sides by $\left(q^a; q^a\right)\left(q^b; q^b\right) / \left(q^{c}; q^{c}\right)$. For \cref{eq:order-10}, repeat the same argument with the only difference that $v = 3$ and $b = 1$ instead (so $c = 1 \cdot 3^2 + 1 \cdot 1^2 = 10$ and $au^2 + bv^2 = 10$). Finally, for \cref{eq:order-21}, take $\alpha = \beta = 1$, $u = 3$, $v = 2$, $a = 1$ and $b = 3$ in \cref{prop:general-type-1}; this leads to $d = 3$, $a' = 1$ and $b' = 2$; thus $c = 1 \cdot 2^2 + 3 \cdot 1^2 = 7$ and $au^2 + bv^2 = 21$.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize the general type-1 identity with three parameter choices.

nodes.name: Sextuple
nodes.statement: For \cref{eq:sextuple}, use \cref{prop:general-type-1} for $\alpha = \beta = u = v = 1$, $a = 1$ and $b = 3$ (so $c = 1 \cdot 3^2 + 3 \cdot 1^2 = 12$ and $au^2 + bv^2 = 4$), then multiply both sides by $\left(q^a; q^a\right)\left(q^b; q^b\right) / \left(q^{c}; q^{c}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Parameters for the sextuple identity

nodes.name: Order 10
nodes.statement: For \cref{eq:order-10}, repeat the same argument with the only difference that $v = 3$ and $b = 1$ instead (so $c = 1 \cdot 3^2 + 1 \cdot 1^2 = 10$ and $au^2 + bv^2 = 10$).
nodes.statement_short: Parameters for the order-10 identity

nodes.name: Order 21
nodes.statement: Finally, for \cref{eq:order-21}, take $\alpha = \beta = 1$, $u = 3$, $v = 2$, $a = 1$ and $b = 3$ in \cref{prop:general-type-1}; this leads to $d = 3$, $a' = 1$ and $b' = 2$; thus $c = 1 \cdot 2^2 + 3 \cdot 1^2 = 7$ and $au^2 + bv^2 = 21$.
nodes.statement_short: Parameters for the order-21 identity

nodes.name: Remark: choice of the order-10 and order-21 identities
nodes.statement: While the freedom in constructing type-1 identities is large, we listed \cref{eq:order-10} and \cref{eq:order-21} since they will lead to identities of generalized eta functions in \cref{subsec:generalized-eta}; in fact, the choices of $a, b, u$ and $v$ were designed to produce the exponents of 10 and 21 in the right-hand sides.

nodes.name: Second septuple product identity
nodes.statement: In $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(-qx^6\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^4\right)$, one has \begin{equation} \left(q^3; q^3\right)\left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle x^3; q^3 \right\rangle = \frac{\vect{-qx^6}{0} + \vect{-qx^6}{4}}{\left(q^3; q^6\right) \left\langle q; q^6 \right\rangle} - \frac{\vect{-qx^6}{1} + \vect{-qx^6}{3}}{\left(q^3; q^6\right) \left\langle q^2; q^6 \right\rangle}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $(q^3;q^3)\langle x;q\rangle\langle qx^2;q^2\rangle\langle x^3;q^3\rangle$ in the paired basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(-qx^6)$.
nodes.label: prop:septuple2

nodes.name: Second septuple product identity (display)
nodes.statement: \left(q^3; q^3\right)\left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle x^3; q^3 \right\rangle = \frac{\vect{-qx^6}{0} + \vect{-qx^6}{4}}{\left(q^3; q^6\right) \left\langle q; q^6 \right\rangle} - \frac{\vect{-qx^6}{1} + \vect{-qx^6}{3}}{\left(q^3; q^6\right) \left\langle q^2; q^6 \right\rangle}.
nodes.label: eq:septuple2

nodes.name: Proof of Second septuple product identity
nodes.statement: Write $(q; q)\left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle = \vect{qx^3}{0} - \vect{qx^3}{1}$ and $\left(q^3; q^3\right)\left\langle x^3; q^3 \right\rangle = \vect{-x^3}{0}$ as in \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple,eq:substitutions-triple}. Multiply these two equalities and apply \cref{lem:m-identities} twice, both times with $a = b = 3$ and $u = v = 1$ (thus $au^2 + bv^2 = 6$ and $ab'^2 + ba'^2 = 6$). Then apply \cref{eq:substitutions-triple} for $a = 6$ and $u = 1$ to express the resulting $q$-coefficients as infinite products, and divide by $(q; q)$ to recover \cref{prop:septuple2}.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply quintuple and triple expansions, apply the multiplication lemma twice, and rewrite coefficients as products.

nodes.name: Expand factors
nodes.statement: Write $(q; q)\left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle = \vect{qx^3}{0} - \vect{qx^3}{1}$ and $\left(q^3; q^3\right)\left\langle x^3; q^3 \right\rangle = \vect{-x^3}{0}$ as in \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple,eq:substitutions-triple}.
nodes.statement_short: Quintuple and triple expansions

nodes.name: Multiply
nodes.statement: Multiply these two equalities and apply \cref{lem:m-identities} twice, both times with $a = b = 3$ and $u = v = 1$ (thus $au^2 + bv^2 = 6$ and $ab'^2 + ba'^2 = 6$).
nodes.statement_short: Apply the multiplication lemma twice

nodes.name: Coefficients as products
nodes.statement: Then apply \cref{eq:substitutions-triple} for $a = 6$ and $u = 1$ to express the resulting $q$-coefficients as infinite products, and divide by $(q; q)$ to recover \cref{prop:septuple2}.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite coefficients and divide

nodes.name: Remark: second septuple identity as possible d=6 case
nodes.statement: We noted in \cref{subsec:dim-bounds} that \cref{thm:bases-proportional,thm:bases-proportional-2} give proportionalities of canonical bases for $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(-qx^d\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^{d-2}\right) \propto \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(f_d)$ when $d \in \{4, 5\}$, corresponding to the octuple and septuple product identities; in this context, \cref{prop:septuple2} may correspond to the case $d = 6$ for some $f_6$. This possibility is supported by the framework in \cref{qtn:characters}, since the $q$-coefficients in the right-hand side of \cref{prop:septuple2} are $M(2, 6)_2$ characters according to the notation in \cite[(5.2)]{andrews1999a2}.

nodes.name: Ewell's octuple product identity
nodes.statement: In $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(-qx^4\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^2\right)$, one has \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} (q; q)\left(q; q^2\right) \left\langle x; q \right\rangle^2 \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle &= \hspace{0.19cm} \left(-q; q^2\right)\left(\vect{-qx^4}{0} + \vect{-qx^4}{2}\right) \\ &- 2\left(-q^2; q^2\right) \vect{-qx^4}{1}. \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Octuple product in the paired canonical basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(-qx^4)$.
nodes.label: prop:octuple

nodes.name: Octuple product identity (display)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} (q; q)\left(q; q^2\right) \left\langle x; q \right\rangle^2 \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle &= \hspace{0.19cm} \left(-q; q^2\right)\left(\vect{-qx^4}{0} + \vect{-qx^4}{2}\right) \\ &- 2\left(-q^2; q^2\right) \vect{-qx^4}{1}. \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:octuple

nodes.name: Proof of Ewell's octuple product identity
nodes.statement: Expand $(q; q)\left\langle x; q\right\rangle = \vect{-x}{0}$ and $(q; q)\left\langle x; q\right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2\right\rangle = \vect{qx^3}{0} - \vect{qx^3}{1}$, multiply the two equalities and apply \cref{lem:m-identities} twice for $a = 3$ and $b = u = v = 1$ (thus $au^2 + bv^2 = 4$ and $ab'^2 + ba'^2 = 12$). Then group terms, apply \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple} with $a = 4$ and $u = 1$ for the coefficient of $\vect{-qx^4}{0} + \vect{-qx^4}{2}$, and \cref{eq:substitutions-triple} with $a = 12$ and $u = 1$ for the coefficient of $\vect{-qx^4}{1}$. To finish, divide everything by $\left(q^2; q^2\right)$ and use that $\left\langle -q; q^4 \right\rangle = \left(-q; q^2\right)$, $\left(q^4; q^4\right)/\left(q^2; q^2\right) = \left(-q^2; q^2\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply triple and quintuple expansions, apply the multiplication lemma, group terms and rewrite coefficients via quintuple/triple substitutions.

nodes.name: Expand and multiply
nodes.statement: Expand $(q; q)\left\langle x; q\right\rangle = \vect{-x}{0}$ and $(q; q)\left\langle x; q\right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2\right\rangle = \vect{qx^3}{0} - \vect{qx^3}{1}$, multiply the two equalities and apply \cref{lem:m-identities} twice for $a = 3$ and $b = u = v = 1$ (thus $au^2 + bv^2 = 4$ and $ab'^2 + ba'^2 = 12$).
nodes.statement_short: Triple and quintuple expansions, multiplication lemma

nodes.name: Coefficients as products
nodes.statement: Then group terms, apply \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple} with $a = 4$ and $u = 1$ for the coefficient of $\vect{-qx^4}{0} + \vect{-qx^4}{2}$, and \cref{eq:substitutions-triple} with $a = 12$ and $u = 1$ for the coefficient of $\vect{-qx^4}{1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Quintuple/triple substitutions for coefficients

nodes.name: Normalize
nodes.statement: To finish, divide everything by $\left(q^2; q^2\right)$ and use that $\left\langle -q; q^4 \right\rangle = \left(-q; q^2\right)$, $\left(q^4; q^4\right)/\left(q^2; q^2\right) = \left(-q^2; q^2\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Divide and simplify products

nodes.name: Proof of the first nonuple product identity
nodes.statement: Recall that the (first) nonuple product in \cref{eq:nonuple} is proportional to \[ \left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle^2 \left\langle x^2; q^2 \right\rangle = \left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle, \] which takes the type-2 form in \cref{eq:type2} for $a = b = u = 1$ and $v = 2$ (and $\alpha = \beta = 1$). After using \cref{eq:substitutions-triple,eq:substitutions-quintuple} and expanding, apply \cref{lem:m-identities} twice for $a = 3, b = 1$, $u = 1$ and $v = 2$, leading to the exponents $au^2 + bv^2 = 7$ in the canonical basis vectors and $ab'^2 + ba'^2 = 3 \cdot 2^2 + 1 \cdot 3^2 = 21$ in the $M_\ell$ coefficients. Then group terms, apply \cref{eq:substitutions-triple} with $a = 21$ and $u = 1$ for the coefficient of $\vect{q^2x^7}{5}$, and \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple} with $a = 7$ and $u = 1$ for the other three $q$-coefficients. Scaling by the appropriate $q$-factor now recovers \cref{eq:nonuple}.
nodes.statement_short: Write the nonuple product as a type-2 product, expand via triple/quintuple substitutions and the multiplication lemma, and rewrite the coefficients as products.

nodes.name: Type-2 form
nodes.statement: Recall that the (first) nonuple product in \cref{eq:nonuple} is proportional to \[ \left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle^2 \left\langle x^2; q^2 \right\rangle = \left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle, \] which takes the type-2 form in \cref{eq:type2} for $a = b = u = 1$ and $v = 2$ (and $\alpha = \beta = 1$).
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite as a type-2 product

nodes.name: Expand
nodes.statement: After using \cref{eq:substitutions-triple,eq:substitutions-quintuple} and expanding, apply \cref{lem:m-identities} twice for $a = 3, b = 1$, $u = 1$ and $v = 2$, leading to the exponents $au^2 + bv^2 = 7$ in the canonical basis vectors and $ab'^2 + ba'^2 = 3 \cdot 2^2 + 1 \cdot 3^2 = 21$ in the $M_\ell$ coefficients.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplication lemma twice

nodes.name: Coefficients as products
nodes.statement: Then group terms, apply \cref{eq:substitutions-triple} with $a = 21$ and $u = 1$ for the coefficient of $\vect{q^2x^7}{5}$, and \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple} with $a = 7$ and $u = 1$ for the other three $q$-coefficients.
nodes.statement_short: Triple and quintuple substitutions

nodes.name: Scale
nodes.statement: Scaling by the appropriate $q$-factor now recovers \cref{eq:nonuple}.
nodes.statement_short: Scale to recover the identity

nodes.name: Second nonuple product identity
nodes.statement: In $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(-q^5 x^{13}\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^3\right)$, one has \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} (q; q)\left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle x^2; q^2 \right\rangle &\left\langle qx^4; q^2 \right\rangle \\ = -&\frac{\vect{-q^5x^{13}}{1} + \vect{-q^5x^{13}}{2}}{\left\langle q^3,q^4,q^5,q^6 ; q^{13}\right\rangle \left\langle q^2 ; q^{26} \right\rangle} + \frac{\vect{-q^5x^{13}}{0} + \vect{-q^5x^{13}}{3}}{\left\langle q,q^2,q^4,q^5 ; q^{13}\right\rangle \left\langle q^6 ; q^{26} \right\rangle} \\[7pt] -\ q&\frac{\vect{-q^5x^{13}}{-1} + \vect{-q^5x^{13}}{4}}{\left\langle q,q^2,q^4,q^6 ; q^{13}\right\rangle \left\langle q^{10} ; q^{26} \right\rangle} -q^2 \frac{\vect{-q^5x^{13}}{-2} + \vect{-q^5x^{13}}{5}}{\left\langle q^2,q^3,q^4,q^5 ; q^{13}\right\rangle \left\langle q^{14} ; q^{26} \right\rangle} \\[7pt] +\ q&\frac{\vect{-q^5x^{13}}{-3} + \vect{-q^5x^{13}}{6}}{\left\langle q,q^2,q^3,q^4 ; q^{13}\right\rangle \left\langle q^{18} ; q^{26} \right\rangle} -q \frac{\vect{-q^5x^{13}}{-4} + \vect{-q^5x^{13}}{7}}{\left\langle q,q^3,q^5,q^6 ; q^{13}\right\rangle \left\langle q^{22} ; q^{26} \right\rangle}, \end{aligned} \end{equation} where we used the common notation $\left\langle q^{a_1}, q^{a_2}, \ldots, q^{a_k}; q^b \right\rangle := \prod_{j=1}^k \left\langle q^{a_j}; q^b \right\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Second nonuple product in the paired canonical basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(-q^5x^{13})$ with level-13 product coefficients.
nodes.label: prop:nonuple2

nodes.name: Second nonuple product identity (display)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} (q; q)\left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle x^2; q^2 \right\rangle &\left\langle qx^4; q^2 \right\rangle \\ = -&\frac{\vect{-q^5x^{13}}{1} + \vect{-q^5x^{13}}{2}}{\left\langle q^3,q^4,q^5,q^6 ; q^{13}\right\rangle \left\langle q^2 ; q^{26} \right\rangle} + \frac{\vect{-q^5x^{13}}{0} + \vect{-q^5x^{13}}{3}}{\left\langle q,q^2,q^4,q^5 ; q^{13}\right\rangle \left\langle q^6 ; q^{26} \right\rangle} \\[7pt] -\ q&\frac{\vect{-q^5x^{13}}{-1} + \vect{-q^5x^{13}}{4}}{\left\langle q,q^2,q^4,q^6 ; q^{13}\right\rangle \left\langle q^{10} ; q^{26} \right\rangle} -q^2 \frac{\vect{-q^5x^{13}}{-2} + \vect{-q^5x^{13}}{5}}{\left\langle q^2,q^3,q^4,q^5 ; q^{13}\right\rangle \left\langle q^{14} ; q^{26} \right\rangle} \\[7pt] +\ q&\frac{\vect{-q^5x^{13}}{-3} + \vect{-q^5x^{13}}{6}}{\left\langle q,q^2,q^3,q^4 ; q^{13}\right\rangle \left\langle q^{18} ; q^{26} \right\rangle} -q \frac{\vect{-q^5x^{13}}{-4} + \vect{-q^5x^{13}}{7}}{\left\langle q,q^3,q^5,q^6 ; q^{13}\right\rangle \left\langle q^{22} ; q^{26} \right\rangle}, \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:nonuple2

nodes.name: Proof of Second nonuple product identity
nodes.statement: The second nonuple product in \cref{eq:nonuple2} can be rewritten (up to a factor of $(q; q)$) as \[ \left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^4; q^2 \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle x; q \right\rangle, \] which takes the form of the type-2 product \cref{eq:type2} for $a = b = v = 1$ and $u = 2$ (and $\alpha = \beta = 1$). As before, use \cref{eq:substitutions-triple,eq:substitutions-quintuple}, then apply \cref{lem:m-identities} twice for $a = 3, b = 1, u = 2$ and $v = 1$ (so that $au^2 + bv^2 = 13$ and $ab'^2 + ba'^2 = 39$). Group terms and apply \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple} with $a = 13$ and $u = 1$ for each of the resulting $q$-coefficients, and scale by the appropriate $q$-factor to conclude.
nodes.statement_short: Type-2 rewriting, multiplication lemma twice, quintuple substitution for each coefficient.

nodes.name: Type-2 form
nodes.statement: The second nonuple product in \cref{eq:nonuple2} can be rewritten (up to a factor of $(q; q)$) as \[ \left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^4; q^2 \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle x; q \right\rangle, \] which takes the form of the type-2 product \cref{eq:type2} for $a = b = v = 1$ and $u = 2$ (and $\alpha = \beta = 1$).
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite as a type-2 product

nodes.name: Expand
nodes.statement: As before, use \cref{eq:substitutions-triple,eq:substitutions-quintuple}, then apply \cref{lem:m-identities} twice for $a = 3, b = 1, u = 2$ and $v = 1$ (so that $au^2 + bv^2 = 13$ and $ab'^2 + ba'^2 = 39$).
nodes.statement_short: Substitutions and multiplication lemma twice

nodes.name: Coefficients as products
nodes.statement: Group terms and apply \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple} with $a = 13$ and $u = 1$ for each of the resulting $q$-coefficients, and scale by the appropriate $q$-factor to conclude.
nodes.statement_short: Quintuple substitution for each coefficient

nodes.name: Remark: nonuple identities are nontrivial at x=1
nodes.statement: What is special about the first and second nonuple product identities, among all identities in this section, is that they do not reduce to trivial equalities when specialized at $x = 1$. In fact, setting $x = 1$ here will lead to new identities of generalized eta functions in \cref{subsec:generalized-eta}.

nodes.name: Squared quintuple product identity
nodes.statement: In $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(q^2x^6\right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^2\right)$, one has \[ \begin{aligned} \frac{(q; q)^2}{\left(q^6; q^6\right)} \left\langle x; q \right\rangle^2 \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle^2 = &\left\langle-q^3; q^6 \right\rangle \left(\vect{q^2x^6}{0} + \vect{q^2x^6}{2}\right)\hspace{0.12cm} - 2q\left\langle-q; q^6 \right\rangle\vect{q^2x^6}{4} \\ +\ q&\left\langle-1; q^6 \right\rangle \left(\vect{q^2x^6}{-1} + \vect{q^2x^6}{3}\right) - 2\left\langle-q^2; q^6 \right\rangle \vect{q^2x^6}{1}. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Square of the quintuple product in the canonical basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(q^2x^6)$.
nodes.label: prop:squared-quintuple

nodes.name: Proof of Squared quintuple product identity
nodes.statement: Square the quintuple product identity $(q; q)\left\langle x; q\right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2\right\rangle = \vect{qx^3}{0} - \vect{qx^3}{1}$, and then proceed exactly as in the proof of \cref{prop:septuple2} (dividing by $(q^6; q^6)$ in the end).
nodes.statement_short: Square the quintuple identity and proceed as for the second septuple identity.

nodes.name: Undecuple product identity
nodes.statement: In $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(q^6 x^{15} \right) \cap \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(x^3 \right)$, one has \[ \begin{aligned} \frac{(q; q)^2}{\left(q^{15}; q^{15}\right)}\left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle x^2q; q^2 \right\rangle^2 &\left\langle x^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle x^4q; q^2 \right\rangle \\ = &-\left\langle -q^6; q^{15} \right\rangle \left(\vect{q^6 x^{15}}{1} + \vect{q^6 x^{15}}{2}\right) \\ &+ \left(\left\langle -q^7; q^{15} \right\rangle + q\left\langle -q^2; q^{15} \right\rangle\right) \left(\vect{q^6 x^{15}}{0} + \vect{q^6 x^{15}}{3}\right) \\ &- q^2 \left\langle -1; q^{15} \right\rangle\left(\vect{q^6 x^{15}}{-1} + \vect{q^6 x^{15}}{4}\right) \\ &- q \left\langle -q^3; q^{15} \right\rangle \left(\vect{q^6 x^{15}}{-2} + \vect{q^6 x^{15}}{5}\right) \\ &+ q\left(\left\langle -q^4; q^{15}\right\rangle + q\left\langle -q; q^{15} \right\rangle\right) \left(\vect{q^6 x^{15}}{-3} + \vect{q^6 x^{15}}{6}\right) \\ &- q\left\langle -q^6; q^{15} \right\rangle \left(\vect{q^6 x^{15}}{-4} + \vect{q^6 x^{15}}{7}\right) \\ &- q^2\left\langle -q^3; q^{15} \right\rangle \left(\vect{q^6 x^{15}}{-5} + \vect{q^6 x^{15}}{8}\right) + 2q^2\left\langle -q^5; q^{15} \right\rangle\vect{q^6 x^{15}}{9}. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Undecuple product in the paired canonical basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(q^6x^{15})$ with level-15 product coefficients.
nodes.label: prop:undecuple

nodes.name: Proof of Undecuple product identity
nodes.statement: Rewrite the undecuple product (up to a factor depending on $q$) as \[ \left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle x^2q ; q^2 \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle \left\langle x^4 q; q^2 \right\rangle, \] which has the form of the type-3 product \cref{eq:type3} for $a = b = u = 1$ and $v = 2$. Apply \cref{lem:m-identities} four times for $a = b = 3$, $u = 1$ and $v = 2$, so that $au^2 + bv^2 = 15$ and $ab'^2 + ba'^2 = 15$. Then group terms, apply \cref{eq:substitutions-triple} with $a = 15$ and $u = 1$ repeatedly, and divide by $\left(q^{15}; q^{15}\right)$ to conclude.
nodes.statement_short: Type-3 rewriting, the multiplication lemma four times, triple substitutions for the coefficients.

nodes.name: Type-3 form
nodes.statement: Rewrite the undecuple product (up to a factor depending on $q$) as \[ \left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle x^2q ; q^2 \right\rangle \cdot \left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle \left\langle x^4 q; q^2 \right\rangle, \] which has the form of the type-3 product \cref{eq:type3} for $a = b = u = 1$ and $v = 2$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite as a type-3 product

nodes.name: Expand
nodes.statement: Apply \cref{lem:m-identities} four times for $a = b = 3$, $u = 1$ and $v = 2$, so that $au^2 + bv^2 = 15$ and $ab'^2 + ba'^2 = 15$.
nodes.statement_short: Multiplication lemma four times

nodes.name: Coefficients as products
nodes.statement: Then group terms, apply \cref{eq:substitutions-triple} with $a = 15$ and $u = 1$ repeatedly, and divide by $\left(q^{15}; q^{15}\right)$ to conclude.
nodes.statement_short: Triple substitutions and division

nodes.name: Question: finitized higher-order product identities
nodes.statement: In \cref{prop:Cauchy}, we reproved a finitized version of Jacobi's triple product identity due to Cauchy; we used that $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f_N) \le 1$, where $f_N(z)$ was a degree-1 rational function in $x$ approaching $-x$ as $N \to \infty$. Are there similar finitized analogues of the higher-order product identities in this section, provable using the finite-dimensionality of the appropriate $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(f_N)$ spaces?
nodes.label: qtn:finitized

nodes.name: Eta quotients and generalized eta quotients
nodes.statement: Recall the notations from \cref{eq:generalized-eta} for the Dedekind eta function $\eta(\tau) := q^{1/24} (q; q)$, and the generalized eta functions $\textnormal E_g(\tau) := q^{N B(g/N)/2}\left\langle q^g; q^N \right\rangle$ of a fixed level $N \ge 1$ (for $\tau \in {\mathbb{H}}^+$). As mentioned after \cref{cor:eta-poly}, these are not to be confused with the Eisenstein series $E_{2k}(\tau)$, which do not appear in this paper. An \emph{eta quotient} \cite{gordon1993multiplicative,martin1997eta} is an expression \[ \prod_{1 \le d \mid n} \eta(d\tau)^{r_d}, \] for some $n \ge 1$ and $r_d \in \mathbb{Z}$; we define \emph{generalized eta quotients} analogously, allowing only functions $\textnormal E_g$ of the same level $N$ (however, $g \in \mathbb{Z}$ may vary).
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions
nodes.statement_short: Recalls $\eta$, $E_g$; eta quotients $\prod\eta(d\tau)^{r_d}$ and their analogues built from $E_g$ of a fixed level.
nodes.label: not:eta

nodes.name: Remark: modularity of eta and generalized eta functions
nodes.statement: $\eta$ is a half-integral weight modular form for the full modular group $\Gamma$, and eta quotients are useful in computing bases of modular forms for congruence subgroups containing $\Gamma_0(n)$. Similarly, the generalized eta functions $\textnormal E_g$ satisfy transformation formulae at the action of $\Gamma_0(N)$ \cite[Corollary 2]{yang2004transformation}; one can design generalized eta quotients that are invariant under the action of $\Gamma_1(N)$, and use them to produce generators of function fields associated to general genus-zero congruence subgroups \cite{yang2004transformation}. The functions $\textnormal E_g$ (and a further generalization $\textnormal E_{g,h}$ thereof) were also studied in \cite{berndt1973generalized}. For our purposes, the generalized eta functions provide the ``right'' normalization of the double infinite products $\left\langle q^g; q^N \right\rangle$, in the sense that when specializing a product identity at a value $x = \pm q^r$, all extraneous powers of $q$ will be encapsulated in the functions $\eta$ and $\textnormal E_g$; this \emph{must} be the case because (non-constant) powers of $q$ do not transform nicely under $\tau \mapsto -1/\tau$. The following lemma provides a few easy facts about $\eta$ and $\textnormal E_g$, with proofs left to the reader.
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions

nodes.name: Basic facts about generalized eta functions
nodes.statement: Let $\tau \in {\mathbb{H}}^+$ and fix a level $N$. \begin{itemize} \item[(i).] If $N$ is odd, $\prod_{g=1}^{\lfloor N/2 \rfloor} \textnormal E_g(\tau) = \frac{\eta(\tau)}{\eta(N\tau)}$. \item[(ii).] If $N$ is even, $\prod_{g=1}^{(N/2)-1} \textnormal E_g(\tau) = \frac{\eta(\tau)}{\eta(N\tau/2)}$. \item[(iii).] For any $g \in \mathbb{Z}$, $\textnormal E_g(\tau) = \textnormal E_{N-g}(\tau) = -\textnormal E_{g+N}(\tau)$. In particular, $\textnormal E_0(\tau) = 0$. \end{itemize}
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions
nodes.statement_short: Products of $E_g$ over $g$ are eta quotients; $E_g=E_{N-g}=-E_{g+N}$.
nodes.label: lem:basic-E

nodes.name: Level-6 generalized eta functions as eta quotients
nodes.statement: For $N \in \{2, 3, 4, 6\}$, each function $\textnormal E_g(\tau)$ can be expressed directly as an eta quotient; for instance, when $N = 6$, quick computations show that \[ \textnormal E_3(\tau) = \frac{\eta(3\tau)^2}{\eta(6\tau)^2} ,\qquad\quad \textnormal E_2(\tau) = \frac{\eta(2\tau)}{\eta(6\tau)} ,\qquad\quad \textnormal E_1(\tau) = \frac{\eta(\tau)\eta(6\tau)}{\eta(2\tau)\eta(3\tau)}. \]
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions

nodes.name: Level-7 generalized eta quotients
nodes.statement: For the level $N = 7$ and $\tau \in {\mathbb{H}}^+$, \begin{align} &\sum_{g=1}^3 \frac{\textnormal E_g(2\tau)}{\textnormal E_{3g}(\tau)} = 2\frac{\eta(14\tau)^2}{\eta(7\tau)^2}, & &\sum_{g=1}^3 \frac{\textnormal E_{3g}(\tau)}{\textnormal E_g(2\tau)} = \frac{\eta(7\tau)^2}{\eta(14\tau)^2}, \\ &\sum_{g=1}^3 \frac{\textnormal E_g(\tau)^2 \textnormal E_{3g}(\tau)}{\textnormal E_{3g}(2\tau)} = 2\frac{\eta(2\tau)^2}{\eta(7\tau)^2}, & &\sum_{g=1}^3 \textnormal E_g(\tau)\textnormal E_{3g}(3\tau) = 0. \end{align}
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions
nodes.statement_short: Four identities for sums over $g$ of level-7 generalized eta quotients.
nodes.label: prop:level-7

nodes.name: Level-7 identities (display)
nodes.statement: &\sum_{g=1}^3 \frac{\textnormal E_g(2\tau)}{\textnormal E_{3g}(\tau)} = 2\frac{\eta(14\tau)^2}{\eta(7\tau)^2}, & &\sum_{g=1}^3 \frac{\textnormal E_{3g}(\tau)}{\textnormal E_g(2\tau)} = \frac{\eta(7\tau)^2}{\eta(14\tau)^2}, \\ &\sum_{g=1}^3 \frac{\textnormal E_g(\tau)^2 \textnormal E_{3g}(\tau)}{\textnormal E_{3g}(2\tau)} = 2\frac{\eta(2\tau)^2}{\eta(7\tau)^2}, & &\sum_{g=1}^3 \textnormal E_g(\tau)\textnormal E_{3g}(3\tau) = 0.
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions
nodes.label: eq:level-7-1

nodes.name: Proof of Level-7 generalized eta quotients
nodes.statement: The first equality in \cref{eq:level-7-1} follows by specializing the nonuple product identity from \cref{prop:nonuple} at $x = 1$; the left-hand side of \cref{eq:nonuple} becomes null due to the factor of $\left\langle x; q\right\rangle$, and the last term in \cref{eq:nonuple} results (after suitable scaling) in the quotient $2\eta(14\tau)^2/\eta(7\tau)^2$ above. The second equality in \cref{eq:level-7-1} is equivalent to an identity of Hickerson; indeed, by dividing the fact that $(4.6)$ equals $(4.8)$ in \cite{hickerson1988seventh} by $-q^3(q; q)\left(q^7; q^7\right)^2$ and simplifying, one obtains: \[ \frac{\left\langle q; q^7 \right\rangle}{\left\langle q^4; q^{14} \right\rangle} - \frac{\left\langle q^2; q^7 \right\rangle}{\left\langle q^6; q^{14} \right\rangle} + \frac{\left\langle q^3; q^7 \right\rangle}{q\left\langle q^2; q^{14} \right\rangle} = \frac{\left\langle q^7; q^{14} \right\rangle}{q}. \] Finally, the two equalities in \cref{eq:level-7-2} follow by specializing our type-1 product identity \cref{eq:order-21} at $x = -q^{1/3}$ (and applying \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple} with $a = 7$ for the specialization of each pair of canonical basis vectors), respectively at $x = 1$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions
nodes.statement_short: Specialize the first nonuple identity at $x=1$, use an identity of Hickerson, and specialize the order-21 identity at $x=-q^{1/3}$ and $x=1$.

nodes.name: Nonuple at x=1
nodes.statement: The first equality in \cref{eq:level-7-1} follows by specializing the nonuple product identity from \cref{prop:nonuple} at $x = 1$; the left-hand side of \cref{eq:nonuple} becomes null due to the factor of $\left\langle x; q\right\rangle$, and the last term in \cref{eq:nonuple} results (after suitable scaling) in the quotient $2\eta(14\tau)^2/\eta(7\tau)^2$ above.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize the first nonuple identity at $x=1$
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions

nodes.name: Hickerson's identity
nodes.statement: The second equality in \cref{eq:level-7-1} is equivalent to an identity of Hickerson; indeed, by dividing the fact that $(4.6)$ equals $(4.8)$ in \cite{hickerson1988seventh} by $-q^3(q; q)\left(q^7; q^7\right)^2$ and simplifying, one obtains: \[ \frac{\left\langle q; q^7 \right\rangle}{\left\langle q^4; q^{14} \right\rangle} - \frac{\left\langle q^2; q^7 \right\rangle}{\left\langle q^6; q^{14} \right\rangle} + \frac{\left\langle q^3; q^7 \right\rangle}{q\left\langle q^2; q^{14} \right\rangle} = \frac{\left\langle q^7; q^{14} \right\rangle}{q}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Equivalent to an identity of Hickerson
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions

nodes.name: Order-21 specializations
nodes.statement: Finally, the two equalities in \cref{eq:level-7-2} follow by specializing our type-1 product identity \cref{eq:order-21} at $x = -q^{1/3}$ (and applying \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple} with $a = 7$ for the specialization of each pair of canonical basis vectors), respectively at $x = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize the order-21 identity
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions

nodes.name: Proof of Eta quotient polynomial
nodes.statement: Letting $X_g(\tau) := \textnormal E_g(2\tau)/\textnormal E_{3g}(\tau)$, \cref{eq:level-7-1} provides identities for $X_1 + X_2 + X_3$ and $\frac{1}{X_1} + \frac{1}{X_2} + \frac{1}{X_3}$. Combining these with the fact that \[ X_1(\tau)X_2(\tau)X_3(\tau) = -\frac{\prod_{g=1}^3 \textnormal E_g(2\tau)}{\prod_{g=1}^3 \textnormal E_g(\tau)} = -\frac{\eta(2\tau)\eta(7\tau)}{\eta(\tau)\eta(14\tau)}, \] which follows from \cref{lem:basic-E}, we obtain the three Vieta identities for $(X - X_1)(X - X_2)(X - X_3)$ that constitute \cref{cor:eta-poly}.
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions
nodes.statement_short: Vieta: the level-7 identities give the elementary symmetric functions of the three quotients.

nodes.name: Level-10 generalized eta quotients
nodes.statement: For the level $N = 10$ and $\tau \in {\mathbb{H}}^+$, \begin{align*} \frac{\textnormal E_1(2\tau)\textnormal E_2(2\tau)}{\textnormal E_1(\tau)\textnormal E_2(\tau)} &= \frac{1}{2}\left( \frac{\eta(2\tau)^4}{\eta(\tau)^2\eta(10\tau)^2} - \frac{\eta(10\tau)^2}{\eta(5\tau)^2} - \frac{\eta(\tau)\eta(5\tau)}{\eta(10\tau)^2} \right), \\ \frac{\textnormal E_3(2\tau)\textnormal E_4(2\tau)}{\textnormal E_3(\tau)\textnormal E_4(\tau)} &= \frac{1}{2}\left( \frac{\eta(2\tau)^4}{\eta(\tau)^2\eta(10\tau)^2} - \frac{\eta(10\tau)^2}{\eta(5\tau)^2} + \frac{\eta(\tau)\eta(5\tau)}{\eta(10\tau)^2} \right). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions
nodes.statement_short: Two level-10 generalized eta quotients expressed through Dedekind eta quotients.

nodes.name: Proof of Level-10 generalized eta quotients
nodes.statement: We obtain separate identities for the sum and the difference of the two quotients above. The equality \[ \frac{\textnormal E_1(2\tau)\textnormal E_2(2\tau)}{\textnormal E_1(\tau)\textnormal E_2(\tau)} + \frac{\textnormal E_3(2\tau)\textnormal E_4(2\tau)}{\textnormal E_3(\tau)\textnormal E_4(\tau)} = \frac{\eta(2\tau)^4}{\eta(\tau)^2\eta(10\tau)^2} - \frac{\eta(10\tau)^2}{\eta(5\tau)^2} \] follows by specializing our type-1 identity \cref{eq:order-10} at $x = -1$. The second equality, \[ \frac{\textnormal E_3(2\tau)\textnormal E_4(2\tau)}{\textnormal E_3(\tau)\textnormal E_4(\tau)} - \frac{\textnormal E_1(2\tau)\textnormal E_2(2\tau)}{\textnormal E_1(\tau)\textnormal E_2(\tau)} = \frac{\eta(\tau)\eta(5\tau)}{\eta(10\tau)^2}, \] is equivalent (after multiplying by $\eta(10\tau)\textnormal E_1(\tau) \textnormal E_2(\tau) \textnormal E_3(\tau) \textnormal E_4(\tau) = \eta(\tau)\eta(10\tau)/\eta(5\tau)$ and a power of $q$) to the fact that \begin{equation} U\left(q, q^{10}\right) - qU\left(q^3, q^{10}\right) = \frac{(q; q)^2}{\left(q^{10}; q^{10}\right)}, \end{equation} where $U(x, q) := (q; q)\left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle^2 \left\langle x^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle q x^4 ; q^2 \right\rangle$ denotes the undecuple product from \cref{prop:undecuple}. Finally, \cref{eq:undecuple-det} is precisely the statement that the determinant of the matrix in \cref{eq:explicit-matrix} equals $1$; we will prove this in the next section (non-circularly), based on a generalization of \cref{prop:2x2-determinant} and 4 identities of Slater \cite[(94),(96),(98),(99)]{slater1952further}, which are also implied by \cref{thm:bases-proportional}.
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions
nodes.statement_short: Sum from specializing the order-10 identity at $x=-1$; difference reduces to a determinant identity for undecuple products proved later via Slater's identities.

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: We obtain separate identities for the sum and the difference of the two quotients above.
nodes.statement_short: Treat sum and difference separately
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions

nodes.name: Sum
nodes.statement: The equality \[ \frac{\textnormal E_1(2\tau)\textnormal E_2(2\tau)}{\textnormal E_1(\tau)\textnormal E_2(\tau)} + \frac{\textnormal E_3(2\tau)\textnormal E_4(2\tau)}{\textnormal E_3(\tau)\textnormal E_4(\tau)} = \frac{\eta(2\tau)^4}{\eta(\tau)^2\eta(10\tau)^2} - \frac{\eta(10\tau)^2}{\eta(5\tau)^2} \] follows by specializing our type-1 identity \cref{eq:order-10} at $x = -1$.
