nodes.statement_short: Specialize the order-10 identity at $x=-1$
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions

nodes.name: Difference
nodes.statement: The second equality, \[ \frac{\textnormal E_3(2\tau)\textnormal E_4(2\tau)}{\textnormal E_3(\tau)\textnormal E_4(\tau)} - \frac{\textnormal E_1(2\tau)\textnormal E_2(2\tau)}{\textnormal E_1(\tau)\textnormal E_2(\tau)} = \frac{\eta(\tau)\eta(5\tau)}{\eta(10\tau)^2}, \] is equivalent (after multiplying by $\eta(10\tau)\textnormal E_1(\tau) \textnormal E_2(\tau) \textnormal E_3(\tau) \textnormal E_4(\tau) = \eta(\tau)\eta(10\tau)/\eta(5\tau)$ and a power of $q$) to the fact that \begin{equation} U\left(q, q^{10}\right) - qU\left(q^3, q^{10}\right) = \frac{(q; q)^2}{\left(q^{10}; q^{10}\right)}, \end{equation} where $U(x, q) := (q; q)\left\langle x; q \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle^2 \left\langle x^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle q x^4 ; q^2 \right\rangle$ denotes the undecuple product from \cref{prop:undecuple}.
nodes.statement_short: Equivalent to an undecuple determinant identity
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions

nodes.name: Determinant identity
nodes.statement: Finally, \cref{eq:undecuple-det} is precisely the statement that the determinant of the matrix in \cref{eq:explicit-matrix} equals $1$; we will prove this in the next section (non-circularly), based on a generalization of \cref{prop:2x2-determinant} and 4 identities of Slater \cite[(94),(96),(98),(99)]{slater1952further}, which are also implied by \cref{thm:bases-proportional}.
nodes.statement_short: It is the determinant of the explicit matrix, proved later
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions

nodes.name: Undecuple determinant identity
nodes.statement: U\left(q, q^{10}\right) - qU\left(q^3, q^{10}\right) = \frac{(q; q)^2}{\left(q^{10}; q^{10}\right)},
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions
nodes.label: eq:undecuple-det

nodes.name: Remark: relating the undecuple identity to the determinant identity
nodes.statement: It would be interesting to see if our undecuple product identity (\cref{prop:undecuple}) can be used to prove \cref{eq:undecuple-det}, or if it can be combined with \cref{eq:undecuple-det} to produce other identities of eta quotients.
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions

nodes.name: Level-13 generalized eta quotients
nodes.statement: For the level $N = 13$ and $\tau \in {\mathbb{H}}^+$, \[ \sum_{g=1}^6 \frac{\textnormal E_{g}(\tau)\textnormal E_{2g}(\tau)\textnormal E_{6g}(\tau)}{\textnormal E_g(2\tau)} = 0. \]
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions
nodes.statement_short: A vanishing sum of six level-13 generalized eta quotients.
nodes.label: prop:level-13

nodes.name: Proof of Level-13 generalized eta quotients
nodes.statement: Specialize the second nonuple product identity from \cref{prop:nonuple2} at $x = 1$; as before, the left-hand side of \cref{eq:nonuple2} becomes null due to the factor of $\left\langle x; q \right\rangle$.
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions
nodes.statement_short: Specialize the second nonuple identity at $x=1$.

nodes.name: Question: polynomial identities for level-13 and other eta quotients
nodes.statement: Is there an analogue of the polynomial identity in \cref{cor:eta-poly} for the level $N = 13$ (or for other levels), building on \cref{prop:level-13}? One could attempt, for example, to determine closed forms (in terms of $\eta$) for the coefficients of $X^4, X^3, X^2$ and $X$ in \[ \prod_{g=1}^6 \left(X - \frac{\textnormal E_{g}(\tau)\textnormal E_{2g}(\tau)\textnormal E_{6g}(\tau)}{\textnormal E_g(2\tau)}\right). \] More broadly, is there a wider class of generalized eta quotients that occur as roots of polynomials whose coefficients are Dedekind eta quotients, and can this be used to compute special values of the $\textnormal E_g$ quotients as algebraic integers?
nodes.section: 4.2 Identities for quotients of generalized eta functions

nodes.name: Two-variable Rogers-Ramanujan sum and its Fourier coefficients
nodes.statement: \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}, n \ge 0} \frac{q^{\binom{m}{2} + \binom{n+1}{2}}}{(q; q)_n} (-x)^{m+n} = \cdots + \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{(q; q)_n} x^0 - \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_n} x^1 + \cdots \quad \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2 -x \right),
nodes.label: eq:two-variable-statement-sum

nodes.name: Rogers' two-variable identity (Rogers, 1894)
nodes.statement: In $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{+}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(1, qx)$, one has (see \cite[p.~292--294]{hardy1979introduction} and \cite[p.~330]{rogers1893second}) \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_n} x^n &= \sum_{n \geq 0}(-1)^n \frac{q^{5\binom{n}{2}+2n}}{(q; q)_n \left(q^n x; q\right)} \left(1 - q^{2n} x\right) x^{2n} \\ &= \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} x^n \left(-q^{2n+2} x; q^2\right). \end{aligned} \end{equation} In fact, the left-hand side lies in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1, qx)$, and thus all the singularities on the right are removable.
nodes.statement_short: $\sum q^{n^2}x^n/(q;q)_n$ equals Rogers' quintic-exponent series and a q-binomial-type series.
nodes.label: prop:rogers

nodes.name: Rogers' identity (display)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_n} x^n &= \sum_{n \geq 0}(-1)^n \frac{q^{5\binom{n}{2}+2n}}{(q; q)_n \left(q^n x; q\right)} \left(1 - q^{2n} x\right) x^{2n} \\ &= \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} x^n \left(-q^{2n+2} x; q^2\right). \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:rogers

nodes.name: Remark: recovering Rogers-Ramanujan from Rogers' identity
nodes.statement: The two Rogers--Ramanujan identities in \cref{eq:rog-ram} can be recovered from the first equality in \cref{eq:rogers} by letting $x \to 1$, respectively $x \to q$, and then using \cref{eq:canonical-formula} with $d = 5$. Also, the series in the left-hand side of \cref{eq:rogers} will reappear in \cref{cor:rogers-type-sums}, which will raise the problem of finding a similar identity for $\sum_{n \geq 0} q^{n^2} (q^4; q^4)_n^{-1} x^{2n} \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2, 1\right)$; see \cref{qtn:rogers-type-sums}.

nodes.name: Proof of Rogers' identity in the T_D framework
nodes.statement: We saw in \cref{ex:two-var-rog-ram,ex:two-var-rog-ram-ctd} that $\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_n} x^n \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1, qx)$, and that $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1, qx) = \dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{+}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(1, qx) = 1$. A significantly lengthier computation shows that the right-hand side lies in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{+}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(1, qx)$ as well; see the function $H_1$ in \cite[p.~292--294]{hardy1979introduction}. Identifying the coefficients of $x^0$, which are equal to $1$ on both sides of \cref{eq:rogers}, completes the proof of the first equality. For the second equality, it is easier to take $x \mapsto x^2$; denote \[ L(z) := \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_n} x^{2n} \qquad\text{and}\qquad R(z) := \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} x^{2n} \left(-q^{2n+2} x^2; q^2\right), \] where $R(z)$ is almost a twisted sum in the sense of \cref{eq:w-coeffs}. Since $L(z/2) \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1, qx)$, one can obtain \[ \begin{cases} L(z) - L(z+\tau/2) = qx^2 L(z+\tau) \\ L(z+\tau/2) - L(z+\tau) = q^2x^2 L(z+3\tau/2) \quad \Rightarrow \quad L \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(1 + qx^2 + q^2 x^2, -q^5 x^4\right). \\ L(z+\tau) - L(z+3\tau/2) = q^3x^2 L(z+2\tau). \end{cases} \] Hence it is natural to attempt to show that $R \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(1 + qx^2 + q^2 x^2, -q^5 x^4\right)$ as well, and this follows with little effort after expanding $R(z) - \left(1 + q^2 x^2\right)R(z+\tau)$. Now from \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii) for $n_0 = -3$ one obtains that $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(1 + qx^2 + q^2 x^2, -q^5 x^4\right) \le 4$, and thus by \cref{lem:proofs-by-fourier} it suffices to check that $\widehat{L}(k) = \widehat{R}(k)$ for $k \in \{-3, -2, -1, 0\}$. But these Fourier coefficients are $0, 0, 0, 1$ respectively for both $L$ and $R$, proving that $L = R$.
nodes.statement_short: Both sides lie in a one-dimensional $\mathcal T(1,qx)$; compare $x^0$ coefficients. For the second equality show both sides lie in a 4-dimensional $\mathcal T$ space and compare four coefficients.

nodes.name: One-dimensional space
nodes.statement: We saw in \cref{ex:two-var-rog-ram,ex:two-var-rog-ram-ctd} that $\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_n} x^n \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1, qx)$, and that $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1, qx) = \dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{+}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(1, qx) = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Left side lies in a one-dimensional space

nodes.name: Right side in space
nodes.statement: A significantly lengthier computation shows that the right-hand side lies in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{+}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}(1, qx)$ as well; see the function $H_1$ in \cite[p.~292--294]{hardy1979introduction}.
nodes.statement_short: Right side lies there too (Hardy-Wright)

nodes.name: First equality
nodes.statement: Identifying the coefficients of $x^0$, which are equal to $1$ on both sides of \cref{eq:rogers}, completes the proof of the first equality.
nodes.statement_short: Compare $x^0$ coefficients

nodes.name: Define L and R
nodes.statement: For the second equality, it is easier to take $x \mapsto x^2$; denote \[ L(z) := \sum_{n \geq 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_n} x^{2n} \qquad\text{and}\qquad R(z) := \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} x^{2n} \left(-q^{2n+2} x^2; q^2\right), \] where $R(z)$ is almost a twisted sum in the sense of \cref{eq:w-coeffs}.
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $x\mapsto x^2$ and define $L$, $R$

nodes.name: Functional equation of L
nodes.statement: Since $L(z/2) \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1, qx)$, one can obtain \[ \begin{cases} L(z) - L(z+\tau/2) = qx^2 L(z+\tau) \\ L(z+\tau/2) - L(z+\tau) = q^2x^2 L(z+3\tau/2) \quad \Rightarrow \quad L \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(1 + qx^2 + q^2 x^2, -q^5 x^4\right). \\ L(z+\tau) - L(z+3\tau/2) = q^3x^2 L(z+2\tau). \end{cases} \]
nodes.statement_short: $L$ lies in a 4-term $\mathcal T$ space

nodes.name: R in same space
nodes.statement: Hence it is natural to attempt to show that $R \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(1 + qx^2 + q^2 x^2, -q^5 x^4\right)$ as well, and this follows with little effort after expanding $R(z) - \left(1 + q^2 x^2\right)R(z+\tau)$.
nodes.statement_short: Check $R$ lies in the same space

nodes.name: Dimension bound
nodes.statement: Now from \cref{prop:upper-bounds}.(ii) for $n_0 = -3$ one obtains that $\dim \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(1 + qx^2 + q^2 x^2, -q^5 x^4\right) \le 4$, and thus by \cref{lem:proofs-by-fourier} it suffices to check that $\widehat{L}(k) = \widehat{R}(k)$ for $k \in \{-3, -2, -1, 0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Space has dimension at most 4

nodes.name: Compare coefficients
nodes.statement: But these Fourier coefficients are $0, 0, 0, 1$ respectively for both $L$ and $R$, proving that $L = R$.
nodes.statement_short: Four coefficients agree

nodes.name: Proof that the Rogers-Ramanujan identities are equivalent to the two-variable statement
nodes.statement: The first equality in \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram} and the membership to $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2 - x\right)$ follow immediately from the expansions \[ (q; q)\left\langle x; q\right\rangle = \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{\binom{m}{2}} (-x)^m \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(-x) \qquad \text{and} \qquad (qx; q) = \sum_{n \ge 0} (-1)^n \frac{q^{\binom{n+1}{2}}}{(q; q)_n} (-x)^n \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1-qx), \] due to \cref{eq:triple} and \cref{eq:basic1}. The second equality in \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram} implies \cref{eq:rog-ram} by identifying the coefficients of $x^0$ as $x^1$, as seen in \cref{eq:two-variable-statement-sum}. Conversely, identifying the coefficients of $x^0$ and $x^1$ is enough to prove an equality in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(qx^2 - x\right)$, by \cref{lem:proofs-by-fourier} (or in this case, directly by \cref{eq:fourier-coeffs-basis}).
nodes.statement_short: Expand via triple product and Euler; the canonical-basis coefficients of $x^0,x^1$ are exactly the Rogers-Ramanujan sums, by Fourier identification.

nodes.name: First equality
nodes.statement: The first equality in \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram} and the membership to $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2 - x\right)$ follow immediately from the expansions \[ (q; q)\left\langle x; q\right\rangle = \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{\binom{m}{2}} (-x)^m \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(-x) \qquad \text{and} \qquad (qx; q) = \sum_{n \ge 0} (-1)^n \frac{q^{\binom{n+1}{2}}}{(q; q)_n} (-x)^n \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1-qx), \] due to \cref{eq:triple} and \cref{eq:basic1}.
nodes.statement_short: Triple product and Euler expansions

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: The second equality in \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram} implies \cref{eq:rog-ram} by identifying the coefficients of $x^0$ as $x^1$, as seen in \cref{eq:two-variable-statement-sum}.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficients of $x^0,x^1$ give the RR identities

nodes.name: Converse
nodes.statement: Conversely, identifying the coefficients of $x^0$ and $x^1$ is enough to prove an equality in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(qx^2 - x\right)$, by \cref{lem:proofs-by-fourier} (or in this case, directly by \cref{eq:fourier-coeffs-basis}).
nodes.statement_short: Fourier identification gives the converse

nodes.name: Twisted two-variable Rogers-Ramanujan
nodes.statement: For $\tau \in {\mathbb{H}}^+$ and $z \in \mathbb{C}$, one has \[ \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \left( q^{n+1}x; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2 + n}x^{2n+1} \left( q^{n+1}x; q\right) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \vspace{0.1cm}\\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2}{1} \end{pmatrix}, \] where \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \vspace{0.1cm}\\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} = \frac{\left(q^{10}; q^{10}\right)}{(q; q)} \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle q; q^{10}\right\rangle \left\langle q^8; q^{20} \right\rangle & -q\left\langle q^4; q^{10} \right\rangle \left\langle q^2; q^{20} \right\rangle \vspace{0.1cm} \\ -\left\langle q^3; q^{10}\right\rangle \left\langle q^4; q^{20} \right\rangle & \left\langle q^2; q^{10} \right\rangle \left\langle q^6; q^{20} \right\rangle \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Two twisted theta series equal an explicit $2\times2$ matrix of level-10/20 products times the canonical basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(qx^2)$.
nodes.label: thm:twisted-rog-ram

nodes.name: Explicit matrix of the twisted Rogers-Ramanujan theorem
nodes.statement: \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \vspace{0.1cm}\\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} = \frac{\left(q^{10}; q^{10}\right)}{(q; q)} \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle q; q^{10}\right\rangle \left\langle q^8; q^{20} \right\rangle & -q\left\langle q^4; q^{10} \right\rangle \left\langle q^2; q^{20} \right\rangle \vspace{0.1cm} \\ -\left\langle q^3; q^{10}\right\rangle \left\langle q^4; q^{20} \right\rangle & \left\langle q^2; q^{10} \right\rangle \left\langle q^6; q^{20} \right\rangle \end{pmatrix}.
nodes.label: eq:explicit-matrix

nodes.name: Remark: twisted theorem generalizes Rogers-Ramanujan by value identification
nodes.statement: One can recover the Rogers--Ramanujan identities by taking $x = 1$ above, as we will see shortly; thus \cref{thm:bases-proportional} is a generalization of \cref{eq:rog-ram} by value identification, unlike \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram}. Also, \cref{cor:3-var-2x2-matrix-ctd} and \cref{eq:slater} will show that the matrix in \cref{eq:explicit-matrix} has determinant equal to $1$.

nodes.name: Proof that the twisted theorem is equivalent to the main theorem
nodes.statement: Using the triple product identity in the form $\vect{-qx}{0} = (q;q) \left(x^{-1}; q\right) (qx; q)$, one can rewrite \cref{thm:bases-proportional} as \[ (q; q)\left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle \begin{pmatrix} \left(x^{-1}; q\right)\vect{qx^2-x}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \left(x^{-1}; q\right)\vect{qx^2-x}{1} \end{pmatrix} = -\vect{-qx}{0} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3} \end{pmatrix}, \] Now recall the formulae for canonical basis vectors from \cref{cor:kind2} (use $y = 1$): \[ \begin{pmatrix} \left(x^{-1}; q\right)\vect{qx^2-x}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \left(x^{-1}; q\right)\vect{qx^2-x}{1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \left(q^{-n+1}x^{-1}; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2+n} x^{2n+1} \left(q^{-n}x^{-1}; q\right) \end{pmatrix}. \] As observed in the proof of \cref{prop:exact-formulae-kind2}, the two series in the right-hand side are just \emph{twisted} versions of the series $\vect{qx^2}{0}$ and $\vect{qx^2}{1}$, so they lie in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2\right)$. But by \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}, we have $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2\right) \subset \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}(1)$, and so these series are invariant under $x \mapsto x^{-1}$; thus \[ \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \left(q^{-n+1}x^{-1}; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n} q^{n^2+n} x^{2n+1} \left(q^{-n}x^{-1}; q\right) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n} q^{n^2} x^{-2n} (q^{-n+1}x; q) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n} q^{n^2+n} x^{-2n-1} (q^{-n}x; q) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n} q^{n^2} x^{2n} (q^{n+1}x; q) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n} q^{n^2+n} x^{2n+1} (q^{n+1}x; q) \end{pmatrix}, \] where all summations are over $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, and we took $n \mapsto -n$ and $n \mapsto -n-1$ in the last equality. Overall, we have found that \cref{thm:bases-proportional} is equivalent to \begin{equation} (q; q) \left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \left( q^{n+1}x; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2 + n}x^{2n+1} \left( q^{n+1}x; q\right) \end{pmatrix} = -\vect{-qx}{0} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3} \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation} Now by applying the multiplication identities from \cref{lem:m-identities} four times, and using \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple} with $a = 10$ on each $q$-coefficient (as in Step 3 from \cref{subsec:higher-order}), we find that \[ \vect{-qx}{0} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3} \end{pmatrix} = (q; q) \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \vspace{0.1cm}\\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{q^2x^6}{2} - \vect{q^2x^6}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{q^2x^6}{3} - \vect{q^2x^6}{-1} \end{pmatrix}, \] where $A(q), B(q), C(q), D(q)$ are exactly as in \cref{eq:explicit-matrix}. Hence to prove that \cref{thm:bases-proportional} is equivalent to \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram}, it suffices to show that \begin{equation} \left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2}{1} \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{q^2x^6}{0} - \vect{q^2x^6}{2} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{q^2x^6}{-1} - \vect{q^2x^6}{3} \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation} Now by \cref{eq:substitutions-triple} and \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple}, we have \[ \begin{aligned} \left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2}{1} \end{pmatrix} &= \left(q^2; q^2\right) \left\langle x^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle -qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle \vspace{0.1cm} \\ x\left\langle -q^2 x^2; q^2 \right\rangle \end{pmatrix} \\ &= \left(q^2; q^2\right) \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle x^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle q^2x^4; q^4 \right\rangle \vspace{0.1cm} \\ -x^3\left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle q^4x^4; q^4 \right\rangle \end{pmatrix} \qquad = \begin{pmatrix} \vect{q^2x^6}{0} - \vect{q^2x^6}{2} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ -x^3\left(\vect{q^5x^6}{0} - q\vect{q^5x^6}{2}\right) \end{pmatrix}, \end{aligned} \] which simplifies to the right-hand side of \cref{eq:to-show-quintuple}, using that $q\vect{q^5 x^6}{2} = \vect{q^5x^6}{-4}$ and $x^3 \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(q^{-3}\right)$. Thus indeed \cref{thm:bases-proportional} $\Leftrightarrow$ \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram}.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the main theorem via the triple product and second-kind canonical formulas into twisted series; the multiplication lemma reduces the equivalence to a quintuple-type identity.

nodes.name: Rewrite main theorem
nodes.statement: Using the triple product identity in the form $\vect{-qx}{0} = (q;q) \left(x^{-1}; q\right) (qx; q)$, one can rewrite \cref{thm:bases-proportional} as \[ (q; q)\left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle \begin{pmatrix} \left(x^{-1}; q\right)\vect{qx^2-x}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \left(x^{-1}; q\right)\vect{qx^2-x}{1} \end{pmatrix} = -\vect{-qx}{0} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3} \end{pmatrix}, \]
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite via the triple product

nodes.name: Second-kind formulas
nodes.statement: Now recall the formulae for canonical basis vectors from \cref{cor:kind2} (use $y = 1$): \[ \begin{pmatrix} \left(x^{-1}; q\right)\vect{qx^2-x}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \left(x^{-1}; q\right)\vect{qx^2-x}{1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \left(q^{-n+1}x^{-1}; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2+n} x^{2n+1} \left(q^{-n}x^{-1}; q\right) \end{pmatrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Insert explicit canonical vectors

nodes.name: Twisted series
nodes.statement: As observed in the proof of \cref{prop:exact-formulae-kind2}, the two series in the right-hand side are just \emph{twisted} versions of the series $\vect{qx^2}{0}$ and $\vect{qx^2}{1}$, so they lie in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: They are twisted series in $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(qx^2)$

nodes.name: Symmetry x->1/x
nodes.statement: But by \cref{prop:monomial-spaces}, we have $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2\right) \subset \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}(1)$, and so these series are invariant under $x \mapsto x^{-1}$; thus \[ \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \left(q^{-n+1}x^{-1}; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n} q^{n^2+n} x^{2n+1} \left(q^{-n}x^{-1}; q\right) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n} q^{n^2} x^{-2n} (q^{-n+1}x; q) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n} q^{n^2+n} x^{-2n-1} (q^{-n}x; q) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n} q^{n^2} x^{2n} (q^{n+1}x; q) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n} q^{n^2+n} x^{2n+1} (q^{n+1}x; q) \end{pmatrix}, \] where all summations are over $n \in \mathbb{Z}$, and we took $n \mapsto -n$ and $n \mapsto -n-1$ in the last equality.
nodes.statement_short: Use the $\mathcal S$-symmetry and reindex

nodes.name: Reformulation
nodes.statement: Overall, we have found that \cref{thm:bases-proportional} is equivalent to \begin{equation} (q; q) \left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \left( q^{n+1}x; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2 + n}x^{2n+1} \left( q^{n+1}x; q\right) \end{pmatrix} = -\vect{-qx}{0} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3} \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Main theorem equivalent to a reformulated identity

nodes.name: Multiplication lemma
nodes.statement: Now by applying the multiplication identities from \cref{lem:m-identities} four times, and using \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple} with $a = 10$ on each $q$-coefficient (as in Step 3 from \cref{subsec:higher-order}), we find that \[ \vect{-qx}{0} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3} \end{pmatrix} = (q; q) \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \vspace{0.1cm}\\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{q^2x^6}{2} - \vect{q^2x^6}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{q^2x^6}{3} - \vect{q^2x^6}{-1} \end{pmatrix}, \] where $A(q), B(q), C(q), D(q)$ are exactly as in \cref{eq:explicit-matrix}.
nodes.statement_short: Expand the right-hand side with the explicit matrix

nodes.name: Reduce
nodes.statement: Hence to prove that \cref{thm:bases-proportional} is equivalent to \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram}, it suffices to show that \begin{equation} \left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2}{1} \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{q^2x^6}{0} - \vect{q^2x^6}{2} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{q^2x^6}{-1} - \vect{q^2x^6}{3} \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Reduces to a quintuple-type identity

nodes.name: Verify
nodes.statement: Now by \cref{eq:substitutions-triple} and \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple}, we have \[ \begin{aligned} \left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2}{1} \end{pmatrix} &= \left(q^2; q^2\right) \left\langle x^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle -qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle \vspace{0.1cm} \\ x\left\langle -q^2 x^2; q^2 \right\rangle \end{pmatrix} \\ &= \left(q^2; q^2\right) \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle x^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle q^2x^4; q^4 \right\rangle \vspace{0.1cm} \\ -x^3\left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle \left\langle q^4x^4; q^4 \right\rangle \end{pmatrix} \qquad = \begin{pmatrix} \vect{q^2x^6}{0} - \vect{q^2x^6}{2} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ -x^3\left(\vect{q^5x^6}{0} - q\vect{q^5x^6}{2}\right) \end{pmatrix}, \end{aligned} \] which simplifies to the right-hand side of \cref{eq:to-show-quintuple}, using that $q\vect{q^5 x^6}{2} = \vect{q^5x^6}{-4}$ and $x^3 \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(q^{-3}\right)$. Thus indeed \cref{thm:bases-proportional} $\Leftrightarrow$ \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram}.
nodes.statement_short: Verify via triple and quintuple substitutions

nodes.name: Reformulation of the main theorem
nodes.statement: (q; q) \left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \left( q^{n+1}x; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2 + n}x^{2n+1} \left( q^{n+1}x; q\right) \end{pmatrix} = -\vect{-qx}{0} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3} \end{pmatrix}.
nodes.label: eq:first-thm-reformulation

nodes.name: Quintuple-type identity to show
nodes.statement: \left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2}{1} \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{q^2x^6}{0} - \vect{q^2x^6}{2} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{q^2x^6}{-1} - \vect{q^2x^6}{3} \end{pmatrix}.
nodes.label: eq:to-show-quintuple

nodes.name: First proof of the twisted two-variable Rogers-Ramanujan theorem
nodes.statement: By \cref{lem:proofs-by-value} for $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2\right)$, it suffices to prove \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram} when $x \in \{1, -1\}$. After noting that $\left(q^{n+1}; q\right) = 0$ for $n < 0$, the statement at $x = 1$ (i.e., $z = 0$) becomes \[ \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2}\left(q^{n+1}; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2 + n}\left(q^{n+1}; q\right) \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \vspace{0.1cm}\\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2}{0}(0)\vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2}{1}(0) \end{pmatrix}. \] Now in last part of the previous proof, we saw (unconditionally, using \cref{lem:m-identities}) that \[ \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \vspace{0.1cm}\\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2}{0}\vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2}{1} \end{pmatrix} = \frac{-\vect{-qx}{0}}{(q; q)\left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3} \end{pmatrix} \] as an identity of meromorphic functions of $z$. Using that $\vect{-qx}{0} = (q; q)\left\langle xq; q\right\rangle$ and letting $z \to 0$, our claim to prove becomes \[ \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2}\left(q^{n+1}; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2 + n}\left(q^{n+1}; q\right) \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} \frac{1}{2} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{-qx^5}{1}(0) + \vect{-qx^5}{2}(0) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{-qx^5}{0}(0) + \vect{-qx^5}{3}(0) \end{pmatrix} \\ = \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^n q^{\frac{5n^2+n}{2}} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^n q^{\frac{5n^2+3n}{2}} \end{pmatrix}, \] which is equivalent to the Rogers--Ramanujan identities from \cref{eq:rog-ram} (which we deduced from \cref{prop:rogers}), after dividing by $(q; q)$ and applying the triple product identity. Next, the statement of \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram} at $x = -1$ (i.e., $z = 1/2$) becomes, after applying the triple product identity in \cref{eq:triple} for $x \mapsto -qx^2$ and $x \mapsto -q^2x^2$, \[ \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} \left(-q^{n+1}; q\right) \\ -\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} \left(-q^{n+1}; q\right) \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \vspace{0.1cm}\\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle -q; q^2 \right\rangle\vspace{0.1cm} \\ -\left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle -q^2; q^2 \right\rangle \end{pmatrix}. \] But since we have already shown that \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram} holds at $x = 1$, we know that \begin{equation} (q; q) \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2}\left(q^{n+1}; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2 + n}\left(q^{n+1}; q\right) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \vspace{0.1cm}\\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle -q; q^2 \right\rangle\vspace{0.1cm}\vspace{0.1cm} \\ \left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle -q^2; q^2 \right\rangle \end{pmatrix}, \end{equation} and by subtracting this from the previous equation it remains to prove that \[ \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} \left(-q^{n+1}; q\right) \\ -\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} \left(-q^{n+1}; q\right) \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} (q; q) \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1} \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \vspace{0.1cm}\\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0\vspace{0.1cm} \\ -2\left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle -q^2; q^2 \right\rangle \end{pmatrix}. \] In the left-hand side, break the sums into $n \ge 0$ and $n < 0$, and use the notation from \cref{eq:mock-theta}. On the right, substitute $B(q) = -q\left(-q; q\right)/\left\langle q^8; q^{20}\right\rangle$ and $D(q) = \left(-q; q\right)/\left\langle q^4; q^{20} \right\rangle$, which follow from \cref{eq:explicit-matrix}. Dividing both sides by $(-q; q)$ and using the triple product identity in the form $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2+n} = \left(q^2; q^2\right) \left\langle -q^2; q^2 \right\rangle$, we see that the claim above is equivalent to \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} f_0 + 2\psi_0(q) \\ f_1 + 2\psi_1(q) \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} \frac{(q; q)}{(-q; q)} \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ -\left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1} \end{pmatrix} + 4q \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2+n} \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle q^8; q^{20} \right\rangle^{-1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \left\langle q^4; q^{20} \right\rangle^{-1} \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation} But \cref{eq:watson} is precisely the content of equations $(3_0) + 2(1_0)$ and $(3_1) + 2(1_1)$ from \cite{watson1937mock}, which completes our proof assuming the work of Watson.
nodes.statement_short: Value identification at $x=\pm1$: at $x=1$ it is the Rogers-Ramanujan identities; at $x=-1$ it reduces to Watson's fifth-order mock theta identities.

nodes.name: Value identification
nodes.statement: By \cref{lem:proofs-by-value} for $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2\right)$, it suffices to prove \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram} when $x \in \{1, -1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $x=\pm1$

nodes.name: x=1
nodes.statement: After noting that $\left(q^{n+1}; q\right) = 0$ for $n < 0$, the statement at $x = 1$ (i.e., $z = 0$) becomes \[ \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2}\left(q^{n+1}; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2 + n}\left(q^{n+1}; q\right) \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \vspace{0.1cm}\\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2}{0}(0)\vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2}{1}(0) \end{pmatrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Specialize at $x=1$

nodes.name: Matrix identity
nodes.statement: Now in last part of the previous proof, we saw (unconditionally, using \cref{lem:m-identities}) that \[ \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \vspace{0.1cm}\\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2}{0}\vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2}{1} \end{pmatrix} = \frac{-\vect{-qx}{0}}{(q; q)\left\langle x^2; q \right\rangle} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3} \end{pmatrix} \] as an identity of meromorphic functions of $z$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the unconditional matrix identity

nodes.name: Rogers-Ramanujan
nodes.statement: Using that $\vect{-qx}{0} = (q; q)\left\langle xq; q\right\rangle$ and letting $z \to 0$, our claim to prove becomes \[ \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2}\left(q^{n+1}; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2 + n}\left(q^{n+1}; q\right) \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} \frac{1}{2} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{-qx^5}{1}(0) + \vect{-qx^5}{2}(0) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{-qx^5}{0}(0) + \vect{-qx^5}{3}(0) \end{pmatrix} \\ = \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^n q^{\frac{5n^2+n}{2}} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^n q^{\frac{5n^2+3n}{2}} \end{pmatrix}, \] which is equivalent to the Rogers--Ramanujan identities from \cref{eq:rog-ram} (which we deduced from \cref{prop:rogers}), after dividing by $(q; q)$ and applying the triple product identity.
nodes.statement_short: At $x=1$ this is the Rogers-Ramanujan identities

nodes.name: x=-1
nodes.statement: Next, the statement of \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram} at $x = -1$ (i.e., $z = 1/2$) becomes, after applying the triple product identity in \cref{eq:triple} for $x \mapsto -qx^2$ and $x \mapsto -q^2x^2$, \[ \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} \left(-q^{n+1}; q\right) \\ -\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} \left(-q^{n+1}; q\right) \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \vspace{0.1cm}\\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle -q; q^2 \right\rangle\vspace{0.1cm} \\ -\left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle -q^2; q^2 \right\rangle \end{pmatrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Specialize at $x=-1$

nodes.name: Subtract
nodes.statement: But since we have already shown that \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram} holds at $x = 1$, we know that \begin{equation} (q; q) \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2}\left(q^{n+1}; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2 + n}\left(q^{n+1}; q\right) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \vspace{0.1cm}\\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle -q; q^2 \right\rangle\vspace{0.1cm}\vspace{0.1cm} \\ \left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle -q^2; q^2 \right\rangle \end{pmatrix}, \end{equation} and by subtracting this from the previous equation it remains to prove that \[ \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} \left(-q^{n+1}; q\right) \\ -\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} \left(-q^{n+1}; q\right) \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} (q; q) \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1} \end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \vspace{0.1cm}\\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0\vspace{0.1cm} \\ -2\left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle -q^2; q^2 \right\rangle \end{pmatrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Subtract the $x=1$ case

nodes.name: Mock theta form
nodes.statement: In the left-hand side, break the sums into $n \ge 0$ and $n < 0$, and use the notation from \cref{eq:mock-theta}. On the right, substitute $B(q) = -q\left(-q; q\right)/\left\langle q^8; q^{20}\right\rangle$ and $D(q) = \left(-q; q\right)/\left\langle q^4; q^{20} \right\rangle$, which follow from \cref{eq:explicit-matrix}. Dividing both sides by $(-q; q)$ and using the triple product identity in the form $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2+n} = \left(q^2; q^2\right) \left\langle -q^2; q^2 \right\rangle$, we see that the claim above is equivalent to \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} f_0 + 2\psi_0(q) \\ f_1 + 2\psi_1(q) \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} \frac{(q; q)}{(-q; q)} \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ -\left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1} \end{pmatrix} + 4q \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2+n} \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle q^8; q^{20} \right\rangle^{-1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \left\langle q^4; q^{20} \right\rangle^{-1} \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite with fifth-order mock theta functions

nodes.name: Watson
nodes.statement: But \cref{eq:watson} is precisely the content of equations $(3_0) + 2(1_0)$ and $(3_1) + 2(1_1)$ from \cite{watson1937mock}, which completes our proof assuming the work of Watson.
nodes.statement_short: Watson's identities finish the proof

nodes.name: Rogers-Ramanujan products via the explicit matrix
nodes.statement: (q; q) \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2}\left(q^{n+1}; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2 + n}\left(q^{n+1}; q\right) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \vspace{0.1cm}\\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle -q; q^2 \right\rangle\vspace{0.1cm}\vspace{0.1cm} \\ \left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle -q^2; q^2 \right\rangle \end{pmatrix},
nodes.label: eq:5-and-10

nodes.name: Watson's fifth-order mock theta identities
nodes.statement: \begin{pmatrix} f_0 + 2\psi_0(q) \\ f_1 + 2\psi_1(q) \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} \frac{(q; q)}{(-q; q)} \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ -\left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle^{-1} \end{pmatrix} + 4q \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2+n} \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle q^8; q^{20} \right\rangle^{-1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \left\langle q^4; q^{20} \right\rangle^{-1} \end{pmatrix}.
nodes.label: eq:watson

nodes.name: Remark: Watson's derivation and the converse implication
nodes.statement: Watson \cite{watson1937mock} deduced his relations $(1_0), (1_1), (3_0)$ and $(3_1)$ using $q$-series manipulations based on the Rogers--Ramanujan identities from \cref{eq:rog-ram}, the formulae in \cref{cor:basic-identities} (Watson's $(E_1)$ and $(E_2)$), and specializations of the triple product identity (Watson's $(J_1)$ and $(J_2)$). The proof above also shows that \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram} \emph{implies} the mock theta identities in \cref{eq:watson} by taking $x = \pm 1$, which is relevant since we will give a self-contained proof of \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram} in \cref{subsec:w-coeffs}.

nodes.name: Derivation of the imaginary Rogers-Ramanujan identities
nodes.statement: Taking $x = i$ in \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram} yields two relatives of the Rogers--Ramanujan identities:
nodes.statement_short: Specialize the twisted theorem at $x=i$.

nodes.name: Imaginary Rogers-Ramanujan identities
nodes.statement: For $\tau \in {\mathbb{H}}^+$, one has \[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^n \frac{q^{n^2}}{(iq; q)_n} &= \frac{\left(q; q^2\right)}{(iq; q)} \left(q^{10}; q^{10}\right) \left\langle q; q^{10} \right\rangle \left\langle q^8; q^{20} \right\rangle , \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^n \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{(iq; q)_n} &= i\frac{\left(q; q^2\right)}{(iq; q)}\left(q^{10}; q^{10}\right) \left\langle q^3; q^{10} \right\rangle \left\langle q^4; q^{20} \right\rangle. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Two Rogers-Ramanujan-type sums with $(iq;q)_n$ denominators equal level-10/20 products.
nodes.label: cor:more-rog-ram

nodes.name: Two-variable Rogers-Ramanujan variation
nodes.statement: In $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(qx^2 - q^{-1}\right)$, one has \[ \frac{(q; q)\left\langle x; q\right\rangle (qx; q)}{(-q; q)^2\left(- x^{-1}; q\right)} = 2\left(-q^2; q^2\right) \vect{qx^2 - q^{-1}}{0} - \left(-q; q^2\right)\vect{qx^2 - q^{-1}}{1}. \]
nodes.statement_short: A product in $\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^-}(qx^2-q^{-1})$ expands in its canonical basis with coefficients $(-q^2;q^2)$, $(-q;q^2)$.
nodes.label: prop:2var-rog-ram-var

nodes.name: Remark: link of the variation with the octuple identity
nodes.statement: The $q$-coefficients in the right-hand side above are the same (up to a sign) as the $q$-coefficients on the right of the octuple identity from \cref{eq:octuple}. Moreover, multiplying the product above by the left-hand side of \cref{thm:bases-proportional-2} yields the octuple product in \cref{eq:octuple}. Hence under \cref{thm:bases-proportional-2}, the octuple identity and \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram-var} are equivalent.

nodes.name: Proof of Two-variable Rogers-Ramanujan variation
nodes.statement: Rewrite the left-hand side as \[ \begin{aligned} \frac{-x^{-1} (q; q)\left\langle x; q\right\rangle^2}{(-q; q)^2\left( x^{-2}; q^2\right)} &= -\frac{x^{-1}}{(-q; q)^2} \left(\left(-q; q^2\right)^2 \vect{x^2}{0} - 2\left(-q^2; q^2\right)^2\vect{x^2}{1}\right) \cdot \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{1}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} x^{-2n} \\ &= 2\frac{\left(-q^2; q^2\right)}{\left(-q; q^2\right)} \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}, n \ge 0} \frac{q^{m^2}}{(q^2; q^2)_n}x^{2m-2n} - \frac{\left(-q; q^2\right)}{\left(-q^2; q^2\right)} \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}, n \ge 0} \frac{q^{m^2+m}}{(q^2; q^2)_n}x^{2m-2n+1}, \end{aligned} \] where we used the squared triple product identity from \cref{prop:squared-triple}, and \cref{eq:basic2} in the first equality and simply multiplied sums out in the second equality. Now using \cref{tbl:spaces}, we see that the left-hand side product lies in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(q(-x)^2 \left(1 - x^{-2} q^{-2}\right)\right) = \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(qx^2 - q^{-1}\right)$, so it is a linear combination of $\vect{qx^2-q^{-1}}{0}$ and $\vect{qx^2-q^{-1}}{1}$. To finish it suffices to identify the coefficients of $x^0$ and $x^1$ in the sum above; this amounts to the identities \begin{equation} \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q^2; q^2)_n} = \left(-q; q^2\right) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{(q^2; q^2)_n} = \left(-q^2; q^2\right), \end{equation} which follow from \cref{eq:basic1} for $q \mapsto q^2$ and $x \mapsto -q$, respectively $x \mapsto -q^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the squared triple identity and the q-binomial expansion; identify $x^0,x^1$ coefficients, which are Euler-type identities.

nodes.name: Expand
nodes.statement: Rewrite the left-hand side as \[ \begin{aligned} \frac{-x^{-1} (q; q)\left\langle x; q\right\rangle^2}{(-q; q)^2\left( x^{-2}; q^2\right)} &= -\frac{x^{-1}}{(-q; q)^2} \left(\left(-q; q^2\right)^2 \vect{x^2}{0} - 2\left(-q^2; q^2\right)^2\vect{x^2}{1}\right) \cdot \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{1}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} x^{-2n} \\ &= 2\frac{\left(-q^2; q^2\right)}{\left(-q; q^2\right)} \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}, n \ge 0} \frac{q^{m^2}}{(q^2; q^2)_n}x^{2m-2n} - \frac{\left(-q; q^2\right)}{\left(-q^2; q^2\right)} \sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}, n \ge 0} \frac{q^{m^2+m}}{(q^2; q^2)_n}x^{2m-2n+1}, \end{aligned} \] where we used the squared triple product identity from \cref{prop:squared-triple}, and \cref{eq:basic2} in the first equality and simply multiplied sums out in the second equality.
nodes.statement_short: Squared triple identity and q-binomial expansion

nodes.name: Space
nodes.statement: Now using \cref{tbl:spaces}, we see that the left-hand side product lies in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(q(-x)^2 \left(1 - x^{-2} q^{-2}\right)\right) = \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(qx^2 - q^{-1}\right)$, so it is a linear combination of $\vect{qx^2-q^{-1}}{0}$ and $\vect{qx^2-q^{-1}}{1}$.
nodes.statement_short: The product lies in $\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^-}(qx^2-q^{-1})$

nodes.name: Coefficients
nodes.statement: To finish it suffices to identify the coefficients of $x^0$ and $x^1$ in the sum above; this amounts to the identities \begin{equation} \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q^2; q^2)_n} = \left(-q; q^2\right) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{(q^2; q^2)_n} = \left(-q^2; q^2\right), \end{equation} which follow from \cref{eq:basic1} for $q \mapsto q^2$ and $x \mapsto -q$, respectively $x \mapsto -q^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Compare $x^0$, $x^1$ coefficients via Euler

nodes.name: Easy Rogers-Ramanujan type identities
nodes.statement: \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q^2; q^2)_n} = \left(-q; q^2\right) \qquad\text{and}\qquad \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{(q^2; q^2)_n} = \left(-q^2; q^2\right),
nodes.label: eq:rog-ram-var

nodes.name: Remark: the variation generalizes the easier identities
nodes.statement: While \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram} generalizes the original Rogers--Ramanujan identities in \cref{eq:rog-ram}, \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram-var} is a generalization of the (much easier) Rogers--Ramanujan type identities in \cref{eq:rog-ram-var}.

nodes.name: Twisted two-variable Rogers-Ramanujan variation
nodes.statement: For $\tau \in {\mathbb{H}}^+$ and $z \in {\mathbb{H}}^-$, \[ \left(x^{-2}; q^2\right) \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \left(-q^{2n+1}; q^2\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2+n} x^{2n+1} \left(-q^{2n+2}; q^2\right) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2}{1} \end{pmatrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: $(x^{-2};q^2)$ times two twisted series equals the canonical basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(qx^2)$.
nodes.label: thm:twisted-rog-ram-var

nodes.name: Proof of Twisted two-variable Rogers-Ramanujan variation
nodes.statement: Take $y = q^{-1}$ in \cref{cor:kind1}, then multiply the results by $\left(-q; q^2\right)$ and $\left(-q^2; q^2\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $y=q^{-1}$ in the first-kind canonical basis corollary and rescale.

nodes.name: Proof that the octuple-vs-variation theorem is equivalent to the twisted variation
nodes.statement: Let $z \in {\mathbb{H}}^-$. Using that $\vect{-x^2}{1} = \left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle$ (by \cref{eq:canonical-formula}) and that $\left\langle x; q \right\rangle = -x (qx; q)\left(x^{-1}; q\right)$, one can rephrase \cref{thm:bases-proportional-2} as \[ \vect{-x^2}{1}\left(x^{-2}; q^2\right) \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2-q^{-1}}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2-q^{-1}}{1} \end{pmatrix} = (q; q) \begin{pmatrix} \vect{-qx^4}{1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{-qx^4}{0} + \vect{-qx^4}{2} \end{pmatrix}. \] Using the formulae for canonical basis vectors from \cref{cor:kind1}, we can further rewrite this as \[ \vect{-x^2}{1}\left(x^{-2}; q^2\right) \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \frac{\left(-q^{n+1}; q^2\right)}{\left(-q; q^2\right)} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2+n} x^{2n+1} \frac{\left(-q^{n+2}; q^2\right)}{\left(-q^2; q^2\right)} \end{pmatrix} = (q; q) \begin{pmatrix} \vect{-qx^4}{1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{-qx^4}{0} + \vect{-qx^4}{2} \end{pmatrix}. \] Now from \cref{lem:m-identities} and the triple product identity from \cref{eq:substitutions-triple} for $a = 4$, we find that \[ \vect{-x^2}{1} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2}{1} \end{pmatrix} = \left(q^4; q^4\right) \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle q^2; q^4 \right\rangle & 0 \vspace{0.1cm} \\ 0 & \left\langle q; q^4 \right\rangle \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{-qx^4}{1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{-qx^4}{0} + \vect{-qx^4}{2} \end{pmatrix}. \] This proves that \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram-var} is equivalent to \cref{thm:bases-proportional-2} since $\left(q^4; q^4\right)\left\langle q^2; q^4 \right\rangle / (q; q) = \left(-q; q^2\right)$ and $\left(q^4; q^4\right)\left\langle q; q^4 \right\rangle / (q; q) = \left(-q^2; q^2\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Rephrase via canonical formulas and first-kind basis formulas; the multiplication lemma gives a diagonal relation whose entries are the right products.

nodes.name: Rephrase
nodes.statement: Let $z \in {\mathbb{H}}^-$. Using that $\vect{-x^2}{1} = \left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle qx^2; q^2 \right\rangle$ (by \cref{eq:canonical-formula}) and that $\left\langle x; q \right\rangle = -x (qx; q)\left(x^{-1}; q\right)$, one can rephrase \cref{thm:bases-proportional-2} as \[ \vect{-x^2}{1}\left(x^{-2}; q^2\right) \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2-q^{-1}}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2-q^{-1}}{1} \end{pmatrix} = (q; q) \begin{pmatrix} \vect{-qx^4}{1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{-qx^4}{0} + \vect{-qx^4}{2} \end{pmatrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Rephrase the theorem using canonical formulas

nodes.name: First-kind formulas
nodes.statement: Using the formulae for canonical basis vectors from \cref{cor:kind1}, we can further rewrite this as \[ \vect{-x^2}{1}\left(x^{-2}; q^2\right) \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \frac{\left(-q^{n+1}; q^2\right)}{\left(-q; q^2\right)} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2+n} x^{2n+1} \frac{\left(-q^{n+2}; q^2\right)}{\left(-q^2; q^2\right)} \end{pmatrix} = (q; q) \begin{pmatrix} \vect{-qx^4}{1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{-qx^4}{0} + \vect{-qx^4}{2} \end{pmatrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Insert first-kind canonical vectors

nodes.name: Multiplication lemma
nodes.statement: Now from \cref{lem:m-identities} and the triple product identity from \cref{eq:substitutions-triple} for $a = 4$, we find that \[ \vect{-x^2}{1} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2}{1} \end{pmatrix} = \left(q^4; q^4\right) \begin{pmatrix} \left\langle q^2; q^4 \right\rangle & 0 \vspace{0.1cm} \\ 0 & \left\langle q; q^4 \right\rangle \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{-qx^4}{1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{-qx^4}{0} + \vect{-qx^4}{2} \end{pmatrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Diagonal relation between bases

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: This proves that \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram-var} is equivalent to \cref{thm:bases-proportional-2} since $\left(q^4; q^4\right)\left\langle q^2; q^4 \right\rangle / (q; q) = \left(-q; q^2\right)$ and $\left(q^4; q^4\right)\left\langle q; q^4 \right\rangle / (q; q) = \left(-q^2; q^2\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Products match

nodes.name: Remark: non-mixing of even and odd powers
nodes.statement: Comparing our main results in \cref{thm:bases-proportional} (equivalent to \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram}) and \cref{thm:bases-proportional-2} (equivalent to \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram-var}), the latter one is characterized by the \emph{non-mixing of even and odd powers of $x$} in the basis vectors $\vect{qx^2 - q^{-1}}{k}$ (which originates from the fact that the symmetry factor $qx^2 - q^{-1}$ only contains even powers). This has several consequences: \begin{itemize} \item[(i).] There is no need for a $2 \times 2$ matrix in \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram-var} (or by a different choice of scalars, the matrix would be diagonal), unlike in \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram}. \item[(ii).] \cref{thm:bases-proportional-2} and \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram-var} were easier to prove than \cref{thm:bases-proportional} and \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram}. \item[(iii).] By identifying even and odd powers of $x$, \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram-var} splits into two identities for $\vect{qx^2 - q^{-1}}{0}$ and $\vect{qx^2 - q^{-1}}{1}$, which are ultimately equivalent to \cref{cor:kind2}, \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram-var} and \cref{thm:bases-proportional-2}. By contrast, \cref{thm:bases-proportional} is stronger than \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram}. \item[(iv).] There is no nonzero entire function in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(qx^2 - q^{-1}\right)$ (i.e., $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2 - q^{-1}\right) = \{0\}$). This is ultimately because $\frac{1}{1-x^2}$ and $\frac{x}{1-x^2}$ (which correspond to the tails of the coefficients of $q^0$ in $\vect{qx^2 - q^{-1}}{0}$ and $\vect{qx^2 - q^{-1}}{1}$) are linearly independent. By contrast, $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2 - x\right)$ is spanned by the left-hand side of \cref{prop:2var-rog-ram}. \end{itemize} The non-mixing phenomenon extends (with respect to residue classes mod $d$) to any $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}}\left(\alpha x^d + \beta\right)$, which is ultimately what allowed us to obtain closed forms for canonical basis vectors of the first kind in \cref{prop:exact-formulae-kind1}. Similarly, the mixing phenomenon is manifested in all nontrivial cases of canonical basis vectors of the second kind, from \cref{prop:exact-formulae-kind2}.

nodes.name: Remark: numerically suggested cross-product identities
nodes.statement: Numerical generation also suggests identities for the cross-products in the (now proven) \cref{thm:bases-proportional,thm:bases-proportional-2}: \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\vect{qx^2 - x}{1}\left(\vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2}\right)\\[-5pt] = \ &\vect{qx^2 - x}{0}\left(\vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3}\right) = \frac{\left(q^{35}; q^{35}\right)}{\left(x^{-1}; q\right)} \Big( \left\langle q^{15}; q^{35} \right\rangle \left(\vect{-q^2 x^7}{0} + \vect{-q^2 x^7}{3}\right) \\[-2pt] &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad -q^2\left\langle q^5; q^{35} \right\rangle \left(\vect{-q^2 x^7}{1} + \vect{-q^2 x^7}{2}\right) \\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\ -q\left\langle q^{10}; q^{35} \right\rangle \left(\vect{-q^2 x^7}{-1} + \vect{-q^2 x^7}{4}\right) \Big), \end{aligned} \end{equation} respectively \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} & \vect{qx^2 - q^{-1}}{1}\vect{-qx^4}{1} \\[-5pt] = \ &\vect{qx^2 - q^{-1}}{0}\left(\vect{-qx^4}{0} + \vect{-qx^4}{2}\right) = \frac{\left(q^2; q^2\right)}{\left(x^{-2}; q^2\right)} \left(\vect{-q^2 x^6}{0} + \vect{-q^2 x^6}{2}\right). \end{aligned} \end{equation} While \cref{eq:cross-product-2} can be proven easily using the results in this section and \cref{lem:m-identities}, \cref{eq:cross-product-1} appears to be more difficult. By specialization at $x = 1$, \cref{eq:cross-product-1} would imply an additional identity for the generalized eta functions of level $N = 7$ (using \cref{eq:generalized-eta}), which would belong in \cref{prop:level-7}: \[ \sum_{g = 1}^3 \textnormal E_g(5\tau) \textnormal E_{3g}(\tau) = - \frac{\eta(\tau)\eta(5\tau)}{\eta(7\tau)\eta(35\tau)}. \]

nodes.name: Cross-product identity for T(qx^2-x) and T(-qx^5)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &\vect{qx^2 - x}{1}\left(\vect{-qx^5}{1} + \vect{-qx^5}{2}\right)\\[-5pt] = \ &\vect{qx^2 - x}{0}\left(\vect{-qx^5}{0} + \vect{-qx^5}{3}\right) = \frac{\left(q^{35}; q^{35}\right)}{\left(x^{-1}; q\right)} \Big( \left\langle q^{15}; q^{35} \right\rangle \left(\vect{-q^2 x^7}{0} + \vect{-q^2 x^7}{3}\right) \\[-2pt] &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad -q^2\left\langle q^5; q^{35} \right\rangle \left(\vect{-q^2 x^7}{1} + \vect{-q^2 x^7}{2}\right) \\ &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\quad\ -q\left\langle q^{10}; q^{35} \right\rangle \left(\vect{-q^2 x^7}{-1} + \vect{-q^2 x^7}{4}\right) \Big), \end{aligned}
nodes.statement_short: Numerically suggested product of canonical vectors of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^-}(qx^2-x)$ and $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(-qx^5)$ in the canonical basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(-q^2x^7)$.
nodes.label: eq:cross-product-1

nodes.name: Cross-product identity for T(qx^2-q^{-1}) and T(-qx^4)
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} & \vect{qx^2 - q^{-1}}{1}\vect{-qx^4}{1} \\[-5pt] = \ &\vect{qx^2 - q^{-1}}{0}\left(\vect{-qx^4}{0} + \vect{-qx^4}{2}\right) = \frac{\left(q^2; q^2\right)}{\left(x^{-2}; q^2\right)} \left(\vect{-q^2 x^6}{0} + \vect{-q^2 x^6}{2}\right). \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:cross-product-2

nodes.name: Twisted sum identities
nodes.statement: Let $0 \neq \alpha \in \mathbb{C}$, $s \in \{\pm 1\}$ and $d, k, a \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $0 \le k \le d-1$ and $1 \le a \mid d$. If $sa = d$ assume that $|y| < \left\vert \alpha q^k \right\vert$, and if $sa = -d$ assume that $|y| < \left\vert q^{d-k}/\alpha\right\vert$. Then \begin{equation} \underbrace{\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} x^{dn+k}}_{\text{Original series $\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}$}} \underbrace{\vphantom{\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}} \left(q^{san}x^{sa} y; q^{a}\right)}_{\text{Twist factor}} = \sum_{\ell=0}^{d-1} W_{k,\ell}(y, q) \vect{\alpha x^d}{\ell}, \end{equation} where $\{W_{k,\ell}(y, q)\}_\ell$ also depend on $\alpha, s, d, a$ (but not on $x$), and are given by \begin{equation} W_{k,\ell}(y, q) = \mathbbm{1}_{\ell \equiv k\ (\textnormal{mod }a)} \cdot q^{a \binom{j}{2}} \sum_{n \ge \mathbbm{1}_{s\ell < sk}} \alpha^{-sn}\ \frac{q^{a \binom{b}{2} n^2 + s(b(\ell-k)-\ell)n + \frac{s-1}{2}dn}}{\left(q^{a}; q^{a}\right)_{bn+j}} (-y)^{bn+j}, \end{equation} where $b := d/a$ and $j := (\ell - k)/(sa)$.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement_short: A theta series twisted by $(q^{san}x^{sa}y;q^a)$ expands in the canonical basis with explicit W-coefficients.
assumptions: Let $0 \neq \alpha \in \mathbb{C}$, $s \in \{\pm 1\}$ and $d, k, a \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $0 \le k \le d-1$ and $1 \le a \mid d$.
nodes.label: lem:t-identities

nodes.name: Twisted series expansion
nodes.statement: \underbrace{\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} x^{dn+k}}_{\text{Original series $\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}$}} \underbrace{\vphantom{\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}} \left(q^{san}x^{sa} y; q^{a}\right)}_{\text{Twist factor}} = \sum_{\ell=0}^{d-1} W_{k,\ell}(y, q) \vect{\alpha x^d}{\ell},
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.label: eq:twisted-series

nodes.name: Formula for W-coefficients
nodes.statement: W_{k,\ell}(y, q) = \mathbbm{1}_{\ell \equiv k\ (\textnormal{mod }a)} \cdot q^{a \binom{j}{2}} \sum_{n \ge \mathbbm{1}_{s\ell < sk}} \alpha^{-sn}\ \frac{q^{a \binom{b}{2} n^2 + s(b(\ell-k)-\ell)n + \frac{s-1}{2}dn}}{\left(q^{a}; q^{a}\right)_{bn+j}} (-y)^{bn+j},
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.label: eq:w-coeffs-value

nodes.name: Remark: mixing of Fourier coefficients
nodes.statement: The condition $\ell \equiv k \pmod{a}$ in \cref{eq:w-coeffs-value} indicates the extent of the non-mixing phenomenon for Fourier coefficients described in the end of \cref{subsec:two-var-generaliz}; there is no mixing when $a = d$, maximum mixing when $a = 1$, and some mixing when $1 < a < d$. Also, the general case of \cref{lem:t-identities} can be recovered from the special case $a = 1$, using the substitutions $d \mapsto b$, $q \mapsto q^a$ and adequate substitutions for $\alpha$; however, it is more convenient to state and prove \cref{lem:t-identities} for a general $a \mid d$.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Proof of Twisted sum identities
nodes.statement: Let $L(z)$ denote the left-hand side of \cref{eq:twisted-series}, where $x = e^{2\pi i z}$. One can check as in the proof of \cref{prop:exact-formulae-kind1} that $L$ converges absolutely and locally uniformly to a well-defined entire function under the given assumptions. It is then immediate that $L \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d \right)$, since it is a twisted version of $\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}$ as in \cref{eq:w-coeffs}; hence $L$ has an expansion as in the right-hand side of \cref{eq:twisted-series}, where $W_{k,\ell}(y, q) = \widehat{L}(\ell)$. Expanding the series of $L(z)$ using \cref{eq:basic1} and identifying the coefficients of $x^\ell$ leads to the formula in \cref{eq:w-coeffs-value}, after a short computation (treating the cases $s \in \{\pm 1\}$ separately).
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement_short: The twisted series lies in $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(\alpha x^d)$; compute its canonical coefficients by expanding the twist with Euler's formula.

nodes.name: Convergence
nodes.statement: Let $L(z)$ denote the left-hand side of \cref{eq:twisted-series}, where $x = e^{2\pi i z}$. One can check as in the proof of \cref{prop:exact-formulae-kind1} that $L$ converges absolutely and locally uniformly to a well-defined entire function under the given assumptions.
nodes.statement_short: Define $L$; it is entire
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Expansion
nodes.statement: It is then immediate that $L \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d \right)$, since it is a twisted version of $\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}$ as in \cref{eq:w-coeffs}; hence $L$ has an expansion as in the right-hand side of \cref{eq:twisted-series}, where $W_{k,\ell}(y, q) = \widehat{L}(\ell)$.
nodes.statement_short: $L$ is twisted, so expands in the canonical basis
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Coefficients
nodes.statement: Expanding the series of $L(z)$ using \cref{eq:basic1} and identifying the coefficients of $x^\ell$ leads to the formula in \cref{eq:w-coeffs-value}, after a short computation (treating the cases $s \in \{\pm 1\}$ separately).
nodes.statement_short: Euler expansion identifies $W_{k,\ell}$
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: A one-variable bilateral summation (case d=1)
nodes.statement: For $y \in \mathbb{C}$ with $|y| < |x|$ and $y \not\in \left\{q^n : n \le 0\right\}$, one has \[ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{q^{\binom{n}{2}}}{\left(y; q \right)_n} x^n = \frac{(q; q)\left\langle -x; q \right\rangle}{(y; q)(-y/x; q)}, \] generalizing \cref{eq:triple}, \cref{eq:basic1} and \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram-var}. In fact, this is a particular case of Ramanujan's $_1\psi_1$ summation from \cref{prop:ramanujan-1psi1} (by taking $x \mapsto -x/a$, $a \to \infty$ and $b = y$).
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement_short: $\sum q^{\binom n2}x^n/(y;q)_n$ equals a ratio of infinite products.
nodes.label: cor:d=1

nodes.name: Proof of the d=1 bilateral summation
nodes.statement: \cref{lem:t-identities} yields $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{\binom{n}{2}}x^n \left(q^n xy; q\right) = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{(-y)^n}{(q; q)_n} \cdot \vect{x}{0}$ for $|y| < 1$; take $y \mapsto y/x$, divide by $(y; q)$, and use \cref{eq:triple},\cref{eq:basic2} to finish. An alternative proof proceeds by noting that both sides lie in the one-dimensional space $\mathcal{T}_D\left(x - y\right)$ (as functions of $z$), for a suitable half-plane $D$.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement_short: Twisted sum lemma with $d=1$, then substitute and divide; alternatively a one-dimensional space argument.

nodes.name: Three-variable 2x2 matrix identity
nodes.statement: Let $y \in \mathbb{C}$ with $|y| \le 1$. Then as an equality of pairs of functions in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2\right)$, \[ \begin{aligned} \left(x^{-1} y; q\right) \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2 - yx}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2 - yx}{1} \end{pmatrix} &= \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \left(q^{n+1}xy; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2+n} x^{2n+1} \left(q^{n+1}xy; q\right) \end{pmatrix} \\ &= \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n(n+1)}}{(q; q)_{2n}} y^{2n} & - \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{(n+1)^2}}{(q; q)_{2n+1}} y^{2n+1} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ -\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n(n+1)}}{(q; q)_{2n+1}} y^{2n+1} & \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_{2n}} y^{2n} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2}{1} \end{pmatrix}. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement_short: $(x^{-1}y;q)$ times the canonical basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb H^-}(qx^2-yx)$ equals twisted series, and a $2\times2$ matrix of Rogers-Ramanujan sums in $y$ times the basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(qx^2)$.
nodes.label: cor:3-var-2x2-matrix

nodes.name: Proof of Three-variable 2x2 matrix identity
nodes.statement: For the first equality, use \cref{cor:kind2} and the symmetry at $x \mapsto x^{-1}$ (due to $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2\right) \subset \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}(1)$). For the second equality, use \cref{lem:t-identities} for $a = 1$, $d = 2$, $s = 1$ and $\alpha = y = q$.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement_short: Second-kind canonical formula with the $x\mapsto x^{-1}$ symmetry, then the twisted sum lemma.

nodes.name: Remark: bottom row from top row
nodes.statement: Concerning the second equality in \cref{cor:3-var-2x2-matrix}, one can deduce the bottom-row identity from the top-row one by taking $x \mapsto x/\sqrt{q}$ and $y \mapsto y\sqrt{q}$; however, the matrix appearing in the formulation above will be relevant later (it turns out to have determinant $1$; see \cref{cor:3-var-2x2-matrix-ctd}).
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Rogers-type sums
nodes.statement: For $\tau \in {\mathbb{H}}^+$ and $z \in \mathbb{C}$, one has \[ (q; q) \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_n} x^{-2n} = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n(n+1)}}{(q; q)_{2n}} x^{2n} \cdot \vect{qx^2}{0} - \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{(n+1)^2}}{(q; q)_{2n+1}} x^{2n+1} \cdot \vect{qx^2}{1}, \] where the left-hand side is (up to a trivial substitution) the sum from \cref{prop:rogers}.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement_short: $(q;q)\sum q^{n^2}x^{-2n}/(q;q)_n$ expands in the basis of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(qx^2)$ with Rogers-Ramanujan type coefficients in $x$.
nodes.label: cor:rogers-type-sums

nodes.name: Proof of Rogers-type sums
nodes.statement: Take $y = x^{-1}$ in \cref{cor:3-var-2x2-matrix} and identify the top row (alternatively, take $x \mapsto x/\sqrt{q}$, then $y = x^{-1}\sqrt{q}$ and identify the bottom row). Afterwards, substitute $x \mapsto x^{-1}$ on both sides, noting that $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2\right) \subset \mathcal{S}_{\mathbb{C}}(1)$.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement_short: Set $y=x^{-1}$ in the three-variable matrix identity and use the $x\mapsto x^{-1}$ symmetry.

nodes.name: Remark: further Rogers-Ramanujan type sums
nodes.statement: More identities of Rogers--Ramanujan type sums follow by plugging in $x \in \{-i, -i/\sqrt{q}\}$ in \cref{cor:rogers-type-sums} and using \cref{prop:rogers}.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Second proof of the twisted two-variable Rogers-Ramanujan theorem
nodes.statement: Taking $y = 1$ in \cref{cor:3-var-2x2-matrix}, the statement of \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram} reduces to an equality of matrices \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n(n+1)}}{(q; q)_{2n}} & - \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{(n+1)^2}}{(q; q)_{2n+1}} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ -\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n(n+1)}}{(q; q)_{2n+1}} & \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_{2n}} \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix}, \end{equation} where $A(q), B(q), C(q), D(q)$ are as in \cref{eq:explicit-matrix}. We note that \cref{eq:slater} is precisely the content of four Rogers--Ramanujan type identities of Slater \cite[(94),(96),(98),(99)]{slater1952further}, and we can prove them using \cref{prop:rogers}. Indeed, taking $q \mapsto q^4$ and then multiplying by $\begin{psmall} -q & q \\ 1 & 1 \end{psmall}$, one easily reduces \cref{eq:explicit-matrix} to \[ \begin{pmatrix} -\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{(n+1)^2}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} & -\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{(n+1)^2}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} & \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}(-1)^n}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} \begin{pmatrix} A\left(q^4\right) & B\left(q^4\right) \\ C\left(q^4\right) & D\left(q^4\right) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} -q & q \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \] which, in light of the symmetry $q \leftrightarrow -q$, boils down to \[ \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} \stackrel{?}{=} D\left(q^4\right) - qC\left(q^4\right) ,\qquad\qquad \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+2n}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} \stackrel{?}{=} A\left(q^4\right) - q^{-1} B\left(q^4\right). \] Now using \cref{eq:explicit-matrix} and the quintuple identity \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple} for $a = 10$, one can expand $(q; q)A(q)$, $(q; q)B(q)$, $(q; q)C(q)$ and $(q; q)D(q)$ as explicit series where the $n$th term has a dominant power of $q^{30\binom{n}{2}}$. By taking $q \mapsto q^4$, adding these series and then using \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple} for $a = 10$ again, one obtains \[ \begin{aligned} \left(q^4; q^4\right) \left(D\left(q^4\right) - qC\left(q^4\right)\right) &\ =\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^n q^{30\binom{n}{2}}\left(q^{13n} + q^{7n+1}\right) \ =\ \left(q^{10}; q^{10}\right)\left\langle -q; q^{10}\right\rangle \left\langle q^{12}; q^{20}\right\rangle , \\ \left(q^4; q^4\right) \left(A\left(q^4\right) - q^{-1}B\left(q^4\right)\right) &\ =\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^n q^{30\binom{n}{2}}\left(q^{11n} + q^{n+3}\right) \ \ =\ \left(q^{10}; q^{10}\right)\left\langle -q^3; q^{10}\right\rangle \left\langle q^{16}; q^{20}\right\rangle . \end{aligned} \] After rearranging the products on the right, it remains to show that \begin{equation} \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} \stackrel{?}{=} \frac{1}{\left(-q^2; q^2\right) \left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle} ,\qquad\qquad \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+2n}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} \stackrel{?}{=} \frac{1}{\left(-q^2; q^2\right) \left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle}. \end{equation} But by taking $x = 1$, respectively $x = q$ in the second equality from \cref{prop:rogers} (and using the Rogers--Ramanujan identities \cref{eq:rog-ram}), one obtains that \begin{equation} \frac{1}{\left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle} = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2n+2}; q^2\right), \qquad\qquad \frac{1}{\left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle} = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2n+3}; q^2\right). \end{equation} The first equality in \cref{eq:known} settles the first equality in \cref{eq:claim} since $\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n = \left(q^2; q^2\right)_n \left(-q^2; q^2\right)_n$. For the second equality in \cref{eq:claim}, write $F(z) := \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n}x^n \left(-q^{2n+2}x; q^2\right)$, and recall that \cref{prop:rogers} implies that $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1, qx)$. In particular we have $F(\tau) = F(0) - q F(2\tau)$, and thus \[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2n+3}; q^2\right) &= \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2n+2}; q^2\right) - \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{(n+1)^2}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2(n+1)+2}; q^2\right) \\ &= \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2n+2}; q^2\right) - \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}\left(1-q^{2n}\right)}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2n+2}; q^2\right) \\ &= \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+2n}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2n+2}; q^2\right) \qquad = \left(-q^2; q^2\right) \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+2n}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} , \end{aligned} \] which settles the second equality in \cref{eq:claim} in light of \cref{eq:known}. This completes our proof.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement_short: Reduce, via the three-variable matrix identity at $y=1$, to four Slater identities, and prove them from Rogers' identity. The key step expands the matrix entries as theta series with dominant power $q^{30\binom n2}$.

nodes.name: Reduce to matrix equality
nodes.statement: Taking $y = 1$ in \cref{cor:3-var-2x2-matrix}, the statement of \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram} reduces to an equality of matrices \begin{equation} \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n(n+1)}}{(q; q)_{2n}} & - \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{(n+1)^2}}{(q; q)_{2n+1}} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ -\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n(n+1)}}{(q; q)_{2n+1}} & \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_{2n}} \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix}, \end{equation} where $A(q), B(q), C(q), D(q)$ are as in \cref{eq:explicit-matrix}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to an equality of matrices
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Slater identities
nodes.statement: We note that \cref{eq:slater} is precisely the content of four Rogers--Ramanujan type identities of Slater \cite[(94),(96),(98),(99)]{slater1952further}, and we can prove them using \cref{prop:rogers}.
nodes.statement_short: It is four Slater identities, proved from Rogers' identity
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Reduce to two identities
nodes.statement: Indeed, taking $q \mapsto q^4$ and then multiplying by $\begin{psmall} -q & q \\ 1 & 1 \end{psmall}$, one easily reduces \cref{eq:explicit-matrix} to \[ \begin{pmatrix} -\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{(n+1)^2}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} & -\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{(n+1)^2}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} & \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}(-1)^n}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} \begin{pmatrix} A\left(q^4\right) & B\left(q^4\right) \\ C\left(q^4\right) & D\left(q^4\right) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} -q & q \\ 1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \] which, in light of the symmetry $q \leftrightarrow -q$, boils down to \[ \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} \stackrel{?}{=} D\left(q^4\right) - qC\left(q^4\right) ,\qquad\qquad \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+2n}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} \stackrel{?}{=} A\left(q^4\right) - q^{-1} B\left(q^4\right). \]
nodes.statement_short: Substitute and use $q\leftrightarrow -q$
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Theta expansions
nodes.statement: Now using \cref{eq:explicit-matrix} and the quintuple identity \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple} for $a = 10$, one can expand $(q; q)A(q)$, $(q; q)B(q)$, $(q; q)C(q)$ and $(q; q)D(q)$ as explicit series where the $n$th term has a dominant power of $q^{30\binom{n}{2}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Expand matrix entries as theta series
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: By taking $q \mapsto q^4$, adding these series and then using \cref{eq:substitutions-quintuple} for $a = 10$ again, one obtains \[ \begin{aligned} \left(q^4; q^4\right) \left(D\left(q^4\right) - qC\left(q^4\right)\right) &\ =\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^n q^{30\binom{n}{2}}\left(q^{13n} + q^{7n+1}\right) \ =\ \left(q^{10}; q^{10}\right)\left\langle -q; q^{10}\right\rangle \left\langle q^{12}; q^{20}\right\rangle , \\ \left(q^4; q^4\right) \left(A\left(q^4\right) - q^{-1}B\left(q^4\right)\right) &\ =\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^n q^{30\binom{n}{2}}\left(q^{11n} + q^{n+3}\right) \ \ =\ \left(q^{10}; q^{10}\right)\left\langle -q^3; q^{10}\right\rangle \left\langle q^{16}; q^{20}\right\rangle . \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: Combine series into products
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Remaining claims
nodes.statement: After rearranging the products on the right, it remains to show that \begin{equation} \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} \stackrel{?}{=} \frac{1}{\left(-q^2; q^2\right) \left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle} ,\qquad\qquad \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+2n}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} \stackrel{?}{=} \frac{1}{\left(-q^2; q^2\right) \left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Remains to show two identities
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Rogers at x=1, q
nodes.statement: But by taking $x = 1$, respectively $x = q$ in the second equality from \cref{prop:rogers} (and using the Rogers--Ramanujan identities \cref{eq:rog-ram}), one obtains that \begin{equation} \frac{1}{\left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle} = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2n+2}; q^2\right), \qquad\qquad \frac{1}{\left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle} = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2n+3}; q^2\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Rogers' identity gives two product formulas
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: First claim
nodes.statement: The first equality in \cref{eq:known} settles the first equality in \cref{eq:claim} since $\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n = \left(q^2; q^2\right)_n \left(-q^2; q^2\right)_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Settles the first claim
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Define F
nodes.statement: For the second equality in \cref{eq:claim}, write $F(z) := \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n}x^n \left(-q^{2n+2}x; q^2\right)$, and recall that \cref{prop:rogers} implies that $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1, qx)$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce Rogers' series $F$
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Second claim
nodes.statement: In particular we have $F(\tau) = F(0) - q F(2\tau)$, and thus \[ \begin{aligned} \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2n+3}; q^2\right) &= \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2n+2}; q^2\right) - \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{(n+1)^2}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2(n+1)+2}; q^2\right) \\ &= \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2n+2}; q^2\right) - \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}\left(1-q^{2n}\right)}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2n+2}; q^2\right) \\ &= \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+2n}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2n+2}; q^2\right) \qquad = \left(-q^2; q^2\right) \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+2n}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} , \end{aligned} \] which settles the second equality in \cref{eq:claim} in light of \cref{eq:known}. This completes our proof.
nodes.statement_short: Functional equation settles the second claim
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Slater's identities (94), (96), (98), (99)
nodes.statement: \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n(n+1)}}{(q; q)_{2n}} & - \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{(n+1)^2}}{(q; q)_{2n+1}} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ -\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n(n+1)}}{(q; q)_{2n+1}} & \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_{2n}} \end{pmatrix} \stackrel{?}{=} \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix},
