nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.label: eq:slater

nodes.name: Two Rogers-Ramanujan type identities to show
nodes.statement: \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} \stackrel{?}{=} \frac{1}{\left(-q^2; q^2\right) \left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle} ,\qquad\qquad \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+2n}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} \stackrel{?}{=} \frac{1}{\left(-q^2; q^2\right) \left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle}.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.label: eq:claim

nodes.name: Rogers-Ramanujan products via Rogers' identity
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{\left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle} = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2n+2}; q^2\right), \qquad\qquad \frac{1}{\left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle} = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} \left(-q^{2n+3}; q^2\right).
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.label: eq:known

nodes.name: Remark: twisted theorem implies Slater's identities
nodes.statement: As indicated in \cref{fig:layout}, the proof above also shows that \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram} implies Slater's identities from \cref{eq:slater}. So while \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram} generalizes the classical Rogers--Ramanujan identities from \cref{eq:rog-ram} (and Watson's identities from \cref{eq:watson}) by value identification, it also generalizes \cref{eq:slater} by Fourier identification.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Second proof of the twisted Rogers-Ramanujan variation
nodes.statement: Taking $a = d = 2$, $\alpha = q$, $s = 1$ and $y \in \left\{-qx^{-2}, -q^2x^{-2}\right\}$ in \cref{lem:t-identities}, one obtains \[ \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \left(-q^{2n+1}; q^2\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2+n} x^{2n+1} \left(-q^{2n+2}; q^2\right) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^n}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} x^{-2n} & 0 \vspace{0.1cm} \\ 0 & \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^n}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} x^{-2n} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2}{0} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \vect{qx^2}{1} \end{pmatrix}. \] But \cref{eq:basic2} implies that $\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^n}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_n} x^{-2n} = \left(x^{-2}; q^2\right)^{-1}$, completing our proof.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement_short: Twisted sum lemma with $a=d=2$ gives a diagonal matrix, identified by the q-binomial theorem.

nodes.name: Twisted canonical basis as change of basis
nodes.statement: \underbrace{\vphantom{\sum_n} \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} x^{dn+k} \left(q^{-an} x^{-a} y; q^a\right) \end{pmatrix}_{0 \le k < d} }_{\text{Twisted canonical basis of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$}} = \underbrace{\vphantom{\sum_n} \begin{pmatrix} W_{k,\ell}(y, q) \end{pmatrix}_{0 \le k, \ell < d} }_{\text{Change-of-basis matrix}} \underbrace{\vphantom{\sum_n} \begin{pmatrix} \vect{\alpha x^d}{\ell} \end{pmatrix}_{0 \le l < d} }_{\text{Canonical basis}},
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.label: eq:twist-change-canonical

nodes.name: y-Interpolation
nodes.statement: Let $V(x, y) := \big( \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} x^{dn+k} \left(q^{-n} x^{-1} y; q\big) \right)_{0 \le k < d}$ denote the column vector in the left-hand side of \cref{eq:twist-change-canonical}, for $1 = a \le d$ and $\alpha, y$ as in \cref{lem:t-identities}. Then \[ V(x, y) = M(y) \cdot V(x, qy), \] where $M(y) = \left(1 + \alpha y q^{-1}\right)^{-1}$ if $d = 1$, $M(y) = \begin{psmall} 1 + \alpha y^2q^{-1} & -\alpha yq^{-1} \\ -y & 1 \end{psmall}$ if $d = 2$, and \[ M(y) = \begin{psmall} 1 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & \alpha y^2q^{-1} & -\alpha yq^{-1} \\ -y & 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -y & 1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ & & & & \ddots & & \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & -y & 1 \end{psmall} \in \mathbb{C}^{d \times d}, \qquad \text{if } d \ge 3. \] So while $V(x, y) \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)^d$, by swapping variables we have $V(y, x) \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(M(x)\right)$ for $d \ge 2$.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement_short: The twisted canonical basis vector $V(x,y)$ satisfies $V(x,y)=M(y)V(x,qy)$ for an explicit matrix $M(y)$.
nodes.label: lem:y-interpolation

nodes.name: Proof of y-Interpolation
nodes.statement: Letting $V_k(x, y)$ be the $k$th coordinate of $V(x, y)$, use the functional equation $\left(q^{-n} x^{-1} y; q\right) = \left(1 - q^{-n} x^{-1} y\right) \left(q^{-n} x^{-1} (qy); q\right)$ to obtain \[ V_k(x, y) = V_k(x, qy) - yV_{k-1}(x, qy), \] for $1 \le k < d$. For $k = 0$, the analogous expansion yields $V_0(x, y) = V_0(x, qy) - \alpha y q^{-1} V_{d-1}(x, y)$; if $d = 1$ this gives $V_0(x, y) = (1 + \alpha y q^{-1})^{-1} V_0(x, qy)$, and if $d \ge 2$ we get $V_0(x, y) = V_0(x, qy) + \alpha y^2 q^{-1} V_{d-2}(qy) - \alpha y q^{-1} V_{d-1}(qy)$ by applying the relation above for $k-1 = d$. Putting these together produces the matrices $M(y)$ above.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement_short: Use the functional equation of the twist factor to relate coordinates at $y$ and $qy$.

nodes.name: Coordinates k>=1
nodes.statement: Letting $V_k(x, y)$ be the $k$th coordinate of $V(x, y)$, use the functional equation $\left(q^{-n} x^{-1} y; q\right) = \left(1 - q^{-n} x^{-1} y\right) \left(q^{-n} x^{-1} (qy); q\right)$ to obtain \[ V_k(x, y) = V_k(x, qy) - yV_{k-1}(x, qy), \] for $1 \le k < d$.
nodes.statement_short: Relation for coordinates $1\le k<d$
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Coordinate 0
nodes.statement: For $k = 0$, the analogous expansion yields $V_0(x, y) = V_0(x, qy) - \alpha y q^{-1} V_{d-1}(x, y)$; if $d = 1$ this gives $V_0(x, y) = (1 + \alpha y q^{-1})^{-1} V_0(x, qy)$, and if $d \ge 2$ we get $V_0(x, y) = V_0(x, qy) + \alpha y^2 q^{-1} V_{d-2}(qy) - \alpha y q^{-1} V_{d-1}(qy)$ by applying the relation above for $k-1 = d$.
nodes.statement_short: Relation for $k=0$
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Matrix M
nodes.statement: Putting these together produces the matrices $M(y)$ above.
nodes.statement_short: Assemble $M(y)$
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Remark: iterating the y-interpolation
nodes.statement: Working in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(M(x)\right)$, our observation in \cref{ex:two-var-rog-ram} suggests iterating the functional equation in \cref{lem:y-interpolation} to obtain an infinite product of matrices; this leads to the following theorem.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha, y \in \mathbb{C}$ with $\alpha \neq 0$, and $d \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $d \ge 2$. Define the $d \times d$ matrices $U = (U_{k, \ell})_{0 \le k, \ell < d}$ and $W = (W_{k, \ell})_{0 \le k, \ell < d}$ by \[ U_{k, \ell} := \sum_{n \ge \mathbbm{1}_{\ell > k}} \alpha^n \frac{q^{d\binom{n}{2} + kn}}{(q; q)_{dn+k-\ell}} y^{dn+k-\ell}, \qquad W_{k, \ell} := \sum_{n \ge \mathbbm{1}_{\ell > k}} \alpha^n \frac{q^{\binom{d}{2}n^2 + (d(k-\ell-1)+\ell)n + \binom{k - \ell}{2}}}{(q; q)_{dn+k-\ell}} (-y)^{dn+k-\ell}. \] Then one has $\det U = \det W = 1$. Moreover, \[ W U = \begin{psmall} 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & -\alpha y q^{-1} \\ 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ & & & \ddots & \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 \end{psmall} \qquad \text{and} \qquad W = \prod_{n \ge 0} M\left(q^n y\right), \] where $M$ is as in \cref{lem:y-interpolation} and the product of matrices is evaluated from left to right.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement_short: The change-of-basis matrices $U$, $W$ between canonical, twisted and third bases have determinant 1, $WU$ is elementary, and $W$ is an infinite product of $M(q^ny)$.
nodes.label: thm:change-of-basis

nodes.name: Remark: inverses and the case d=1
nodes.statement: One can compute $U^{-1}$ and $W^{-1}$ explicitly based on \cref{thm:change-of-basis}, and thus all minors of $U$ and $W$ as well. Also, the case $d = 1$ is not included in \cref{thm:change-of-basis} since it is essentially equivalent to \cref{cor:d=1}, and since then we have $\det U = (\det W)^{-1} = \left(-\alpha y q^{-1}; q\right)$ (for $|\alpha y| < |q|$).
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Proof of Change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement: Assume without loss of generality that $|y| \le 1$, by the uniqueness of analytic continuation; then we have $1 - q^{-1} x^{-1} y \neq 0$ in $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < -\textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$, and thus the canonical basis vectors of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}} \left(\alpha x^d \left(1 - q^{-1} x^{-1} y\right) \right)$ are well-defined by \cref{prop:canonical-basis-vectors}. Now consider the following three elements of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)^d$: \begin{center} \small \begin{tikzcd} [column sep = -0.5cm] & \begin{pmatrix} \vect{\alpha x^d}{k} \end{pmatrix}_{0 \le k < d} \arrow{rd}{=\ U \ \cdot} \\ \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} x^{dn+k} \left(q^{-n} x^{-1} y; q\right) \end{pmatrix}_{0 \le k < d} \arrow{rr}{=\ WU\ \cdot} \arrow{ru}{=\ W\ \cdot} && \begin{pmatrix} \left(x^{-1}y; q\right)\vect{\alpha x^d\left(1 - q^{-1}x^{-1}y\right)}{k} \end{pmatrix}_{0 \le k < d} \end{tikzcd} \end{center} where the arrows indicate claimed relationships. The ``$= W \cdot\ $'' arrow is precisely the relation from \cref{eq:twist-change-canonical} for $a = 1$. The ``$= U \cdot\ $'' relation follows from \cref{eq:basic2} by expanding \[ \frac{1}{\left(x^{-1}y; q\right)} \vect{\alpha x^d}{k} = \sum_{m \ge 0} \frac{\left(-x^{-1}y\right)^m}{(q; q)_m} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} x^{dn+k}, \] and identifying Fourier coefficients in the canonical basis of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}} \left(\alpha x^d \left(1 - q^{-1} x^{-1} y\right) \right)$. The ``$= WU\ \cdot$'' relation follows from the previous two, and will be helpful in computing $WU$. Next, the fact that $W = \prod_{n \ge 0} M\left(q^n y\right)$ follows immediately by iterating \cref{lem:y-interpolation}, using that \[ \lim_{p \to \infty} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} x^{dn+k} \left(q^{-n} x^{-1} (q^p y); q\right) = \vect{\alpha x^d}{k}. \] In particular, this shows that $\det W = 1$ (since each $\det M\left(q^n y\right) = 1$), and in particular that $\left(\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}\right)_{0 \le k < d}$ is invertible is indeed a basis of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$ as well. Hence we can compute $(WU)^{-1}$ as the unique change-of-basis matrix satisfying \[ \begin{pmatrix} \left(x^{-1}y; q\right)\vect{\alpha x^d\left(1 - q^{-1}x^{-1}y\right)}{k} \end{pmatrix}_{0 \le k < d} = (WU)^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} x^{dn+k} \left(q^{-n} x^{-1} y; q\right) \end{pmatrix}_{0 \le k < d}. \] But by \cref{prop:exact-formulae-kind2} for $g(-z) = 1 - q^{-1}x^{-1}y$, we have \[ \left(x^{-1}y; q\right)\vect{\alpha x^d\left(1 - q^{-1}x^{-1}y\right)}{k} = \begin{cases} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{d\binom{n}{2}} x^{dn} \left(q^{-n+1}x^{-1}y; q\right), & k = 0, \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} x^{dn+k} \left(q^{-n}x^{-1}y; q\right), & k > 0. \end{cases} \] Using the relationship $V_0(x, qy) = V_0(x, y) + \alpha y q^{-1}$ from the proof of \cref{lem:y-interpolation}, this proves that \[ (WU)^{-1} = \begin{psmall} 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & \alpha y q^{-1} \\ 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ & & & \ddots & \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 \end{psmall} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad WU = \begin{psmall} 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & -\alpha y q^{-1} \\ 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ & & & \ddots & \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 \end{psmall}. \] Finally, from $\det W = 1$ and $\det (WU) = 1$ we also deduce that $\det U = 1$.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement_short: Relate three bases of $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(\alpha x^d)$; iterate y-interpolation for $W$ (determinant 1) and compute $WU$ from the second-kind canonical formula.

nodes.name: WLOG
nodes.statement: Assume without loss of generality that $|y| \le 1$, by the uniqueness of analytic continuation; then we have $1 - q^{-1} x^{-1} y \neq 0$ in $\{\textnormal{Im}\ z < -\textnormal{Im}\ \tau\}$, and thus the canonical basis vectors of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}} \left(\alpha x^d \left(1 - q^{-1} x^{-1} y\right) \right)$ are well-defined by \cref{prop:canonical-basis-vectors}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $|y|\le1$
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Three bases
nodes.statement: Now consider the following three elements of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)^d$: \begin{center} \small \begin{tikzcd} [column sep = -0.5cm] & \begin{pmatrix} \vect{\alpha x^d}{k} \end{pmatrix}_{0 \le k < d} \arrow{rd}{=\ U \ \cdot} \\ \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} x^{dn+k} \left(q^{-n} x^{-1} y; q\right) \end{pmatrix}_{0 \le k < d} \arrow{rr}{=\ WU\ \cdot} \arrow{ru}{=\ W\ \cdot} && \begin{pmatrix} \left(x^{-1}y; q\right)\vect{\alpha x^d\left(1 - q^{-1}x^{-1}y\right)}{k} \end{pmatrix}_{0 \le k < d} \end{tikzcd} \end{center} where the arrows indicate claimed relationships.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce three tuples in $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(\alpha x^d)^d$
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: W relation
nodes.statement: The ``$= W \cdot\ $'' arrow is precisely the relation from \cref{eq:twist-change-canonical} for $a = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Twisted sum lemma
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: U relation
nodes.statement: The ``$= U \cdot\ $'' relation follows from \cref{eq:basic2} by expanding \[ \frac{1}{\left(x^{-1}y; q\right)} \vect{\alpha x^d}{k} = \sum_{m \ge 0} \frac{\left(-x^{-1}y\right)^m}{(q; q)_m} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} x^{dn+k}, \] and identifying Fourier coefficients in the canonical basis of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{H}^{\textnormal{-}\hspace{-0.03cm}}} \left(\alpha x^d \left(1 - q^{-1} x^{-1} y\right) \right)$.
nodes.statement_short: q-binomial expansion
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: WU relation
nodes.statement: The ``$= WU\ \cdot$'' relation follows from the previous two, and will be helpful in computing $WU$.
nodes.statement_short: Composite relation
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Product formula for W
nodes.statement: Next, the fact that $W = \prod_{n \ge 0} M\left(q^n y\right)$ follows immediately by iterating \cref{lem:y-interpolation}, using that \[ \lim_{p \to \infty} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} x^{dn+k} \left(q^{-n} x^{-1} (q^p y); q\right) = \vect{\alpha x^d}{k}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Iterate y-interpolation
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: det W
nodes.statement: In particular, this shows that $\det W = 1$ (since each $\det M\left(q^n y\right) = 1$), and in particular that $\left(\vect{\alpha x^d}{k}\right)_{0 \le k < d}$ is invertible is indeed a basis of $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(\alpha x^d\right)$ as well.
nodes.statement_short: $\det W=1$
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Characterize (WU)^{-1}
nodes.statement: Hence we can compute $(WU)^{-1}$ as the unique change-of-basis matrix satisfying \[ \begin{pmatrix} \left(x^{-1}y; q\right)\vect{\alpha x^d\left(1 - q^{-1}x^{-1}y\right)}{k} \end{pmatrix}_{0 \le k < d} = (WU)^{-1} \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \alpha^n q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} x^{dn+k} \left(q^{-n} x^{-1} y; q\right) \end{pmatrix}_{0 \le k < d}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Characterize the inverse change of basis
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Second-kind formula
nodes.statement: But by \cref{prop:exact-formulae-kind2} for $g(-z) = 1 - q^{-1}x^{-1}y$, we have \[ \left(x^{-1}y; q\right)\vect{\alpha x^d\left(1 - q^{-1}x^{-1}y\right)}{k} = \begin{cases} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{d\binom{n}{2}} x^{dn} \left(q^{-n+1}x^{-1}y; q\right), & k = 0, \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{d\binom{n}{2}+kn} x^{dn+k} \left(q^{-n}x^{-1}y; q\right), & k > 0. \end{cases} \]
nodes.statement_short: Explicit third basis
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Compute WU
nodes.statement: Using the relationship $V_0(x, qy) = V_0(x, y) + \alpha y q^{-1}$ from the proof of \cref{lem:y-interpolation}, this proves that \[ (WU)^{-1} = \begin{psmall} 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & \alpha y q^{-1} \\ 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ & & & \ddots & \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 \end{psmall} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad WU = \begin{psmall} 1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & -\alpha y q^{-1} \\ 0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 & 0 \\ & & & \ddots & \\ 0 & 0 & \cdots & 0 & 1 \end{psmall}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Compute $WU$
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: det U
nodes.statement: Finally, from $\det W = 1$ and $\det (WU) = 1$ we also deduce that $\det U = 1$.
nodes.statement_short: $\det U=1$
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Determinant one of the three-variable 2x2 matrix
nodes.statement: The $2\times 2$ matrix from \cref{cor:3-var-2x2-matrix} has constant determinant $1$. In fact, it can be written as an infinite product (evaluated left-to-right) \[ \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n(n+1)}}{(q; q)_{2n}} y^{2n} & -\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{(n+1)^2}}{(q; q)_{2n+1}} y^{2n+1} \vspace{0.3cm} \\ -\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n(n+1)}}{(q; q)_{2n+1}} y^{2n+1} & \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_{2n}} y^{2n} \end{pmatrix} = \prod_{n \ge 0} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -q^n y & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -q^{n+1} y \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}. \] In particular, this establishes \cref{prop:2x2-determinant} by taking $y = -x$.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement_short: The matrix of Rogers-Ramanujan sums in $y$ has determinant 1 and is an infinite product of elementary matrices; gives the 2x2 determinant identity.
nodes.label: cor:3-var-2x2-matrix-ctd

nodes.name: Proof of determinant one of the three-variable matrix
nodes.statement: Taking $d = 2$ and $\alpha = q$ in \cref{thm:change-of-basis}, the matrix in \cref{cor:3-var-2x2-matrix} is precisely $U^{-1}$. But \[ \begin{aligned} U^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & y \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} W &= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & y \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \prod_{n \ge 0} M\left(q^n y\right) \\ &= \begin{pmatrix} 1 & y \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \prod_{n \ge 0} \begin{pmatrix} 1 + q^{2n}y^2 & 1 - q^n y \\ -q^n y & 1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & y \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \prod_{n \ge 0} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & -q^n y \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ -q^n y & 1 \end{pmatrix}, \end{aligned} \] which completes our proof by noting that $\begin{psmall} 1 & y \\ 0 & 1 \end{psmall} \begin{psmall} 1 & -y \\ 0 & 1 \end{psmall} = 1$.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.statement_short: Identify the matrix with $U^{-1}$ for $d=2$, $\alpha=q$ and expand $W$ as a product of $M(q^ny)$.

nodes.name: Remark: determinant identity as a functional equation for F
nodes.statement: Denoting \[ F(z) := \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_n} x^{2n} \qquad \Rightarrow \qquad \frac{1}{2} \begin{pmatrix} F(z) + F(z+1/4) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ F(z) - F(z+1/4) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{4n^2}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_{2n}} x^{4n} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ q\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{4(n^2+n)}}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)_{2n+1}} x^{4n+2} \end{pmatrix}, \] the fact that the determinant in \cref{cor:3-var-2x2-matrix-ctd} is $1$ can be rephrased as (taking $q \mapsto q^4$) \[ \frac{F(z) + F\left(z + \frac{1}{4}\right)}{2} \frac{F\left(z + \tau\right) + F\left(z + \tau + \frac{1}{4}\right)}{2} - \frac{F(z) - F\left(z + \frac{1}{4}\right)}{2} \frac{F\left(z + \tau\right) - F\left(z + \tau + \frac{1}{4}\right)}{2} = 1, \] which further simplifies to $F(z)F(z + \tau + 1/4) + F(z + 1/4)F(z + \tau) = 2$. This follows in turn from the fact that $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2, 1\right)$ (which is easily checked); indeed, a short computation then shows that $F(z)F(z + \tau + 1/4) + F(z + 1/4)F(z + \tau) \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}(1)$, so it must be a constant.
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities

nodes.name: Question: a Rogers-type identity for sum q^{n^2} x^{2n}/(q^4;q^4)_n
nodes.statement: Note that taking $q \mapsto q^4$ in \cref{cor:3-var-2x2-matrix} connects Rogers' $\sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_n} x^n$ from \cref{prop:rogers} to our function $F(z)$ from the previous remark. Moreover, the relations immediately preceding \cref{eq:claim} yield that \[ F(0) = \frac{1}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^n q^{30\binom{n}{2}}\left(q^{13n} + q^{7n+1}\right), \qquad F(\tau) = \frac{1}{\left(q^4; q^4\right)}\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^n q^{30\binom{n}{2}}\left(q^{11n} + q^{n+3}\right). \] Combining these clues with the fact that $F \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2, 1\right)$, one is inclined to believe that there is a Rogers-type identity (similar to the first equality in \cref{prop:rogers}) for $F(z)$, in which the right-hand side contains dominant powers of $q^{30\binom{n}{2}}$ rather than $q^{5\binom{n}{2}}$. This would imply similar identities for the four sums in the matrix from \cref{prop:2x2-determinant} (thus generalizing \cref{eq:slater}), and due to \cref{cor:rogers-type-sums}, it would likely recover \cref{prop:rogers} as well. Can the reader guess such an identity for $F(z)$, and prove it by identifying Fourier coefficients in $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2, 1\right)$?
nodes.section: 5.2 W-coefficients, second proofs of main theorems and change-of-basis identities
nodes.label: qtn:rogers-type-sums

nodes.name: Proof of Fifth-order mock theta sums
nodes.statement: Consider \cref{eq:first-thm-reformulation}, which is just a reformulation of \cref{thm:bases-proportional} (or \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram}). Dividing both sides by $(q; q)\left(1 - x^2\right)$ yields \[ \left(qx^2; q\right)\left(qx^{-2}; q\right) \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \left( q^{n+1}x; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2 + n}x^{2n+1} \left( q^{n+1}x; q\right) \end{pmatrix} = -\left\langle qx; q \right\rangle \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^n q^{5\binom{n}{2} + 2n} \frac{x^{5n+1} - x^{-5n+2}}{1-x^2} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^n q^{5\binom{n}{2} + n} \frac{x^{5n} - x^{-5n+3}}{1-x^2} \end{pmatrix} \] where we used that $\vect{-qx}{0} = (q; q) \left\langle qx; q \right\rangle$. Now take $x \to -1$, and divide by $(-q; q)$ to obtain \[ (q; q)^2 \left(q; q^2\right) \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(-q; q)_n} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ -\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{q^{n^2 + n}}{(-q; q)_n} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{5\binom{n}{2} + 2n} (10n-1) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{5\binom{n}{2} + n} (10n-3) \end{pmatrix}. \] In the left-hand side, break the sums into $n \ge 0$ and $n < 0$, reindex and use our notations in \cref{eq:finite-product-negative} and \cref{eq:mock-theta}. In the right-hand side, substitute $n \mapsto -n$; this recovers \cref{cor:mock-theta-fifth}.
nodes.statement_short: Divide the reformulated main theorem by $(q;q)(1-x^2)$ and let $x\to-1$; split sums and reindex.

nodes.name: Start
nodes.statement: Consider \cref{eq:first-thm-reformulation}, which is just a reformulation of \cref{thm:bases-proportional} (or \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram}).
nodes.statement_short: Start from the reformulated main theorem

nodes.name: Divide
nodes.statement: Dividing both sides by $(q; q)\left(1 - x^2\right)$ yields \[ \left(qx^2; q\right)\left(qx^{-2}; q\right) \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \left( q^{n+1}x; q\right) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2 + n}x^{2n+1} \left( q^{n+1}x; q\right) \end{pmatrix} = -\left\langle qx; q \right\rangle \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^n q^{5\binom{n}{2} + 2n} \frac{x^{5n+1} - x^{-5n+2}}{1-x^2} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} (-1)^n q^{5\binom{n}{2} + n} \frac{x^{5n} - x^{-5n+3}}{1-x^2} \end{pmatrix} \] where we used that $\vect{-qx}{0} = (q; q) \left\langle qx; q \right\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Divide by $(q;q)(1-x^2)$

nodes.name: Limit x->-1
nodes.statement: Now take $x \to -1$, and divide by $(-q; q)$ to obtain \[ (q; q)^2 \left(q; q^2\right) \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(-q; q)_n} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ -\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{q^{n^2 + n}}{(-q; q)_n} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{5\binom{n}{2} + 2n} (10n-1) \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{5\binom{n}{2} + n} (10n-3) \end{pmatrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Take the limit $x\to-1$

nodes.name: Mock theta form
nodes.statement: In the left-hand side, break the sums into $n \ge 0$ and $n < 0$, reindex and use our notations in \cref{eq:finite-product-negative} and \cref{eq:mock-theta}.
nodes.statement_short: Split sums into mock theta functions

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: In the right-hand side, substitute $n \mapsto -n$; this recovers \cref{cor:mock-theta-fifth}.
nodes.statement_short: Reindex to obtain the corollary

nodes.name: Remark: identities for sums of fifth-order mock theta functions
nodes.statement: Both \cref{cor:mock-theta-fifth} and \cref{eq:watson} give identities for the sums of fifth-order mock theta functions $f_j(q) + 2\psi_j(q)$ (for $j \in \{0, 1\}$), using the notation from \cref{eq:mock-theta}. To list other such identities, we need:

nodes.name: Third- and fifth-order mock theta functions
nodes.statement: Following standard notation \cite{andrews1989ramanujan,chen2012partition,andrews1986fifth,andersen2016vector}, define the third-order mock theta functions introduced by Ramanujan \cite[p.~220]{ramanujan1995ramanujan} \[ \phi(q) := \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(-q^2; q^2\right)_n}, \qquad\qquad \psi(q) := \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q; q^2\right)_n}, \] and the fifth-order mock theta functions (in addition to those from \cref{eq:mock-theta}) \[ \begin{aligned} F_0(q) := \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{2n^2}}{\left(q; q^2\right)_n},& \qquad\qquad F_1(q) := \sum_{n \ge 1} \frac{q^{2n^2 - 2n}}{\left(q; q^2\right)_n}, \\ \phi_0(q) := \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2} \left(-q; q^2\right)_n,& \qquad\qquad \phi_1(q) := \sum_{n \ge 1} q^{n^2} \left(-q; q^2\right)_{n-1}. \end{aligned} \] Specializing \cref{thm:bases-proportional} and \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram} will lead to identities of fifth-order mock theta functions, while \cref{thm:bases-proportional-2} and \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram-var} correspond to third-order mock theta functions. For further readings on mock theta functions and mock modular forms, see \cite{gordon2012survey,zagier2009ramanujan,bringmann2017harmonic}.
nodes.statement_short: Ramanujan's third-order $\phi,\psi$ and fifth-order $F_0,F_1,\phi_0,\phi_1$ mock theta functions.
nodes.label: not:mock-theta

nodes.name: Sums of mock theta functions
nodes.statement: Let $\tau \in {\mathbb{H}}^+$. Concerning third-order mock theta functions and the Dedekind eta function, one has \[ \begin{aligned} \phi(q) + 2\sum_{n \ge 1} q^n \left(-q^2; q^2\right)_{n-1} = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(-q^2; q^2\right)_n} &= q^{\frac{1}{24}} \frac{\eta(2\tau)^7}{\eta(\tau)^3 \eta(4\tau)^3}, \\ 1 + 2\psi(q) + q\sum_{n \ge 0} \left(-q^2\right)^n\left(q; q^2\right)_n = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(q; q^2\right)_{n+1}} &= q^{\frac{1}{24}}\frac{\eta(2\tau)^7}{\eta(\tau)^3\eta(4\tau)^3}, \end{aligned} \] where the two right-hand sides happen to be equal. Concerning fifth-order mock theta functions and the generalized eta functions $\textnormal E_g$ of level $N = 5$ from \cref{eq:generalized-eta}, one has \[ \begin{aligned} f_0(q) + 2\psi_0(q) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(-q; q)_n} &= q^{\frac{1}{60}} \left(\frac{\eta(\tau)^2}{\eta(2\tau)\textnormal E_1(\tau)} + 4\frac{\eta(4\tau)^2}{\eta(2\tau) \textnormal E_2(4\tau)} \right), \\ f_1(q) + 2\psi_1(q) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{(-q; q)_n} &= q^{-\frac{11}{60}} \left(-\frac{\eta(\tau)^2}{\eta(2\tau)\textnormal E_2(\tau)} + 4\frac{\eta(4\tau)^2}{\eta(\tau) \textnormal E_1(4\tau)} \right), \\ F_0(q) + \phi_0(-q) - 1 = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{q^{2n^2}}{(q; q^2)_n} &= q^{\frac{1}{120}} \Bigg( \frac{\eta(4\tau)^6} {\eta(\tau) \eta(2\tau)^2 \eta(q^8)^2 \textnormal E_1(8\tau)} \\ &\qquad + 2\frac{\eta(2\tau)^4 \eta(8\tau)^4} {\eta(\tau) \eta(4\tau)^6 \textnormal E_2(2\tau)} - 4\frac{\eta(2\tau)^2 \eta(8\tau)^6} {\eta(\tau) \eta(4\tau)^6 \textnormal E_1(8\tau)} \Bigg), \\ F_1(q) + q^{-1} \phi_1(-q) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \frac{q^{2n^2-2n}}{(q; q^2)_n} &= q^{-\frac{71}{120}} \Bigg(-\frac{\eta(4\tau)^6} {\eta(\tau) \eta(2\tau)^2 \eta(q^8)^2 \textnormal E_2(8\tau)} \\ &\qquad + 2\frac{\eta(2\tau)^4 \eta(8\tau)^4} {\eta(\tau) \eta(4\tau)^6 \textnormal E_1(2\tau)} + 4\frac{\eta(2\tau)^2 \eta(8\tau)^6} {\eta(\tau) \eta(4\tau)^6 \textnormal E_2(8\tau)} \Bigg). \end{aligned} \] (The advantage of writing the right-hand sides above in terms of $\eta$ and $\textnormal E_g$ is knowing which powers of $q$ are required to make the left-hand sides behave nicely under modular transformations.)
nodes.statement_short: Bilateral completions of third- and fifth-order mock theta functions equal eta and generalized-eta quotients.
nodes.label: prop:mock-theta-sums

nodes.name: Remark: observations on the mock theta sums
nodes.statement: There are a few things to notice about \cref{prop:mock-theta-sums}: \begin{itemize} \item[(i).] The first two identities might lead to formulae for $\phi(q) \pm 2\psi(q)$, as in \cite[(1.4) and (1.5)]{chen2012partition}. \item[(ii).] The next two identities are just a convenient reformulation of \cref{eq:watson}, which can be derived from equations $(1_0)$ to $(3_1)$ from Watson's paper \cite{watson1937mock}. \item[(iii).] Taking $q \mapsto q^2$, the left-hand sides of the last two identities can be given similar but not trivially equivalent formulae, using the same equations $(1_0)$ to $(3_1)$ of Watson \cite{watson1937mock}. \item[(iv).] One can regard the left-hand sides as ``completions'' of mock theta functions (not in the sense of harmonic Maass forms), since they correspond to sums over $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ rather than $n \ge 0$ or $n \ge 1$; thus the fifth-order mock theta functions ``complete'' each other in this sense. \item[(v).] \cref{prop:mock-theta-sums} contains three pairs of (almost) twin identities, where each pair interchanges $\textnormal E_1 \leftrightarrow \textnormal E_2$. This supports the parallelism between the two classes of fifth-order mock theta functions defined by Ramanujan (i.e., those indexed by $0$ and those indexed by $1$). \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Proof of Sums of mock theta functions
nodes.statement: The first equality in each of the identities from \cref{prop:mock-theta-sums} follows immediately from \cref{not:mock-theta} and \cref{eq:finite-product-negative}, so we focus on the second equalities. We also leave the trivial conversion from the notations $\left(q^N; q^N\right)$ and $\left\langle q^g; q^N \right\rangle$ to (generalized) eta functions to the reader. The third-order identities follow by taking $x \in \{iq^{-1/2}, q^{-1/2}\}$ in \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram-var}, or from the obvious substitutions in \cref{cor:d=1}. The first two fifth-order identities are equivalent to \cref{eq:watson} (which, as we have seen, follows by taking $x = 1$ and $x = -1$ in \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram}). For the last two fifth-order identities, take $q \mapsto q^2$ and $x = q^{-1}$ in \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram}, and use the facts that \[ \begin{aligned} A(q) = \frac{1}{\left\langle -q; q^2\right\rangle} \left(\frac{(q; q)}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle} - 2\frac{\left(q^4; q^4\right)^2}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)^2} B(q) \right),& \qquad\qquad B(q) = \frac{-q\left(q^2; q^2\right)}{(q; q)\left\langle q^8; q^{20} \right\rangle }, \\ C(q) = \frac{1}{\left\langle -q; q^2\right\rangle} \left(\frac{(q; q)}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle} - 2\frac{\left(q^4; q^4\right)^2}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)^2} D(q) \right),& \qquad\qquad D(q) = \frac{\left(q^2; q^2\right)}{(q; q)\left\langle q^4; q^{20} \right\rangle}, \end{aligned} \] which follow from \cref{eq:5-and-10} and \cref{eq:explicit-matrix}.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize the twisted variation (third order) and the twisted theorem at $x=\pm1$ and $x=q^{-1}$ with $q\mapsto q^2$ (fifth order).

nodes.name: First equalities
nodes.statement: The first equality in each of the identities from \cref{prop:mock-theta-sums} follows immediately from \cref{not:mock-theta} and \cref{eq:finite-product-negative}, so we focus on the second equalities. We also leave the trivial conversion from the notations $\left(q^N; q^N\right)$ and $\left\langle q^g; q^N \right\rangle$ to (generalized) eta functions to the reader.
nodes.statement_short: First equalities by definitions

nodes.name: Third order
nodes.statement: The third-order identities follow by taking $x \in \{iq^{-1/2}, q^{-1/2}\}$ in \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram-var}, or from the obvious substitutions in \cref{cor:d=1}.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize the twisted variation

nodes.name: Fifth order, first two
nodes.statement: The first two fifth-order identities are equivalent to \cref{eq:watson} (which, as we have seen, follows by taking $x = 1$ and $x = -1$ in \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram}).
nodes.statement_short: Equivalent to Watson's identities

nodes.name: Fifth order, last two
nodes.statement: For the last two fifth-order identities, take $q \mapsto q^2$ and $x = q^{-1}$ in \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram}, and use the facts that \[ \begin{aligned} A(q) = \frac{1}{\left\langle -q; q^2\right\rangle} \left(\frac{(q; q)}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle q; q^5 \right\rangle} - 2\frac{\left(q^4; q^4\right)^2}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)^2} B(q) \right),& \qquad\qquad B(q) = \frac{-q\left(q^2; q^2\right)}{(q; q)\left\langle q^8; q^{20} \right\rangle }, \\ C(q) = \frac{1}{\left\langle -q; q^2\right\rangle} \left(\frac{(q; q)}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)\left\langle q^2; q^5 \right\rangle} - 2\frac{\left(q^4; q^4\right)^2}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)^2} D(q) \right),& \qquad\qquad D(q) = \frac{\left(q^2; q^2\right)}{(q; q)\left\langle q^4; q^{20} \right\rangle}, \end{aligned} \] which follow from \cref{eq:5-and-10} and \cref{eq:explicit-matrix}.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize the twisted theorem at $x=q^{-1}$ with $q\mapsto q^2$

nodes.name: Truncations of canonical basis vectors
nodes.statement: Indeed, writing $F_{\ge j}(z)$ for $\sum_{n \ge j} \widehat{F}(n) x^n$ in ${\mathbb{H}}^-$, \cref{cor:kind1,cor:kind2} imply that \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} &\vect{qx^2-q^{-1}}{0}_{\ge 0} = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(-q; q^2\right)_n} x^{2n} , \qquad\qquad \vect{qx^2-q^{-1}}{1}_{\ge 0} = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{\left(-q^2; q^2\right)_n} x^{2n+1} , \\ &\qquad \vect{qx^2-x}{0}_{\ge 1} = \sum_{n \ge 1} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \left(q^{-n+1} x^{-1}; q\right)_{n-1} \ =\ \sum_{n \ge 1} q^{\binom{n+1}{2}} (-x)^{n+1} (qx; q)_{n-1}, \\ &\qquad \vect{qx^2-x}{1}_{\ge 1} = \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2+n} x^{2n+1} \left(q^{-n} x^{-1}; q\right)_n \ =\ -\sum_{n \ge 0} q^{\binom{n+1}{2}} (-x)^{n+1} (qx; q)_n, \end{aligned} \end{equation} which generalize the summations of $1 + \psi(-q)$, $\phi(q)$, $\psi_0(q)$, respectively $-\psi_1(q)$ from \cref{not:mock-theta} and \cref{eq:mock-theta} (by taking $x = i$, $x = 1$ and $x = -1$).
nodes.statement_short: The nonnegative-power truncations of $[qx^2-q^{-1};k]$ and $[qx^2-x;k]$ are explicit series generalizing $\phi$, $\psi$, $\psi_0$, $\psi_1$.

nodes.name: Truncated canonical basis vectors
nodes.statement: \begin{aligned} &\vect{qx^2-q^{-1}}{0}_{\ge 0} = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{\left(-q; q^2\right)_n} x^{2n} , \qquad\qquad \vect{qx^2-q^{-1}}{1}_{\ge 0} = \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{\left(-q^2; q^2\right)_n} x^{2n+1} , \\ &\qquad \vect{qx^2-x}{0}_{\ge 1} = \sum_{n \ge 1} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \left(q^{-n+1} x^{-1}; q\right)_{n-1} \ =\ \sum_{n \ge 1} q^{\binom{n+1}{2}} (-x)^{n+1} (qx; q)_{n-1}, \\ &\qquad \vect{qx^2-x}{1}_{\ge 1} = \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2+n} x^{2n+1} \left(q^{-n} x^{-1}; q\right)_n \ =\ -\sum_{n \ge 0} q^{\binom{n+1}{2}} (-x)^{n+1} (qx; q)_n, \end{aligned}
nodes.label: eq:truncations

nodes.name: Individual mock theta functions as double sums
nodes.statement: Let $\tau \in {\mathbb{H}}^+$. Using \cref{not:mock-theta} and \cref{eq:explicit-matrix}, one has \begin{gather*} \begin{pmatrix} \psi_0(q) \\ \psi_1(q) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{2n > m \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}(-1)^m}{(q; q)_m} \vspace{0.1cm}\\ \sum_{2n \ge m \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+n}(-1)^m}{(q; q)_m} \end{pmatrix}, \\ \begin{pmatrix} \phi_1(q) \\ \phi_0(q) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A\left(q^2\right) & B\left(q^2\right) \\ C\left(q^2\right) & D\left(q^2\right) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} q\sum_{2n > m \ge 0} \frac{q^{2n^2-2n} (-q)^m}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_m} \vspace{0.1cm}\\ \sum_{2n \ge m \ge 0} \frac{q^{2n^2} (-q)^m}{\left(q^2; q^2\right)_m} \end{pmatrix}. \end{gather*} Similar but simpler identities can be given for the third-order mock theta functions $\psi(q)$ and $\phi(q)$.
nodes.statement_short: $(\psi_0,\psi_1)$ and $(\phi_1,\phi_0)$ equal the explicit matrix times vectors of double sums.
nodes.label: prop:mock-theta-individual

nodes.name: Proof of Individual mock theta functions as double sums
nodes.statement: From \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram-var} and \cref{cor:kind2}, one obtains \[ \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2-x}{0} \vspace{0.1cm}\\ \vect{qx^2-x}{1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \left(x^{-1}; q\right)^{-1} \vect{qx^2}{0} \vspace{0.1cm}\\ \left(x^{-1}; q\right)^{-1} \vect{qx^2}{1} \end{pmatrix}. \] Writing $\left(x^{-1}; q\right)^{-1} = \sum_{m \ge 0} (q; q)^{-m} x^{-m}$ and restricting to powers $x^n$ with $n \ge 0$ yields \[ \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2-x}{0}_{\ge 1} \vspace{0.1cm}\\ \vect{qx^2-x}{1}_{\ge 1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{2n > m \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_m} x^{2n-m} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{2n\ge m \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{(q; q)_m} x^{2n+1-m} \end{pmatrix}. \] Taking $x = -1$ recovers the first claimed equality in light of \cref{eq:truncations}. The second claimed equality follows analogously by taking $q \mapsto q^2$ above, and then $x = -q^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Express $[qx^2-x;k]$ via the matrix and $(x^{-1};q)^{-1}$, truncate to nonnegative powers, and set $x=-1$ (resp. $q\mapsto q^2$, $x=-q^{-1}$).

nodes.name: Matrix form
nodes.statement: From \cref{thm:twisted-rog-ram-var} and \cref{cor:kind2}, one obtains \[ \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2-x}{0} \vspace{0.1cm}\\ \vect{qx^2-x}{1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \left(x^{-1}; q\right)^{-1} \vect{qx^2}{0} \vspace{0.1cm}\\ \left(x^{-1}; q\right)^{-1} \vect{qx^2}{1} \end{pmatrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Express canonical vectors via the explicit matrix

nodes.name: Truncate
nodes.statement: Writing $\left(x^{-1}; q\right)^{-1} = \sum_{m \ge 0} (q; q)^{-m} x^{-m}$ and restricting to powers $x^n$ with $n \ge 0$ yields \[ \begin{pmatrix} \vect{qx^2-x}{0}_{\ge 1} \vspace{0.1cm}\\ \vect{qx^2-x}{1}_{\ge 1} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} A(q) & B(q) \\ C(q) & D(q) \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{2n > m \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(q; q)_m} x^{2n-m} \vspace{0.1cm} \\ \sum_{2n\ge m \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2+n}}{(q; q)_m} x^{2n+1-m} \end{pmatrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to nonnegative powers

nodes.name: x=-1
nodes.statement: Taking $x = -1$ recovers the first claimed equality in light of \cref{eq:truncations}.
nodes.statement_short: Specialize to get $\psi_0,\psi_1$

nodes.name: Second identity
nodes.statement: The second claimed equality follows analogously by taking $q \mapsto q^2$ above, and then $x = -q^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Analogous specialization

nodes.name: Remark: the generalized mock theta function G(y,q) and double twists
nodes.statement: The mock theta conjectures (given different proofs in \cite{hickerson1988proof,folsom2008short}) relate the fifth-order mock theta functions to special values of the widely studied function \cite{ramanujan1988lost,dyson1944some,bringmann2010dyson,andrews2018four} \begin{equation} G(y, q) := \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(qy; q)_n (q/y; q)_n}, \end{equation} for $y \in \mathbb{C}$. The natural approach to this function in the context of this section is to consider the generalization \[ G(x, y, q) := \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}x^{2n}}{(qxy; q)_n (qx/y; q)_n} = \left(\frac{1}{(qxy; q)(qx/y; q)} \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2}x^{2n} \left(q^{n+1}xy; q\right) \left(q^{n+1}x/y; q\right) \right)_{\ge 0}, \] where $F_{\ge 0}$ indicates the truncation to nonnegative powers of $x$ as before. The sum over $n \in \mathbb{Z}$ above is a doubly-twisted version of the series $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \in \mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2\right)$, in the sense of \cref{eq:w-coeffs}; hence it also belongs to $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2\right)$, and can be expanded using a similar argument to \cref{lem:t-identities}. This leads to the following statement, which is ultimately a consequence of \cref{prop:fractional}.

nodes.name: Generalized mock theta function G(y,q)
nodes.statement: G(y, q) := \sum_{n \ge 0} \frac{q^{n^2}}{(qy; q)_n (q/y; q)_n},
nodes.label: eq:generalized-mock-theta

nodes.name: Double twists
nodes.statement: Let $y \in \mathbb{C}^\times$. In $\mathcal{T}_{\mathbb{C}}\left(qx^2\right)$, one has \[ \begin{aligned} (q; q)^2 \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} x^{2n} \left(q^{n+1} xy; q \right) \left(q^{n+1} x/y; q \right) &= \vect{qx^2}{0}\sum_{\substack{d \in \mathbb{Z} \\ d \textnormal{ even}}} \Big(q^{\frac{d^2 + 2|d|}{4}} \sum_{n \ge 0} (-1)^n q^{\binom{n+1}{2} + |d|n}\Big) y^d \\ &- \vect{qx^2}{1} \sum_{\substack{d \in \mathbb{Z} \\ d \textnormal{ odd}}} \Big(q^{\frac{(|d|+1)^2}{4}} \sum_{n \ge 0} (-1)^n q^{\binom{n+1}{2} + |d|n}\Big) y^d. \end{aligned} \]
nodes.statement_short: A doubly twisted theta series in $\mathcal T_{\mathbb C}(qx^2)$ expands in the canonical basis with coefficients that are Laurent series in $y$.
nodes.label: prop:double-twist

nodes.name: Proof of Double twists
nodes.statement: In light of the discussion above and \cref{lem:proofs-by-fourier}, it suffices to identify coefficients of $x^0$ and $x^1$ on both sides. Denoting the left-hand side by $L(z)$, \cref{eq:basic1} gives \[ L(z) = (q; q)^2 \sum_{\substack{n \in \mathbb{Z} \\ m, p \ge 0}} \frac{q^{n^2 + \binom{m}{2} + \binom{p}{2} + (n+1)(m+p)}}{(q; q)_m (q; q)_p} (-y)^{m-p} x^{2n+m+p}. \] Collecting coefficients of $y^d$ in $\widehat{L}(0)$ and $\widehat{L}(1)$ for $d \in \mathbb{Z}$, a short computation yields \[ \widehat{L}(0) = \sum_{d \in \mathbb{Z}, \text{ even}} q^{\frac{d^2 + 2|d|}{4}} S(|d|)\ y^{2d}, \qquad\qquad\qquad \widehat{L}(1) = - \sum_{d \in \mathbb{Z}, \text{ odd}} q^{\frac{\left(|d| + 1\right)^2}{4}} S(|d|)\ y^d, \] where $S(|d|) = (q; q)^2 \sum_{p \ge 0} \frac{q^p}{(q; q)_{p+|d|} (q; q)_p}$. But by \cref{eq:basic2}, $S(|d|)$ is precisely the coefficient of $x^{|d|}$ in $(q; q)^2 (x; q)^{-1} (q/x; q)^{-1}$ (for $|q| < |x| < 1$), which is expanded in \cref{prop:fractional}. Collecting terms in the right-hand side of \cref{eq:inverse} gives $S(|d|) = \sum_{n \ge 0} (-1)^n q^{\binom{n+1}{2} + |d|n}$, as we wanted.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $x^0,x^1$ coefficients by expanding with Euler's formula; the inner sums are coefficients of $(q;q)^2/\langle x;q\rangle$ from the double-product quotient proposition.

nodes.name: Reduce
nodes.statement: In light of the discussion above and \cref{lem:proofs-by-fourier}, it suffices to identify coefficients of $x^0$ and $x^1$ on both sides.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $x^0$, $x^1$ coefficients

nodes.name: Expand L
nodes.statement: Denoting the left-hand side by $L(z)$, \cref{eq:basic1} gives \[ L(z) = (q; q)^2 \sum_{\substack{n \in \mathbb{Z} \\ m, p \ge 0}} \frac{q^{n^2 + \binom{m}{2} + \binom{p}{2} + (n+1)(m+p)}}{(q; q)_m (q; q)_p} (-y)^{m-p} x^{2n+m+p}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Euler expansion of $L$

nodes.name: Collect
nodes.statement: Collecting coefficients of $y^d$ in $\widehat{L}(0)$ and $\widehat{L}(1)$ for $d \in \mathbb{Z}$, a short computation yields \[ \widehat{L}(0) = \sum_{d \in \mathbb{Z}, \text{ even}} q^{\frac{d^2 + 2|d|}{4}} S(|d|)\ y^{2d}, \qquad\qquad\qquad \widehat{L}(1) = - \sum_{d \in \mathbb{Z}, \text{ odd}} q^{\frac{\left(|d| + 1\right)^2}{4}} S(|d|)\ y^d, \] where $S(|d|) = (q; q)^2 \sum_{p \ge 0} \frac{q^p}{(q; q)_{p+|d|} (q; q)_p}$.
nodes.statement_short: Coefficients in terms of $S(|d|)$

nodes.name: Identify S
nodes.statement: But by \cref{eq:basic2}, $S(|d|)$ is precisely the coefficient of $x^{|d|}$ in $(q; q)^2 (x; q)^{-1} (q/x; q)^{-1}$ (for $|q| < |x| < 1$), which is expanded in \cref{prop:fractional}.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $S$ via the double-product quotient

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Collecting terms in the right-hand side of \cref{eq:inverse} gives $S(|d|) = \sum_{n \ge 0} (-1)^n q^{\binom{n+1}{2} + |d|n}$, as we wanted.
nodes.statement_short: Read off $S(|d|)$

nodes.name: Question: applications of double twists to mock theta functions
nodes.statement: Can one use \cref{prop:double-twist} to: \begin{itemize} \item[(i).] Obtain a \cref{prop:mock-theta-sums}-type formula for the sum $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} q^{n^2} (-q; q)_n^{-2}$ (by specialization at $xy = x/y = -1$), and a \cref{prop:mock-theta-individual}-type formula for the third-order mock theta function $f(q) := \sum_{n \ge 0} q^{n^2} (-q; q)_n^{-2}$ (see, e.g., \cite{chen2012partition})? \item[(ii).] Obtain relevant identities for the sum $G(y, q)$ from \cref{eq:generalized-mock-theta}, via its generalization $G(x, y, q)$? \end{itemize}
nodes.label: qtn:double-twist
